-# Appendix: Reference Data & Market Context
-
-## A. MPP Protocol Reference
-
-### What is MPP?
-Machine Payments Protocol, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs (March 2026). An HTTP authentication scheme that standardizes the 402 Payment Required status code.
-
-### Core Flow
-1. Client requests resource -> `GET /endpoint`
-2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)
-3. Client pays (signs blockchain tx, provides card token, etc.)
-4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
-5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header
-
-### Transaction Modes
-- **Charge (one-time):** Immediate settlement per request. Good for discrete API calls
-- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency
-
-### SDKs
-| Language | Package | Install |
-|----------|---------|---------|
-| TypeScript | mppx | npm install mppx |
-| Python | pympp | pip install pympp |
-| Rust | mpp-rs | cargo add mpp |
-
-### Key Resources
-- Protocol overview: mpp.dev/overview
-- Server quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/server
-- Agent quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/agent
-- IETF spec: paymentauth.org
-- Stripe blog: stripe.com/blog/machine-payments-protocol
-
-## B. UK Open Government Licence (OGL v3) Summary
-
-**Permits:** Copy, publish, distribute, transmit, adapt, exploit commercially and non-commercially
-**Requires:** Acknowledge the source, provide link to licence
-**Does NOT require:** Payment, registration, or permission
-
-### OGL-Covered Datasets Used
-- Companies House basic company data
-- Land Registry Price Paid Data
-- Land Registry CCOD/OCOD
-- EPC Register
-- Charity Commission register
-- CQC provider data
-- FHRS food hygiene ratings
-- Ofsted inspection data
-- Census / ONS statistical data
-- The Gazette (insolvency notices)
-- Met Office DataPoint
-- police.uk crime data
-- HMRC trade statistics
-
-### NOT OGL (require separate licensing)
-- Ordnance Survey premium products (AddressBase, MasterMap)
-- Royal Mail PAF (postcode/address data)
-- Land Registry National Polygon Dataset (GBP 4,500+/yr)
-- Individual Land Registry title registers (GBP 3/title, no bulk redistribution)
-
-## C. Competitor Pricing Reference
-
-### UK Company Data
-
-| Provider | Model | Price Point | Enrichment Level |
-|----------|-------|-------------|------------------|
-| Companies House API | Free | 0 (rate-limited) | Raw data only |
-| Endole | Pay-as-you-go | GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Scored, basic network |
-| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | GBP 10K+/yr minimum | Full credit scoring |
-| Beauhurst | Annual subscription | GBP 5K-30K/yr | Growth/innovation signals |
-| OpenCorporates | API subscription | $500+/mo | Cross-jurisdiction, no scoring |
-| DueDil (now Creditsafe) | API credits | GBP 0.50-2.00/check | Compliance/KYB focused |
-
-### Our Proposed Positioning
-- Below Endole on basic lookups (GBP 0.05 vs 0.25)
-- Comparable to Endole on enriched (GBP 0.25)
-- Below DueDil on compliance checks (GBP 1.00 vs 1.50+)
-- Zero friction: no signup, no subscription, no API key
-
-### International Data Products (for comparison)
-
-| Provider | Data Type | Per-Query Price |
-|----------|-----------|-----------------|
-| Clearbit | Company enrichment | $0.05-0.25 |
-| Apollo.io | Contact + company | $0.01-0.05 |
-| BuiltWith | Technology profiles | $0.10-0.50 |
-| SimilarWeb | Traffic data | $0.01-0.10 |
-| Crunchbase | Startup/funding | $0.05-0.20 |
-
-## D. Companies House Data Schema (Key Fields)
-
-### Company Profile
-- company_number (PK)
-- company_name
-- company_status (active, dissolved, liquidation, etc.)
-- company_type (ltd, plc, llp, etc.)
-- date_of_creation
-- date_of_cessation
-- registered_office_address (premises, address_line_1, address_line_2, locality, region, postal_code, country)
-- sic_codes (array of 5-digit codes)
-- accounts.next_due, accounts.last_made_up_to
-- confirmation_statement.next_due, confirmation_statement.last_made_up_to
-- has_charges, has_insolvency_history
-- jurisdiction
-
-### Officer (Director/Secretary)
-- officer_id
-- company_number (FK)
-- name (surname, forename)
-- officer_role (director, secretary, llp-member, etc.)
-- appointed_on, resigned_on
-- date_of_birth (month, year only)
-- nationality
-- country_of_residence
-- occupation
-- address (correspondence address, not residential)
-
-### PSC (Person of Significant Control)
-- psc_id
-- company_number (FK)
-- name or corporate_name
-- natures_of_control (array: ownership-of-shares-25-to-50-percent, voting-rights-75-to-100-percent, etc.)
-- nationality, country_of_residence
-- date_of_birth (month, year)
-- address
-- ceased_on (if no longer a PSC)
-- For corporate PSCs: identification.legal_authority, identification.place_registered, identification.registration_number
-
-### Charges
-- charge_id
-- company_number (FK)
-- status (outstanding, fully-satisfied, part-satisfied)
-- created_on, delivered_on, satisfied_on
-- persons_entitled (lender names)
-- particulars (description of charged property)
-- classification (nature-of-charge, etc.)
-
-## E. Financial Health Score Methodology (Draft)
-
-### Input Variables
-
-**From Accounts (40% weight):**
-- Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (target: > 1.5)
-- Debt to equity = total liabilities / net assets (target: < 2.0)
-- Net assets trend (increasing = positive signal)
-- Revenue growth YoY (where available)
-- Profit margin (where available)
-
-**From Filing Behaviour (25% weight):**
-- Average days late (0 = perfect, >30 = concerning)
-- Percentage of filings late
-- Currently overdue filings count
-- Trend: improving or worsening
-
-**From Charges (15% weight):**
-- Active charges count
-- Recent charge activity (new charges in last 12 months)
-- Charge satisfaction rate
-
-**From Gazette/Insolvency (15% weight):**
-- Winding-up petitions (severe negative signal)
-- Strike-off action (moderate negative)
-- Administrative receiver appointed (severe)
-
-**From Company Age/Status (5% weight):**
-- Companies < 2 years old get a slight penalty (less track record)
-- Dormant companies scored separately
-
-### Score Bands
-- 80-100: Strong financial position
-- 60-79: Adequate, no immediate concerns
-- 40-59: Caution, some risk indicators
-- 20-39: Significant risk, multiple negative signals
-- 0-19: Severe risk, active insolvency indicators
-
-### Known Limitations
-- ~60% of UK companies file micro-entity or abbreviated accounts with minimal financial detail
-- Score for these companies relies heavily on filing behaviour and charges (lower confidence)
-- Financial data can be up to 21 months old at time of filing (9 month filing deadline + 12 month accounting period)
-- Score should always be accompanied by confidence indicator and data freshness
-
-## F. GDPR Compliance Plan
-
-### Personal Data Processed
-- Director/secretary names
-- Director date of birth (month/year only)
-- Director correspondence addresses (not residential)
-- PSC names, nationality, country of residence
-
-### Lawful Basis
-- Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f))
-- Data is published by Companies House under statutory authority
-- Processing serves legitimate business interests (credit checking, due diligence, compliance)
-- Balanced against individual rights: data is already public, we add enrichment not new personal data
-
-### Required Actions
-1. Privacy policy explaining processing activities
-2. Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) documented
-3. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for systematic profiling
-4. Right to object mechanism (suppression list)
-5. Data subject access request (DSAR) process
-6. Respect Companies House residential address suppression
-7. Do not attempt to derive full dates of birth
-8. Consider ICO registration if not already registered
-
-## G. Potential Product Expansion Path
-
-```
-Phase 1 (Months 1-2): Company Intelligence API
-  |
-  v
-Phase 2 (Months 2-4): + Property Intelligence
-  |
-  v
-Phase 3 (Months 4-6): + Planning Pipeline + Trade Intelligence
-  |
-  v
-Phase 4 (Months 6-12): + Climate Risk + Tech/Hiring Signals
-  |
-  v
-Phase 5 (Year 2): + Niche products (Care, Charity, Food, Hyperlocal)
-  |
-  v
-Phase 6 (Year 2+): International expansion (US SEC, EU company registries)
-```

-# MPP Protocol Research
-
-## Overview
-- MPP = Machine Payments Protocol
-- Co-created by Tempo Labs and Stripe, launched March 2026
-- Open protocol for machine-to-machine payments over HTTP
-- Standardizes HTTP 402 Payment Required status code
-- Submitted to IETF as "Payment HTTP Authentication Scheme" (paymentauth.org)
-
-## How It Works
-- Challenge-credential-receipt cycle over HTTP
-- Server returns 402 with WWW-Authenticate: Payment header
-- Client fulfills payment, retries with Authorization: Payment header
-- Server verifies, returns resource + Payment-Receipt header
-- Payment-method agnostic: stablecoins (Tempo), cards (Stripe), Lightning
-
-## Transaction Modes
-- Charge: one-time, immediate settlement per request
-- Session: streaming payment channel, sub-cent costs
-
-## Submission Modes
-- Pull (default): Client signs tx, sends to server. Server broadcasts
-- Push: Client broadcasts tx itself, sends tx hash to server
-
-## SDK Support
-- TypeScript: mppx (npm install mppx)
-- Python: pympp (pip install pympp)
-- Rust: mpp-rs (cargo add mpp)
-- Framework middleware: Hono, Express, Next.js, Elysia, Fetch API
-
-## Agent Discoverability
-- llms.txt file (like robots.txt for AI agents)
-- mpp.dev/services directory listing
-- MCP transport support for JSON-RPC tool calls
-
-## Current Services on MPP
-- Browserbase (headless browsers, pay per session)
-- PostalForm (physical mail, pay per letter)
-- Stripe Climate (carbon contributions)
-- Quick Intel (blockchain data queries)
-- Very few data/intelligence products listed yet
-
-## Hacker News Reception (key points)
-- Per-query pricing for bursty workloads seen as genuinely useful
-- Hard spending caps for agents compelling
-- Skepticism about "protocol" label (it's an HTTP auth scheme)
-- Security concerns: prompt injection could cause misleading purchases
-- Missing B2B primitives: no invoices, refunds, or bills of lading
-- Open question on consumer banking regulation (Regulation E)
-
-## Competing/Adjacent Standards
-- x402 (any blockchain payments)
-- L402 (Bitcoin Lightning)
-- ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol, also from Stripe)

-# UK Open Data Sources Research
-
-## Companies House
-- Free REST API (600 req/5 min), free bulk data (CSV/JSON, daily), streaming API
-- ~5M active companies, officers, PSCs, charges, filing history, iXBRL accounts
-- OGL v3 licence, explicitly allows commercial redistribution
-- Competitors using this data: Endole (GBP 0.25-0.80/report), Creditsafe (enterprise), Beauhurst (GBP 5K+/yr)
-- Key enrichment: financial scoring from iXBRL, director networks, filing risk signals, UBO chains, phoenix detection
-
-## Land Registry
-- Price Paid Data: free bulk CSV, every residential transaction since 1995, OGL
-- CCOD: ~3.5M corporate-owned titles, free, OGL, includes CH company numbers
-- OCOD: ~100K overseas-owned titles, free, OGL
-- Individual title registers: GBP 3/title, NO bulk redistribution allowed
-- National Polygon Dataset: GBP 4,500+/yr, restricted licence
-- Key enrichment: AVM, corporate portfolio mapping, area analytics
-
-## EPC Register
-- Free bulk download, ~20M certificates
-- Energy rating (A-G), floor area, wall type, heating, estimated costs
-- OGL, commercially redistributable
-- Cross-references with property transactions by address matching
-
-## Weather/Climate
-- Met Office DataPoint: free API, OGL, UK forecasts and observations
-- Met Office MIDAS Open: historic observations, free via CEDA archive
-- ERA5/Copernicus: free, global reanalysis 1940-present, hourly, commercial OK
-- NOAA: free, public domain (US government), global datasets
-- Open-Meteo: free for non-commercial, paid for commercial (from ~EUR 15/mo)
-- Key enrichment: location-specific interpolation, climate risk scoring
-
-## Other Valuable Sources (all OGL unless noted)
-- The Gazette: insolvency notices, winding-up petitions (OGL)
-- ICO Register: data controller registrations
-- FCA Register: regulated firms and individuals (API)
-- Charity Commission: ~170K charities, trustees, financials (API + bulk)
-- Ofsted: school/nursery ratings (API + bulk)
-- CQC: ~30K health/social care providers (API + bulk)
-- FHRS: ~500K food business ratings (API)
-- Census 2021: demographics down to output area (~300 people)
-- ONS Nomis: labour market data (API)
-- police.uk: crime data by location (API)
-- HMRC Trade: imports/exports by commodity/country
-- Planning applications: per-council, no national aggregation (scraping needed)
-- TfL/BODS: transport data (APIs, OGL)
-
-## Legal Framework
-- OGL v3 covers most UK government data, explicitly permits commercial use
-- GDPR applies to director/PSC personal data, use legitimate interest basis
-- UK database right (sui generis): cannot bulk-extract "substantial part" of someone else's DB
-- Building your own enriched database from primary sources is fine
-- Computer Misuse Act applies to unauthorized access, but public web pages generally OK
-- No specific UK anti-scraping statute

-# Data-as-a-Service Business Models Research
-
-## Successful Companies Built on Public Data
-
-### Company/Business Data
-- Clearbit (acquired by HubSpot ~$150M): email/domain enrichment, $0.05-0.25/record
-- ZoomInfo ($6B+ revenue): contact + company data, enterprise $15K-100K+/yr
-- Apollo.io: aggressive freemium, $0.01-0.05/record, disrupted ZoomInfo pricing
-- OpenCorporates: 200+ registries normalized, API from $500/mo
-
-### UK-Specific
-- Endole: Companies House enrichment, GBP 0.25-0.80/report, pay-as-you-go
-- DueDil (acquired by Creditsafe): compliance/KYB, GBP 0.50-2.00/check
-- Beauhurst: high-growth company intelligence, GBP 5K-30K/yr subscriptions
-- Creditsafe: enterprise credit scoring, hundreds of millions GBP revenue
-
-### Other Verticals
-- BuiltWith: tech stack detection, $295-995/mo, ~$0.10-0.50/lead
-- SimilarWeb (~$200M ARR): web traffic estimation, $125+/mo
-- Crunchbase: startup/funding data, $49/mo to $49K/yr API
-
-## Pricing Models That Work
-
-### Per-Query Pricing Bands
-| Price | Use Case | Examples |
-|-------|----------|---------|
-| $0.001-0.01 | High-volume, low-enrichment | Email validation, basic lookups |
-| $0.01-0.10 | Medium enrichment | Company profiles, basic financials |
-| $0.10-0.50 | Rich enrichment | Full reports, multi-source |
-| $0.50-2.00 | Compliance/regulatory | KYB, AML screening |
-| $2.00-10.00 | Deep investigative | Full director history, risk analysis |
-
-### Credit-Based Systems
-- Most common for data products
-- Psychological benefit: spending "5 credits" vs "$0.50"
-- Variable pricing per endpoint without complex billing
-- Pre-purchase drives upfront revenue
-- Expiry (30-365 days) drives recurring purchases
-
-### Key Pricing Principle
-Price on decision value, not production cost. A GBP 0.50 risk score preventing a GBP 50K bad debt is trivially justified. Same data sold as "public records lookup" only commands GBP 0.05.
-
-## High-Value Enrichment Patterns
-
-1. **Cross-referencing**: Combining 3-5 public datasets creates proprietary insights. Each additional source adds disproportionate value
-2. **Entity resolution**: Linking "J Smith" across companies. Hardest and most valuable enrichment
-3. **Scoring/classification**: Financial health, risk, growth signals. The defensible moat
-4. **Historical tracking**: Change detection, trend analysis. Best as monitoring subscriptions
-5. **NLP extraction**: Structured data from unstructured filings (PDFs, iXBRL). Transforms free PDFs into valuable structured data
-6. **Geocoding/spatial**: Address normalization, proximity analysis, area profiling
-
-## Competitive Moat
-- The data is public, so raw data is not the moat
-- Moat is: enrichment quality + freshness + cross-referencing + API convenience + MPP-native access
-- Network effects possible via monitoring (more customers = better signal on what data to prioritize refreshing)
-
-## Unit Economics Sweet Spot
-- GBP 0.10-1.00 per enriched record for UK company data
-- Below 0.05: hard to sustain unless billions of queries
-- 0.10-0.30: basic enrichment over free Companies House data
-- 0.30-1.00: multi-source enrichment
-- 1.00-5.00: compliance/regulated use cases
-- Above 5.00: needs to be a "report" with significant analysis

-# Data Peers: MCP Registries, Skills Registries & API Data Services
-
-> Research date: 2026-03-22
-> Mode: ultradeep
-> Sources: 40+
-
----
-
-## Executive Summary
-
-The landscape of how AI agents discover and consume tools, data, and capabilities has crystallized around three complementary layers in 2026: **MCP registries** (protocol-level tool discovery), **skills registries** (procedural knowledge distribution), and **API data services** (structured data delivery). MCP, originally introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, has become the de facto standard for agent-tool connectivity, now governed by the Linux Foundation with adoption from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. The ecosystem has grown explosively from ~100 servers at launch to nearly 19,000 listed on community directories. Meanwhile, the Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io) has emerged as the cross-platform format for distributing procedural knowledge, with 89,000+ skills tracked on skills.sh. API data services are rapidly evolving from traditional developer tools into AI-native infrastructure, with MCP servers and structured schemas becoming key differentiators.
-
----
-
-## 1. MCP Registries
-
-### 1.1 The Official MCP Registry
-
-**URL:** https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io
-**Operator:** MCP project (Linux Foundation, community-driven)
-**Launched:** September 8, 2025 (preview)
-**API Version:** v0.1 (frozen October 2025, no breaking changes)
-
-The canonical upstream registry for publicly available MCP servers. It is intentionally minimal, providing a REST API and basic search but no polished browsing UI. Third-party registries (Smithery, Glama, MCP.so) layer discovery UX on top of it.
-
-**Technical Details:**
-- **API Base:** `https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/`
-- **Key Endpoints:**
-  - `GET /v0/servers` - List/search servers (supports `search`, `limit` max 100, `cursor`, `offset`)
-  - `GET /v0/servers/{name}/versions/{version}` - Single server detail
-  - `GET /v0/version` - Registry version
-- **Data Model:** Each server entry contains name (GitHub-style namespace like `io.github.owner/repo`), description, version, repository URL, packages (npm/pypi/docker), transport type (stdio/sse/streamable-http), and metadata (status, publish date, latest flag)
-- **Namespace Auth:** Server names follow reverse-DNS tied to verified GitHub accounts. An `mcpName` field in `package.json` must match, preventing impersonation
-- **Publishing:** Via `mcp-publisher` CLI (`brew install mcp-publisher` on macOS), supports `init`, `login github`, `publish` commands
-- **Moderation:** Community members can flag servers for spam/malicious code. Maintainers can denylist entries
-- **Health Checks:** All servers pinged every 5 seconds for liveness
-- **Schema:** JSON Schema 2020-12, versioned at `https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/2025-09-29/server.schema.json`
-- **No auth required for reads** (public GET endpoints)
-
-**Governance:** Community-owned, backed by Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, Microsoft. The registry itself is open-source and supports sub-registries, allowing organizations to create opinionated downstream catalogs.
-
-**2026 Roadmap Items:**
-- **MCP Server Cards:** A `.well-known` URL standard for exposing structured server metadata, enabling discovery by browsers/crawlers/registries without connecting
-- **Stateless transport:** Evolving Streamable HTTP for load-balanced, multi-instance deployments
-- **Governance WG:** Contributor ladder (participant -> contributor -> facilitator -> lead -> core maintainer), delegation model for WGs, quarterly charter reviews
-
-[Source: registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, Nordic APIs, MCP Blog]
-
----
-
-### 1.2 MCP.so
-
-**URL:** https://mcp.so
-**Operator:** Third-party community
-**Server Count:** ~18,871 (as of March 2026)
-
-The largest community-driven MCP directory. Tracks explosive growth from ~100 servers at MCP's November 2024 launch to nearly 19,000. Features include a call-volume leaderboard, filters (Featured, Latest, Official, Hosted), and tag/category browsing. Submission is via GitHub issues.
-
-[Source: mcp.so, Nordic APIs]
-
----
-
-### 1.3 Glama.ai
-
-**URL:** https://glama.ai/mcp/servers
-**Operator:** Glama
-**Server Count:** ~9,000+ production-ready
-
-Takes an editorial stance, filtering out duplicates, demos, and low-quality entries. Uses Firecracker VM isolation for enterprise-grade security. Provides AI chat for discovery and extensive category/status filters. Also hosts and runs MCP servers for users (not just metadata).
-
-[Source: Composio comparison, Nordic APIs, Glama blog]
-
----
-
-### 1.4 Smithery
-
-**URL:** https://smithery.ai
-**Operator:** Third-party
-**Server Count:** 2,800+ verified
-
-Positioned as the "Docker Hub for MCP." Cloud platform for deploying MCP agents with CLI and Docker options. Free tier for basic hosting, paid plans for more tools and security. Best for experimentation, discovery, and prototyping, not enterprise-grade gateway use.
-
-[Source: Composio comparison]
-
----
-
-### 1.5 OpenTools Registry
-
-**URL:** https://opentools.com/registry
-**Operator:** OpenTools
-**Tagline:** "One API to use any LLM with every MCP tool"
-
-A unified API layer for LLM tool use. OpenAI SDK-compatible API (`api.opentools.com` as base URL) that lets developers pass MCP tools directly in the `tools` parameter when calling any supported LLM. Task-centric discovery curated to exclude duplicates and abandoned projects. Authentication via Clerk.
-
-**API Example:**
-```python
-from openai import OpenAI
-client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.opentools.com", api_key="<KEY>")
-completion = client.chat.completions.create(
-    model="anthropic/claude-3.7-sonnet",
-    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Compare top 5 EVs"}],
-    tools=[{"type": "mcp", "ref": "firecrawl"}]
-)
-```
-
-[Source: opentools.com, Nordic APIs]
-
----
-
-### 1.6 GitHub MCP Registry
-
-**URL:** https://github.com/mcp
-**Operator:** GitHub/MCP community
-
-Showcases reference servers and community contributions. Hosts servers for NuGet, Azure services, Azure DevOps, Stripe, Elasticsearch, and Microsoft documentation. Visibility influenced by stars, forks, and repo activity.
-
-[Source: GitHub, Nordic APIs]
-
----
-
-### 1.7 Composio
-
-**URL:** https://composio.dev
-**Operator:** Composio
-**Integrations:** 500+ pre-built (Slack, GitHub, Notion, Stripe, etc.)
-
-An agentic integration platform providing a single unified MCP Gateway endpoint. Key differentiator: provides **working integrations** with managed auth (full OAuth, RBAC, PII redaction), not just discovery. Enterprise-grade with OpenTelemetry observability, rate limiting, and governance. Works with Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and any MCP-compatible client.
-
-[Source: Composio blog, comparison pages]
-
----
-
-### 1.8 guMCP (Gumloop)
-
-**URL:** https://gumloop.com/mcp
-**Operator:** Gumloop
-**License:** GPL-3.0
-
-Free, open-source hosted MCP servers. Aims to build the largest MCP server collection with a unified backend. Dual transport (stdio + SSE). SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, HIPAA compliant. No monetization intent ("Use it, have fun"). New servers added almost daily.
-
-[Source: Gumloop blog, GitHub]
-
----
-
-### 1.9 MCP-Get
-
-**URL:** https://mcp-get.com
-**Operator:** Third-party
-
-Functions as both registry and monitoring service. Real-time server status/activity monitoring with uptime insights. Useful for developers who need operational reliability data on servers they depend on.
-
-[Source: Nordic APIs]
-
----
-
-### 1.10 Mastra MCP Registry Registry
-
-**URL:** https://mastra.ai/mcp-registry-registry
-**Operator:** Mastra
-
-A meta-registry that catalogs other registries rather than servers directly. "Registry of registries" providing a cross-ecosystem view. Also available as an MCP server (`@mastra/mcp-registry-registry`) for programmatic querying.
-
-[Source: Mastra blog, Nordic APIs]
-
----
-
-### Registry Comparison Table
-
-| Registry | Server Count | Type | Best For | Auth/Security |
-|----------|-------------|------|----------|---------------|
-| **Official MCP** | Unknown (canonical) | Metadata catalog | Upstream truth, API consumption | Namespace auth via GitHub |
-| **MCP.so** | ~18,871 | Community directory | Broadest discovery | Community moderation |

-## 5. Key Trends & Analysis
-
-### 5.1 The Three-Layer Architecture
-
-The 2026 agent infrastructure has settled into three complementary layers:
-
-1. **Protocol Layer (MCP):** How agents connect to tools and data. Standardized transport, authentication, discovery. The "USB-C for AI."
-2. **Knowledge Layer (Skills):** How agents learn procedures. Progressive disclosure, cross-platform SKILL.md format. Behavioral instructions in natural language.
-3. **Data Layer (API Services):** Where agents get real-world information. Traditional API marketplaces evolving into MCP-native, RAG-pipeline-ready, agent-friendly infrastructure.
-
-### 5.2 Convergence Signals
-
-- **Skills Over MCP Interest Group** is exploring skill distribution through MCP primitives
-- MCP adopted **progressive discovery** in January 2026, narrowing the original context-efficiency advantage of Skills
-- OpenAI deprecated Assistants API in favor of MCP (sunset mid-2026)
-- API providers building native MCP servers (Alpha Vantage, Apify, Pipedream, Zapier)
-
-### 5.3 Market Fragmentation
-
-The MCP registry space is notably fragmented: 7+ registries cataloging overlapping sets of servers, with no single authoritative count. The official registry is intentionally minimal, leaving room for opinionated downstream catalogs. Mastra's "registry of registries" is a direct response to this fragmentation.
-
-### 5.4 Context Window Economics
-
-Every MCP server loads tool definitions at session startup. Token costs were a hidden tax (66,000+ tokens before any conversation), but on-demand tool discovery (default since January 2026) reduced startup cost by ~95%. Agents can realistically connect to only 2-3 MCP servers before accuracy drops, pushing the ecosystem toward progressive disclosure patterns.
-
-### 5.5 Enterprise vs. Community
-
-| Dimension | Community | Enterprise |
-|-----------|-----------|------------|
-| Discovery | MCP.so, Glama, Smithery | Official registry + sub-registries |
-| Hosting | Self-hosted, guMCP (free) | Composio, Azure API Center |
-| Auth | Basic/none | OAuth, RBAC, PII redaction |
-| Compliance | Community moderation | SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA |
-| Skills | skills.sh open ecosystem | Private skills in `.claude/skills/` |

-## 6. Architectural Implications
-
-### For Building a Data/Tool Registry:
-- The official MCP registry API is public, versioned (v0), and supports cursor-based pagination, keyword search, and namespace authentication
-- Sub-registries can ingest from the official upstream and augment with custom metadata
-- Server Cards (`.well-known`) will enable passive discovery without connecting
-- The SKILL.md format is lightweight (YAML frontmatter + markdown) and already cross-platform

-### For Consuming Data Services:

-- Apify is the leading web data extraction layer with dynamic tool discovery
-- Unified.to is purpose-built for real-time B2B data into RAG pipelines
-
-### For the Skills Ecosystem:
-- 89,000+ skills on skills.sh, installed via `npx skills add`
-- Cross-platform by design (19+ supported agents)
-- Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat
-- The Skills Over MCP IG may merge skills into the MCP protocol itself

-# Research Report: Niche Data Businesses You Could Build, Inspired by YC W26 Patterns
-
-## Executive Summary
-
-- **The Agent Economy Needs Data Infrastructure:** 56 of 198 YC W26 companies are building AI agents, yet most lack access to domain-specific, high-quality data. The picks-and-shovels opportunity is in supplying the data layer these agents consume, not building agents themselves [1][2].

-- **The AI Training Dataset Market Is Exploding:** Valued at $3.59B in 2025, projected to reach $23.18B by 2034 (22.9% CAGR). Synthetic data generation alone grew 36% in adoption and is on track for $3.4B by 2030 [4][5].
-- **Agent Memory and Context Infrastructure Is the New Database Layer:** Startups like Mem0 ($24M Series A), Letta, and Zep are building the memory/knowledge graph layer agents need. This is foundational infrastructure with massive TAM [6].
-- **Underserved Verticals Present the Highest-Margin Opportunities:** Healthcare ($164B AI market by 2030), legal ($32.5B legal tech by 2026), construction ($2.1T industry with analog workflows), and supply chain ($50B AI market by 2031) all have massive data gaps that solo founders or small teams can exploit [7][8][9][10].
-
-**Primary Recommendation:** Build a niche data business that curates, structures, or generates domain-specific datasets for one underserved vertical, then compound your data moat through a flywheel of agent usage and feedback.

-## Introduction
-
-### Research Question
-What niche data businesses could you build, informed by the patterns visible in YC's W26 batch, where 85% of companies are AI-first, a third are building agents, and the dominant playbook is "vertical AI coding agent for [industry]"?
-
-This question matters because the article reveals a structural shift: the copilot era lasted 18 months, and we are now in the replacement era. Every $50K-$150K/yr knowledge worker role is getting an AI agent pointed at it. But agents need data to function, and most industries lack the structured, high-quality, domain-specific datasets these agents require. The infrastructure layer beneath the agent wave is where durable, defensible businesses can be built.
-
-### Scope & Methodology
-This research investigated niche data business opportunities across 12 dimensions: AI training datasets, synthetic data generation, data-as-a-service, agent memory/context infrastructure, domain-specific datasets, data labeling/annotation, compliance data, geospatial data, real-time data feeds, agent payment/exchange protocols, web scraping/collection, and data moat strategies. The analysis focused on identifying gaps where data businesses could serve the emerging agent economy described in the YC W26 batch.
-
-Research was conducted using 15 parallel web searches across industry reports, VC analyses, market research firms (Grand View Research, Precedence Research, Mordor Intelligence), tech publications (TechCrunch, VentureBeat), and startup databases (Crunchbase, Tracxn, SeedTable). Over 40 unique sources were consulted, covering the period from 2024 through March 2026, with emphasis on 2025-2026 data.
-
-### Key Assumptions
-- The agent economy trend visible in YC W26 represents a durable structural shift, not a temporary hype cycle
-- Data businesses can be built by solo founders or small teams, given current AI tooling
-- The shift from general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific models will accelerate demand for curated vertical datasets
-- Compliance and regulatory requirements will tighten, increasing the value of clean, governed data
-- The reader is evaluating business ideas they could personally build, favoring capital-efficient approaches

-## Main Analysis
-
-### Finding 1: Agent Memory and Context Infrastructure Is the Most Underbuilt Layer
-
-The entire YC W26 batch is building agents, but agents are stateless by default. Traditional LLMs start each interaction without context or memory. This creates a massive infrastructure gap: autonomy without memory does not scale [6].
-
-Three startups currently dominate this nascent space. Mem0 raised a $24M Series A in October 2025 and was selected as AWS's exclusive memory provider. It uses a hybrid datastore combining vector, key-value, and graph stores. Letta (formerly MemGPT) implements an OS-inspired memory hierarchy with "sleep-time compute," where background agents reorganize memory during idle periods. Zep (Graphiti) stores memory as a temporal knowledge graph that tracks how facts change over time [6].
-
-The broader context layer is evolving rapidly. IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent in March 2026 specifically to make "real-time data the engine of enterprise AI and agents" [11]. Nimble raised $47M in February 2026 to give AI agents access to real-time web data, with their CEO noting that "trusted live web data is increasingly becoming a prerequisite for AI agents performing critical business decisions" [11].
-
-Gartner recently classified Knowledge Graphs as a "Critical Enabler" with immediate impact on generative AI, and the convergence of GraphRAG (retrieval-augmented generation powered by knowledge graphs) with agent architectures is creating what practitioners call an "AI-ready knowledge fabric" [6].
-
-The niche data business opportunity here is not building another Mem0, but rather building the domain-specific memory and context layers that vertical agents need. A construction agent needs memory structured around projects, permits, schedules, and subcontractors. A legal agent needs memory structured around cases, precedents, statutes, and deadlines. These vertical memory schemas are intensely domain-specific and represent defensible data businesses that horizontal memory platforms will not build.
-
-**Sources:** [6], [11]
-
----
-
-### Finding 2: Domain-Specific Training Datasets Are the New Gold
-
-The AI training dataset market was valued at $3.59B in 2025 and is projected to reach $23.18B by 2034, with a 22.9% CAGR [4]. But the real story is the shift from volume to specificity. As foundation model capabilities commoditize, a16z's January 2025 report explicitly identifies proprietary data models as the foundation of durable AI moats [3].
-
-The rise of Small Language Models (SLMs) is accelerating this shift dramatically. Niche industries are moving toward SLMs with fewer than 30B parameters, which require hyper-specific, curated datasets rather than general internet crawls [12]. Domain-specific models like Diabetica-7B (for diabetes) and PatentBERT (for IP research) demonstrate that focused datasets produce superior performance within their domains [12].
-
-The business model is straightforward: curate, clean, and structure datasets for underserved verticals, then sell them as fine-tuning packages or API-accessible data products. The top 8 players in the training dataset market hold only 43% market share, indicating significant room for specialized entrants [4]. Scale AI's revenue climbed to $870M in 2024 and is tracking $2B in 2025, while Meta invested $15B for a 49% stake in the company at a $29B+ valuation, confirming that proprietary training data is an irreplaceable AI asset [13].
-
-The highest-margin opportunity is in regulated verticals where data is scarce, hard to access, and requires domain expertise to structure. Healthcare AI datasets alone are expected to surpass $2.5B by 2026 [13]. Automotive OEMs processing more than 3 million labels per month for Level 4 autonomy represent another concentrated demand pool [13].
-
-**Sources:** [3], [4], [12], [13]
-

-
-### Finding 3: Synthetic Data for Regulated Industries Is a $3.4B Opportunity
-
-The synthetic data generation market was estimated at $576M in 2024 and is projected to reach $3.4B by 2030, growing at a 34.43% CAGR, one of the fastest-growing segments in AI infrastructure [5]. NVIDIA's acquisition of Gretel in March 2025 validated the strategic importance of this category [5].
-
-The opportunity is sharpest in regulated industries where real data is expensive, legally constrained, or ethically problematic to collect. In healthcare, MDClone partners with hospitals to generate synthetic health data, Syntegra builds synthetic data engines purpose-built for healthcare, and Octopize MD provides synthetic medical data for research [5]. In finance, Synthera AI generates realistic yield curves, stock prices, and FX rates [5]. In automotive, Waymo supplements millions of miles of real driving with billions of miles of simulated scenarios [5].
-
-The regulatory tailwind is powerful: 72% of enterprises report data privacy constraints limiting access to production datasets, which is increasing demand for synthetic data by 40% in pilot deployments [5]. GDPR, CCPA, and the 2026 EU AI Act are all pushing organizations toward synthetic alternatives.
-
-For a solo founder or small team, the play is building a synthetic data generation service for one specific vertical. Healthcare synthetic data is particularly attractive because HIPAA constraints make real data nearly impossible to share, yet AI model development requires massive, diverse datasets. A service that takes a hospital's data schema and generates statistically faithful synthetic records, enabling AI research without exposing patient data, could command premium pricing ($10K-$100K per engagement) with relatively low infrastructure costs.
-
-**Sources:** [5]

-### Finding 4: Compliance Data Automation Is a Growing, Capital-Efficient Niche
-
-The compliance automation market is surging as regulatory complexity compounds. Vanta, Drata, Sprinto, and Delve have built substantial businesses automating SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and ISO 27001 compliance [14]. But the deeper opportunity lies in the compliance data layer itself, not just the automation tooling.
-
-The EU AI Act (2026), evolving GDPR enforcement, DORA for financial services, and BCBS 239 for banking are all creating new categories of compliance data that organizations must collect, structure, and maintain [14]. Regulatory compliance AI can reduce audit cycles by up to 70% and audit prep time by 75-90% [14].
-
-The niche data business opportunity is building compliance data products for specific regulatory frameworks in specific industries. For example: a continuously-updated dataset of AI Act requirements mapped to specific technical implementations. Or a structured database of HIPAA violation precedents, enforcement actions, and remediation patterns. Or a real-time feed of SEC regulatory changes mapped to fintech product categories.
-
-These data products become more valuable over time as regulatory history accumulates, creating a natural data moat. A startup that doesn't have SOC 2 might lose a $100K contract [14], meaning compliance data products have direct, quantifiable ROI for buyers. The global data governance market is projected to grow from $5.38B in 2025 to $18.07B by 2032 [14].

-### Finding 5: Healthcare Data Products Are the Largest Vertical Opportunity
-
-Healthcare was the largest vertical in YC W26 with 22 companies, and the healthcare AI market is projected to reach $164.16B by 2030, growing at 49.1% CAGR [7]. AI-enabled healthcare startups captured 62% of all digital health venture funding in H1 2025, raising an average of $34.4M per round, an 83% premium over non-AI startups [7].
-
-The data opportunities are specific and actionable. Ambient scribes, which auto-generate clinical notes from doctor-patient conversations, became healthcare AI's first breakout category with $600M in revenue in 2025, a 2.4x year-over-year increase [7]. This entire category depends on structured medical transcription data, clinical ontologies, and EHR-compatible output schemas.
-
-Autonomous medical coding platforms like XpertCoding automate over 94% of claims with 99%+ accuracy, but they require continuously updated coding datasets (ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS) enriched with payer-specific rules and denial pattern data [7]. Clinical trial data infrastructure is another gap, where Harbor is building an AI-enabled system of record for clinical trial data to replace legacy electronic data capture systems [7].
-
-The niche data business plays in healthcare include: curated medical terminology datasets for specific specialties, structured payer denial pattern databases for revenue cycle optimization, de-identified clinical outcome datasets for AI training, and EHR integration schema libraries that map AI outputs to Epic/Cerner data models. The key constraint is HIPAA compliance, but this is also the moat. Anyone with healthcare data expertise who can navigate compliance has a significant barrier to entry working in their favor.
-
-**Sources:** [7]

-### Finding 6: Construction and Real Estate Data Remain Structurally Underserved
-
-The construction industry is worth $2.1T in North America alone, yet its data infrastructure remains largely analog and fragmented [15]. PropTech received $16.7B in VC investment in 2025, a 67.9% increase year-over-year, with AI-centered proptech growing at 42% annually [15]. Despite this capital influx, significant gaps persist between AI use cases being piloted and available product options.
-
-Construction errors cost the global industry $1.6T annually [12]. Large companies use digital twins, but SMB contractors rarely have access to such tools. The underserved areas include: scheduling data, procurement data, labor tracking, cost control, site safety records, permit databases, and subcontractor performance data [15].
-
-Bedrock Robotics, valued at $1.75B, was created by former Waymo and Segment executives to automate construction using sensor data [15]. ServiceTitan, which raised ~$625M in its IPO, addresses the $600B+ field service industry [15]. Both validate the market size but leave enormous white space in the data layer.
-
-A niche data business in construction could focus on: a structured database of building permits cross-referenced with contractor performance data, a materials pricing index updated in real-time for specific regions, or a standardized data schema for construction project management that makes AI agent integration possible. The industry's fragmentation is the opportunity, as no single incumbent owns the data layer, and the transition from paper-based to digital workflows creates a one-time window to become the data backbone.

-### Finding 7: Agent Payment and Transaction Data Infrastructure Is Nascent
-
-The YC W26 batch explicitly identified agent economy infrastructure as a category, with companies like Sponge building financial infrastructure for the agent economy [1]. The broader market is moving fast: OpenAI and Stripe launched ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol), Google introduced AP2, and AWS/Coinbase launched x402 for pay-per-use agent transactions [16].
-
-Visa predicts millions of consumers will use AI agents to complete purchases by the 2026 holiday season and is working with 100+ partners [16]. Mastercard joined Google's Universal Commerce Protocol [16]. Stripe and Paradigm are building a Layer 1 blockchain optimized for agent settlement, raising $500M at a $5B valuation [16].
-
-The data business opportunity here is in transaction intelligence for the agent economy. As agents begin transacting autonomously, businesses will need: fraud detection datasets specific to agent behavior patterns (which differ fundamentally from human patterns), pricing intelligence data that agents can consume programmatically, and transaction analytics dashboards that show agent spending patterns versus human patterns. Natural, a fintech startup, raised $9.8M to build payments infrastructure for agentic payments [16].
-
-This is an early-stage opportunity, likely 12-18 months from meaningful revenue, but the upside is large because whichever data businesses establish themselves early will benefit from compounding network effects as agent transaction volume scales.
-
-**Sources:** [1], [16]

-### Finding 8: Legal Data Products Have High Margins and Low Competition
-
-Legal tech is projected to reach $32.54B by 2026, with AI adoption in law firms jumping from 19% in 2023 to 79% in 2024 [17]. Harvey raised $750M in 2025 alone at an $8B valuation, and Ivo achieved a sixfold revenue increase since early 2025 [17].

This requires structured court records data, judicial behavior databases, and case outcome pattern datasets.

-Legal information is "much less structured" than code and "lacks equivalent, battle-tested building blocks" [17]. This structural complexity is exactly what creates a data moat: whoever structures and standardizes legal data first owns the substrate on which legal AI agents operate.
-
-Specific niche data businesses include: a structured database of federal and state court opinions with judicial sentiment analysis, a regulatory change tracker that maps new regulations to specific industry impacts in real-time, a patent landscape intelligence dataset for specific technology domains, and a contract clause library with outcome data showing which clauses correlate with disputes.
-
-Antidote raised $5M in seed funding for AI-powered billing compliance for law firms [17]. Tradespace reported clients cutting legal spend 50% with AI-powered IP management [17]. Both validate that legal data products have direct, measurable ROI.

-### Finding 10: Web Data Collection for AI Training Is Entering a Compliance-First Era
-
-70% of all generative AI models and LLMs are now trained primarily on scraped web data [19]. The AI web scraping market is projected to grow from $886M in 2025 to $4.37B by 2035 [19]. But the legal landscape is tightening: Cloudflare now blocks many AI crawlers by default, publishers are drafting "machine access" policies, and the era of scraping without consequence is ending [19].
-
-This creates a massive opportunity for compliance-first data collection services. Between 2025 and 2030, AI data scraping is evolving from largely unregulated bulk collection to controlled, contract-and-standards-based access [19]. 82% of enterprises now demand real-time data pipelines [19].
-
-The niche play is building a curated, licensed, compliance-verified data collection service for a specific domain. Rather than competing with Bright Data or Zyte on breadth, focus on one vertical: restaurant menu and pricing data for food-tech AI, job posting structured data for HR-tech agents, product specification data for e-commerce agents, or academic paper metadata and citation graphs for research AI.
-
-The market is bifurcating between low-cost semi-legal scraping operations and enterprise-grade providers investing in identity, logging, and consent architecture [19]. The latter commands significantly higher margins and creates defensible relationships with data consumers who cannot afford regulatory risk.

-### Finding 11: Data Labeling for Specialized Domains Commands Premium Pricing

Highly skilled annotators doing in-depth reviews command $50-$100 per task, and AI labs willingly pay [13].

Automotive OEMs process 3M+ labels monthly for autonomous driving [13]. 3D/point-cloud annotation workflows are growing at 22.45% CAGR, the fastest among data types [13].
-
-The solo founder opportunity is building a boutique labeling service for one specialized domain: medical imaging annotation for a specific condition (dermatology, radiology subspecialty), financial document annotation for fraud detection models, or robotics manipulation data labeling for specific industrial tasks. The expertise requirement is the moat.

-## Synthesis & Insights
-
-### Patterns Identified
-
-**Pattern 1: The Data Layer Beneath Every Agent Category**
-Every YC W26 agent company, whether in healthcare, legal, finance, or construction, has an implicit data dependency that most have not solved. The AI sales rep needs prospect data. The AI SRE needs incident pattern data. The AI accountant needs chart-of-accounts schemas and payer rules. Each vertical agent category creates a corresponding vertical data business opportunity. The pattern is consistent: agent companies focus on workflow and UX, leaving the data layer as an externality they would prefer to buy rather than build.
-
-**Pattern 2: Compliance as Moat Accelerator**
-In every vertical examined, regulatory complexity increases the value of structured data. HIPAA makes healthcare data scarce. GDPR makes European consumer data expensive. The EU AI Act creates new documentation requirements. SOC 2 gates enterprise sales. Rather than viewing compliance as a cost, the most defensible data businesses treat it as the barrier that prevents commodity competitors from entering. The harder it is to collect, structure, and govern data in a given domain, the more valuable a clean data product becomes.
-
-**Pattern 3: The Flywheel from Data Product to Data Moat**
-The strongest data businesses are those where product usage generates more data, which improves the product, which attracts more users. A labeling service that also trains models on labeled data gets better at pre-labeling, reducing costs and improving quality. A legal dataset that tracks which predictions were accurate improves its prediction accuracy. A synthetic data generator that gets feedback on model performance generates more realistic synthetics. This flywheel dynamic, visible in companies from Abridge to Scale AI, is the key to building durable competitive advantage.
-
-### Novel Insights
-
-**Insight 1: The "Agent Schema" Business**
-No single source explicitly described this, but the convergence of agent memory infrastructure (Finding 1), domain-specific datasets (Finding 2), and underserved verticals (Findings 5-8) points to a new category: the "agent schema" business. This is a company that defines and maintains the canonical data structures an AI agent needs to operate in a specific industry. For construction, this means the schema for projects, permits, materials, labor, and inspections. For healthcare, the schema for encounters, diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes. The company that owns the schema owns the interoperability layer, similar to how HL7/FHIR became the backbone of health data exchange.
-
-**Insight 2: Data Businesses Have Higher Capital Efficiency Than Agent Businesses**
-The YC W26 batch is dominated by agent companies that will compete fiercely on UX, model capability, and go-to-market speed. Data businesses, by contrast, face less direct competition and require less capital to start. A curated dataset can be built by one person with domain expertise. A synthetic data service needs one engineer and one domain expert. A labeling service needs a network of vetted annotators. These are $0-$50K to launch versus $500K-$5M for an agent company. Yet data businesses can achieve similar or higher margins because data is resold repeatedly with near-zero marginal cost.
-
-### Implications
-
-**For You:**
-The optimal strategy is to pick one vertical from the YC W26 batch, deeply understand its data gaps, and build a focused data product. Healthcare and legal have the highest margins due to regulatory barriers. Construction and supply chain have the lowest competition. Agent infrastructure (memory, context, evaluation) has the highest upside but requires more technical depth. The choice depends on your domain expertise and appetite for regulatory complexity.
-
-**Broader Implications:**
-The agent economy will create a parallel "data economy" worth tens of billions within 5 years. The companies that build the data substrate for agents will be as foundational as AWS was for cloud computing. Early movers who establish domain-specific data products now will compound their advantage as agent adoption scales.
-
-**Second-Order Effects:**
-As agents consume more structured data, the value of unstructured data decreases. Data businesses that structure, annotate, and govern data will capture value from data businesses that merely collect and store it. The web scraping era gives way to the data curation era.

-## Limitations & Caveats
-
-### Counterevidence Register
-
-**Contradictory Finding 1: Data Moats May Be Eroding**
-Some analysts argue that increasingly powerful foundation models reduce the need for proprietary data, as models can "learn" domain specifics from smaller fine-tuning sets or even zero-shot [3]. However, the weight of evidence from a16z, venture funding data, and Meta's $15B Scale AI investment suggests data moats are strengthening, not weakening, for domain-specific applications [3][13].
-
-**Contradictory Finding 2: 40% of Agentic AI Deployments May Be Canceled**
-Gartner predicts that 40% of agentic AI deployments will be canceled by 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, or poor risk controls [6]. If agent adoption stalls, the data businesses serving agents would face reduced demand. This risk is mitigated by the breadth of agent adoption (168 of 198 YC W26 companies are AI-first) and by the fact that data products can serve both agent and human consumers.
-
-### Known Gaps
-- Revenue data for domain-specific data businesses is scarce, as most are private and early-stage
-- The research focused primarily on US/English-language markets, potentially underweighting opportunities in Asia-Pacific and Europe
-- Long-term defensibility of specific data moats remains theoretical until proven by multi-year market data
-
-### Areas of Uncertainty
-- How quickly agent-to-agent protocols (ACP, AP2, x402) will achieve meaningful transaction volume
-- Whether AI model capabilities will advance fast enough to reduce the need for domain-specific training data
-- The pace and specifics of regulatory enforcement (EU AI Act, state-level AI laws) that would accelerate compliance data demand
-

-## Recommendations
-
-### Immediate Actions
-
-1. **Pick One Vertical and Map Its Data Gaps**
-   - What: Choose one industry from the YC W26 batch (healthcare, legal, construction, supply chain) and create a comprehensive map of what data agents in that vertical need but cannot easily access
-   - Why: Findings 1-11 all converge on domain specificity as the highest-value strategy
-   - How: Interview 10-20 builders in that vertical, analyze existing data products, identify gaps
-   - Timeline: 2-4 weeks
-
-2. **Build a Minimum Viable Data Product**
-   - What: Create a small, curated dataset or data API that addresses one specific gap identified in step 1
-   - Why: Data businesses can be validated with minimal capital, a $50K dataset that 10 companies would pay $5K for is a $50K business with 100% margins
-   - How: Combine web collection, public records, and domain expertise to structure data that is currently unstructured or scattered
-   - Timeline: 4-8 weeks after gap identification
-
-3. **Establish Compliance Foundations Early**
-   - What: If targeting a regulated vertical, set up data governance, privacy policies, and compliance documentation from day one
-   - Why: Compliance is the moat (Finding 4). Starting compliant is 10x easier than retrofitting compliance later
-   - How: Use tools like Comp AI (open source) or Vanta for baseline compliance
-   - Timeline: Concurrent with product development
-
-### Next Steps
-
-1. **Design the Flywheel**
-   - Identify how product usage can generate more data, improving the product
-   - Plan the progression from static dataset to dynamic data service to platform
-
-2. **Test Pricing with Pre-Sales**
-   - Before building the full product, approach 5-10 potential customers with a description and pricing
-   - Validate willingness to pay and optimal price point
-
-3. **Monitor Agent Protocol Adoption**
-   - Track ACP, AP2, and x402 adoption rates for timing on agent payment data opportunities
-   - The transaction intelligence category (Finding 7) has high upside but requires market maturation
-
-### Further Research Needs
-
-1. **Competitive Landscape Mapping for Specific Verticals**
-   - What: For your chosen vertical, map every existing data product, its pricing, and its gaps
-   - Why: The 40+ source overview here identifies opportunity categories but not specific competitive dynamics within each
-
-2. **Data Acquisition Cost Analysis**
-   - What: For your chosen data product, estimate the cost per record of data collection, cleaning, and structuring
-   - Why: Unit economics determine whether the business is viable for a solo founder versus requiring VC funding
-
-3. **Regulatory Deep Dive for Target Vertical**
-   - What: Map specific regulatory requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, industry-specific) that affect data collection, storage, and sale in your chosen vertical
-   - Why: Compliance determines both cost structure and competitive moat depth

-## Appendix: Methodology
-
-### Research Process
-
-This report was generated through an ultradeep research process spanning 8 phases. Phase 1 (SCOPE) defined the research boundaries around niche data businesses derivable from YC W26 patterns. Phase 2 (PLAN) identified 12 search angles covering the full spectrum of data business categories. Phase 3 (RETRIEVE) executed 15 parallel web searches across market research databases, VC analyses, startup databases, and tech publications, yielding 40+ unique sources.
-
-Phase 4 (TRIANGULATE) cross-verified market size claims across multiple research firms (Grand View Research, Precedence Research, Mordor Intelligence, Fortune Business Insights) and validated startup funding data against primary sources (TechCrunch, Crunchbase). Phase 5 (SYNTHESIZE) identified 3 cross-cutting patterns and 2 novel insights not explicitly stated in any single source. Phases 6-7 (CRITIQUE/REFINE) stress-tested each business idea against counterevidence and market reality. Phase 8 (PACKAGE) assembled this report.
-
-### Sources Consulted
-
-**Total Sources:** 41
-
-**Source Types:**
-- Market research reports: 12
-- VC/investor analyses: 8
-- Tech news articles: 9
-- Industry publications: 7
-- Startup databases: 5
-
-**Geographic Coverage:** Primarily US-focused, with European and Asia-Pacific market data where available.
-
-**Temporal Coverage:** 2024-March 2026, with emphasis on 2025-2026 data.
-
-### Verification Approach
-
-**Triangulation:** Market size claims were verified across 2-3 independent research firms where possible. Startup funding amounts were cross-referenced against primary announcements. Trend claims were validated against multiple independent sources.
-
-**Credibility Assessment:** Sources were weighted by methodology rigor, recency, and author expertise. Market research firms received higher weight for quantitative claims. VC analyses received higher weight for strategic insights. Average credibility score: 72/100.
-
-**Quality Control:** All citations were verified against source material. Market projections from different research firms were noted where they diverge significantly. Speculative claims are labeled as such.

-# Intent-Centric Data Environments: A Novel Architecture for Agent Data Markets
-
-> Research date: 2026-03-23
-> Sources: Paradigm (intents), Anoma (intent machines), envrunai (environments), DataFetch (product context)
-> Category: architectural synthesis / R&D exploration
-
----
-
-## Executive Summary
-
-This document synthesizes three paradigms into a novel architecture for how AI agents should consume data services:
-
-1. **Intent-based architecture** (from crypto/Paradigm/Anoma): Users declare *what* they want, solvers figure out *how*
-2. **Governed execution environments** (from envrunai/env.run): Software as typed, branchable, governable codebases that agents navigate by writing code
-3. **Agent-native data APIs** (from DataFetch): Per-query paid data enrichment for autonomous agents
-
-The synthesis: **A data API that presents itself as a typed TypeScript environment where the agent's "query" is executable code composed against intent-shaped interfaces, with branching for cheap exploration against mock data before committing to paid execution against real data.**
-
-This is not a query language. It is not an API. It is a *data environment* that agents inhabit, explore, and execute within.
-
----
-
-## Part 1: What We Learn From Each Paradigm
-
-### 1.1 Intent Architecture (Paradigm / Anoma)
-
-**Core paper**: [Intent-Based Architectures and Their Risks](https://www.paradigm.xyz/2023/06/intents) (Paradigm, June 2023)
-
-**Key insight**: A transaction is imperative ("do A then B, pay C, get X"). An intent is declarative ("I want X, I'll pay up to C"). The system finds the path.
-
-**Formal definition**: "A signed set of declarative constraints which allow a user to outsource transaction creation to a third party without relinquishing full control."
-
-**Architecture layers**:
-- **User layer**: Express desired outcome + constraints
-- **Propagation layer**: Intents are broadcast to a network of potential executors
-- **Solver layer**: Third parties find satisfying computational paths, potentially netting multiple intents together
-- **Settlement layer**: Verified execution, final state change
-
-**What transfers to data**:
-
-| Crypto Intent Concept | Data Environment Analog |
-|----------------------|------------------------|
-| Intent (declarative constraint) | Agent's TypeScript program describing desired data derivative |
-| Solver (finds execution path) | DataFetch's server-side query planner + enrichment engine |
-| Settlement (verified execution) | Provenance receipt proving computation over identified datasets |
-| Counterparty discovery | Agent discovering data sources via llms.txt / environment manifest |
-| Batch execution (multiple intents → one tx) | Multiple data requirements resolved in a single computation pass |
-| Order netting (overlapping intents matched) | Shared intermediate computations cached across agent requests |
-
-**Critical Paradigm warning that applies here**: "The worst-case outcome is a world in which using an intent-based application entails signing an intent that disappears and then somehow materialises as a transaction with no clarity on how or by whom it was created." The provenance receipt is the answer to this in the data context. The agent must be able to verify *what data was used*, *what computation was performed*, and *what the freshness guarantees are*.
-
-### 1.2 Anoma's Intent Machine
-
-**Key technical elements**:
-
-- **Intent Machine** replaces the Virtual Machine. Instead of executing instructions, it matches and satisfies declarative constraints.
-- **Typhon** (consensus/network): Gossips intents, orders transactions, handles settlement
-- **Taiga** (privacy/execution): Executes state transitions with zero-knowledge proofs, handles information flow control
-- **Solvers**: Specialized nodes that match compatible intents. Can net overlapping requirements. Charge fees for resolution.
-- **Information flow control**: Three intent types, transparent (everyone sees everything), shielded (who is hidden, what is visible), private (both hidden). Users choose per-intent.
-- **Heterogeneous trust**: Different parties can have different security preferences and still achieve atomic settlement.
-
-**What transfers to data**:
-
-The information flow control model maps directly to data access tiers:
-- **Transparent**: Public data queries (Companies House, Land Registry), the agent sees the data and the computation
-- **Shielded**: The agent gets results but the underlying data source is abstracted (third-party proprietary data contributed to the enrichment, agent doesn't see which provider)
-- **Private**: Both the query and the result are private (enterprise use case, compliance-sensitive queries)
-
-The solver model maps to DataFetch's enrichment engine: the agent doesn't specify *which* data sources to query or *how* to join them. It describes the desired output shape. DataFetch's solver determines the optimal data path.
-
-### 1.3 Governed Execution Environments (envrunai)
-
-**Core thesis**: Code agents are better at navigating filesystems and writing code than at calling structured APIs. The right interface for an agent to consume a service is something that looks and feels like a codebase.
-
-**Key mechanisms**:
-
-- **Typed TypeScript interfaces**: Not the execution language, but the *interface description language*. Agents read `.ts` module files to understand what the service can do, then write code against those types.
-- **Mock data / service emulation**: Agents prototype against synthetic data with identical schemas but randomized values. Cheap exploration before committing to real execution.
-- **Branching**: Git-like branching of state. Agent creates exploration branches, tests approaches in parallel, commits the winning trajectory. Branches are cheap (copy-on-write).
-- **Governance / invariants**: Hard constraints (deterministic, fail-closed), soft verifiers (advisory signals), relative ranking (multi-candidate comparison). The environment tells the agent what it *can't* do, not what it *should* do.
-- **Convergence thesis**: LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time. The LLM is the expensive bootstrap; the code it produces is the durable output.
-- **Code mode advantages**: 99%+ context pruning vs tool-call-per-step. The agent chains calls together, surfaces only high-signal decision points for model judgment.
-
-**What transfers to data**:
-
-This is the execution model. The agent doesn't call endpoints. It writes TypeScript against typed data interfaces, branches to explore query strategies cheaply, and commits to the approach that produces the desired derivative.
-

-## Part 2: The Synthesis, Intent-Centric Data Environments
-
-### 2.1 The Core Idea
-
-DataFetch's data is not exposed as REST endpoints, SQL schemas, or GraphQL types. It is exposed as **a typed TypeScript environment** that agents clone, explore, and execute within.
-
-The interfaces are not one-to-one mirrors of the underlying data. They are **intent-shaped**: they represent the *kinds of questions agents want to answer*, not the *tables that store the data*.
-
-```
-Traditional API:         GET /companies?sic_code=6201&incorporated_after=2023-01-01
-SQL:                     SELECT * FROM companies WHERE sic_code = '6201' AND ...
-Intent-centric env:      const targets = await market.findCompetitors({ sector: "data-enrichment", backed_by: "Y Combinator", vintage: { from: 2023 } });
-```
-
-The difference is not syntactic. The agent doesn't need to know that "data enrichment" maps to SIC codes 6201, 6202, 6311, or that "backed by Y Combinator" requires joining a Crunchbase-derived investor table. The intent interface absorbs that complexity. The DataFetch solver resolves it.
-
-### 2.2 How It Works End-to-End
-
-```
-┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
-│                        AGENT CONTEXT                             │
-│                                                                  │
-│  1. Agent clones DataFetch environment (typed .ts modules)       │
-│  2. Reads interfaces: market.ts, company.ts, property.ts, ...   │
-│  3. Branches to explore query strategies against MOCK DATA       │
-│  4. Writes TypeScript composing interfaces toward desired output │
-│  5. Tests against mock data (free/cheap, fast)                   │
-│  6. Commits winning approach                                     │
-│  7. Submits for REAL EXECUTION (paid via MPP)                    │
-│                                                                  │
-└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
-                               │
-                               │  Intent (TypeScript program + MPP payment)
-                               ▼
-┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
-│                    DATAFETCH SOLVER                               │
-│                                                                  │
-│  1. Receives TypeScript intent                                   │
-│  2. Validates against governance (invariants, rate limits)       │
-│  3. Plans execution: which data sources, join strategy, caching  │
-│  4. Executes computation server-side                             │
-│  5. Generates provenance receipt                                 │
-│  6. Returns derivative data + receipt                            │
-│                                                                  │
-│  Internal resolution (invisible to agent):                       │
-│  - Companies House bulk data (2026-03-22 snapshot)               │
-│  - Crunchbase YC batch cross-reference                           │
-│  - LinkedIn headcount signals                                    │
-│  - Geocoding + postcode-to-city resolution                       │
-│  - Entity resolution across sources                              │
-│                                                                  │
-└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
-                               │
-                               │  Derivative data + provenance receipt
-                               ▼
-┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
-│                        AGENT CONTEXT                             │
-│                                                                  │
-│  Receives compact result:                                        │
-│  - 47 companies matching intent                                  │
-│  - Headcount + London presence for each                          │
-│  - Provenance: sources, versions, filters applied, query hash    │
-│  - Drill-down endpoints for any row (paid, on-demand)            │
-│                                                                  │
-│  Agent stays focused on its actual task (due diligence report,   │
-│  investment memo, competitive analysis) — never held 10K rows    │
-│  in context                                                      │
-│                                                                  │
-└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
-```
-
-### 2.3 The Interface Layer: Intent-Shaped Types
-
-The key design decision: interfaces represent **analytical intents**, not data schemas.
-
-**Bad (schema-mirror)**:
-```typescript
-// This is just a typed API. The agent still needs domain knowledge
-// to compose meaningful queries.
-interface CompaniesTable {
-  getById(number: string): Company;
-  search(query: { name?: string; sic?: string[]; postcode?: string }): Company[];
-  getOfficers(companyNumber: string): Officer[];
-}
-```
-
-**Good (intent-shaped)**:
-```typescript
-// modules/market.ts
-// These interfaces encode domain intelligence.
-// The agent describes WHAT it wants to know.
-
-export interface MarketIntelligence {
-  /** Find companies competing in a market segment */
-  findCompetitors(criteria: {
-    sector: string | string[];        // Natural language or SIC codes
-    backed_by?: string;               // Investor name
-    vintage?: { from?: number; to?: number };
-    status?: 'active' | 'dissolved' | 'all';
-  }): Promise<CompanySet>;
-
-  /** Enrich a set of companies with people intelligence */
-  enrichWithTeam(
-    companies: CompanySet,
-    dimensions: ('headcount' | 'leadership' | 'location_breakdown')[]
-  ): Promise<EnrichedCompanySet>;
-
-  /** Filter by geographic presence */
-  whereTeamIn(
-    companies: EnrichedCompanySet,
-    location: string                   // City, region, or country
-  ): Promise<EnrichedCompanySet>;
-
-  /** Score and rank by a composite metric */
-  rankBy(
-    companies: EnrichedCompanySet,
-    metric: 'growth_rate' | 'financial_health' | 'hiring_velocity' | 'funding_recency'

-// modules/property.ts
-export interface PropertyIntelligence {

-
-  /** Estimate current value based on comparables */

-
-  /** Cross-reference with planning applications */
-  findNearbyDevelopment(
-    properties: PropertySet,
-    radius_km: number
-  ): Promise<DevelopmentContext>;
-}
-
-// modules/risk.ts
-export interface RiskIntelligence {

-  assessRisk(company: Company): Promise<RiskProfile>;
-

-
-The agent's "query" becomes:
-```typescript
-// The agent writes this against mock data first (free),
-// then submits for real execution (paid).
-
-import { market } from './modules/market';
-
-const ycDataEnrichment = await market.findCompetitors({
-  sector: 'data enrichment',
-  backed_by: 'Y Combinator',

-});

-
-### 2.4 The Mock Data / Branching Model
-
-Directly from envrunai's spec, adapted for data:
-
-**Mock data layer**: DataFetch publishes synthetic datasets with identical schemas and realistic distributions but no real values. When an agent clones the environment, it gets these mocks. The agent can:
-
-1. Write and test query logic against mocks (free, instant)
-2. Iterate on the composition of interfaces
-3. Branch to try different approaches in parallel
-4. Compare results across branches (even with mock data, the *shape* and *cardinality* of results reveals whether the query logic is sound)
-
-**Commit to real execution**: When the agent is satisfied with its approach, it submits the TypeScript program for execution against real data. This is the moment MPP payment is triggered. The DataFetch solver executes the program server-side, substituting real data for mocks, and returns the result with provenance.
-
-```
-exploration/approach-1    → mock: 47 results, looks right
-exploration/approach-2    → mock: 2,300 results, too broad
-exploration/approach-3    → mock: 0 results, criteria too narrow
-                              ↓
-Agent commits approach-1 for real execution → £2.50 via MPP
-                              ↓
-Real result: 52 companies + enrichment + provenance receipt
-```
-
-**Why this matters for token economics**: The agent burns minimal tokens during exploration (mock data is small, fast, local). The expensive real execution happens once, after the agent has converged on its approach. This inverts the traditional pattern where the agent calls 15 API endpoints, pulls data into context at each step, reasons about it, calls more endpoints, etc.
-
-### 2.5 Provenance: The Trust Layer
-
-Drawing from Anoma's settlement verification and the Paradigm article's warning about opacity:
-
-Every real execution returns a **provenance receipt**:
-
-```typescript
-interface ProvenanceReceipt {
-  // What was computed
-  query_hash: string;              // SHA-256 of the submitted TypeScript program
-  execution_id: string;            // Unique, referenceable
-
-  // What data was used
-  sources: {
-    name: string;                  // "companies-house-bulk"
-    version: string;               // "2026-03-22"
-    record_count: number;          // How many records were in scope
-    license: string;               // "OGL-v3"
-  }[];
-
-  // What happened
-  filters_applied: string[];       // Human-readable summary of filtering steps
-  joins_performed: string[];       // Which sources were cross-referenced
-  rows_before_filter: number;
-  rows_after_filter: number;
-  computation_duration_ms: number;
-
-  // Reproducibility
-  reproducible_until: string;      // Date until which re-execution would yield same result
-  deterministic: boolean;          // Whether re-execution is guaranteed identical
-
-  // Drill-down
-  drill_down_available: boolean;
-  drill_down_cost: string;        // "£5.00" — cost to retrieve underlying data
-  drill_down_endpoint: string;
-}
-```
-
-This is the "evidence that we're not lying over the conclusion." The agent (or its human principal) can verify:
-- The result came from identified, versioned datasets
-- The filtering and joining logic is auditable
-- The result is reproducible within a time window
-- The underlying data is retrievable at additional cost if needed
-
-### 2.6 Interface Evolution
-
-Intent-shaped interfaces are not static. They evolve as:
-
-1. **DataFetch adds data sources**: New sources enable new intent interfaces. Adding LinkedIn data enables `enrichWithTeam`. Adding planning data enables `findNearbyDevelopment`.
-2. **Agent usage patterns reveal demand**: If agents keep composing `findCompetitors` → `enrichWithTeam` → `whereTeamIn`, DataFetch can offer that as a single optimized intent (`findCompetitorsByTeamLocation`).
-3. **Community contribution**: Like envrunai's permissionless compiled wrappers, third parties could propose new intent interfaces over DataFetch's data, pending governance review.
-
-Versioning follows semver, like envrunai:
-- **Major**: Breaking changes to existing interfaces
-- **Minor**: New interfaces or new optional parameters
-- **Patch**: Bug fixes in resolution logic
-
-Agents pin to version ranges: `"datafetch": "^2.1.0"`.

-## Part 3: Why This Is Different
-
-### 3.1 Comparison to Existing Approaches
-
-| Approach | What the agent does | Token cost | Trust model |
-|----------|-------------------|------------|-------------|
-| **REST API** | Call endpoints one by one, join in context | High (data in context at every step) | Trust the API provider |
-| **GraphQL** | Write a query specifying exact shape | Medium (single request, but agent must know schema) | Trust the API provider |
-| **SQL/analytical query** | Write a precise query in a query language | Medium (must know schema + query language) | Trust the database |
-| **Natural language → API** | Describe in English, middleware translates to API calls | High (middleware is another LLM burning tokens) | Trust two LLMs |
-| **Intent-centric environment** | Write TypeScript against intent-shaped types, branch to explore, commit for execution | Low (mock exploration is free, real execution is one-shot) | Provenance receipt, reproducible |
-
-### 3.2 The Three Advantages
-
-**1. Token efficiency through compute offloading**
-
-The agent's context window never holds intermediate data. It holds intent code (small) and derivative results (small). All the heavy joining, filtering, and enrichment happens server-side. This is not just cheaper, it's *architecturally necessary* as agent workloads scale. An agent doing due diligence across 500 companies cannot hold all that data in context.
-
-**2. Provenance without cryptographic overhead**
-
-PySyft requires SMPC, ZKPs, differential privacy. Anoma requires Taiga's zero-knowledge proofs. DataFetch's data is mostly public (OGL-licensed). The trust problem is not "prove you didn't see my data" but "prove you actually computed this over real data and didn't make it up." A signed provenance receipt with dataset versions, query hash, and reproducibility window is sufficient. No cryptographic ceremony needed.
-
-**3. Exploration before commitment**
-
-The branching model means the agent can try multiple query strategies at near-zero cost (mock data, no MPP charge). This is unique. Every other data API charges you the moment you call it, even if the results aren't what you wanted. The mock-then-commit model aligns cost with value: you only pay when you've confirmed the approach produces what you need.
-
-### 3.3 The Convergence Play
-
-From envrunai's convergence thesis: LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time. Applied to data queries:
-
-1. First time an agent needs "YC SaaS competitors with London teams," it writes the TypeScript intent from scratch, explores with mocks, commits
-2. That trajectory gets saved as a reusable function (envrunai's extensions model)
-3. Next time any agent needs similar intelligence, the trajectory runs deterministically, no LLM reasoning needed
-4. Over time, the most common analytical intents become deterministic workflows, reducing cost toward zero marginal token spend
-
-DataFetch becomes not just a data provider but a **library of proven analytical trajectories** that agents can invoke. The collective intelligence of all agent queries compounds into an asset.
-
