# HuggingFace Hub as DataFetch PoC Domain: R&D Scouting Brief

> Research date: 2026-03-31
> Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api, https://github.com/huggingface/skills
> Category: platform
> Context: Evaluating HF Hub datasets as an alternative PoC domain for DataFetch's
> environment-first interaction model (see kb/product_design.md)

---

## Overview

HuggingFace Hub is the dominant repository for ML models and datasets, hosting 2M+
models and 500K+ datasets. It exposes a comprehensive REST API, a Dataset Viewer API
for row-level access, and client libraries in Python and JS. The question is whether
wrapping HF Hub's dataset discovery and exploration behind DataFetch's typed folder
interfaces would demonstrate the environment-first thesis better than (or alongside)
the UK business data domain.

## The Idea

Instead of UK Companies House data, use HuggingFace Hub datasets as the domain:
- Agent enters a DataFetch environment folder with typed interfaces for dataset
  discovery, exploration, comparison, and download
- Mock data: cached metadata for ~1000 popular datasets (sizes, schemas, tags, stats)
- Intent interfaces: `findDatasets`, `compareSchemas`, `sampleRows`, `assessQuality`
- `explore()` returns dataset metadata, column statistics, sample rows (free)
- `purchase()` downloads full dataset slices or runs compute-heavy analysis (paid)

## How HF Hub Works Today

### Two API Surfaces

**1. Hub REST API** (huggingface.co/api/*)
- `GET /api/datasets` -- list/search datasets with filters (tags, author, sort)
- `GET /api/datasets/{ns}/{repo}` -- dataset metadata
- `GET /api/datasets/{ns}/{repo}/tree/{rev}/` -- browse files
- `GET /datasets/{ns}/{repo}/resolve/{rev}/{path}` -- download specific files
- `GET /api/trending?type=dataset` -- trending datasets
- `GET /api/quicksearch?q=...&type=dataset` -- cross-type search
- `GET /api/datasets-tags-by-type` -- available filter tags
- Full OpenAPI spec at `huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.json`
- Markdown version for agents at `huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.md`

**2. Dataset Viewer API** (datasets-server.huggingface.co/*)
- `/is-valid` -- check if dataset is viewable
- `/splits` -- list configs and splits
- `/first-rows` -- preview first 100 rows
- `/rows` -- paginate rows (max 100 per page)
- `/search` -- text search within columns
- `/filter` -- predicate-based row filtering with sort
- `/parquet` -- get parquet shard URLs for direct download
- `/size` -- row counts and byte sizes per split
- `/statistics` -- column-level stats (distribution, mean, median)
- `/croissant` -- ML-specific metadata in Croissant format

All endpoints are free, unauthenticated for public datasets. Gated datasets require
a Bearer token.

- Source: [HF Hub API docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api)
- Source: [Dataset Viewer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/dataset-viewer/index)
- Source: [OpenAPI spec (markdown)](https://huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.md)

### Existing Agent Tooling

**HF MCP Server:** Official MCP server that gives Claude/Codex/Cursor access to search
models, datasets, Spaces, and papers from within the editor. Exposes Gradio-based tools.

**HF Datasets Skill:** A SKILL.md file (for OpenClaw-style agents) that teaches the
agent the Dataset Viewer API workflow: validate, resolve splits, preview rows, paginate,
search, filter, get parquet URLs, query via SQL with `npx parquetlens`.

**Semantic Search MCP:** Community-built server enabling embedding-based similarity
search over HF models and datasets (intent-based, not keyword).

- Source: [HF MCP Server docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/agents-mcp)
- Source: [HF Datasets Skill](https://github.com/huggingface/skills/blob/main/skills/huggingface-datasets/SKILL.md)

### Known Pain Points

| Problem | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| **Discovery is broken at scale** | 500K+ datasets, basic tag filtering only. No domain-specific vocabulary, no free-form topics (GitHub-style). Finding the right dataset for a task is genuinely hard. |
| **Tag/metadata quality is inconsistent** | Many datasets have no tags, wrong tags, or missing metadata. No quality enforcement. |
| **No cross-dataset comparison** | Want to compare 3 NER datasets? You must manually fetch each, parse schemas, compare. No built-in tooling. |
| **No quality signals** | No freshness scores, no completeness metrics, no "this dataset is better than that one" signals beyond download count. |
| **Pagination is clunky for agents** | 100 rows max per request. Agent must loop, track offsets, handle partial flags. Token-expensive. |
| **No composition** | Can't join or cross-reference datasets. Each is an island. |
| **SQL access requires extra tooling** | `npx parquetlens` works but is a separate tool the agent must discover and learn. |

- Source: [GitHub issue #4702: domain-specific discovery](https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/issues/4702)
- Source: [HF criticisms search](https://www.allaboutai.com/ai-reviews/hugging-face/)

---

## Fit Assessment: HF Hub as DataFetch PoC Domain

### Where It Fits Well

**1. The discovery problem is real and painful.**
Finding the right dataset on HF Hub is a genuinely unsolved problem. An intent-shaped
interface like `findDatasets({ task: "named-entity-recognition", language: "en",
minRows: 10000, hasLabels: true })` would be meaningfully better than the current
tag-based search. This directly demonstrates the thesis.

**2. Cross-dataset comparison is the killer use case.**
No existing tool lets an agent say "compare these 5 text classification datasets by
schema overlap, label distribution, and row count." This requires the kind of
multi-step composition that the environment model excels at.

**3. The data is free.**
HF Hub APIs are free for public datasets. No payment integration needed for the PoC.
This removes the MPP dependency from Phase 1 entirely, making the benchmark faster
to build.

**4. The audience is the right audience.**
DataFetch targets code agent users (Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex). These users
already interact with HF Hub for ML work. The domain is immediately relevant.

**5. Mock data is trivial to generate.**
Cache metadata for 1000 popular datasets (via `/api/datasets?sort=downloads&limit=1000`
plus `/size` and `/statistics` for each). Synthetic schema + stats data is easy.

**6. Enrichable<T> maps naturally.**
- Free tier: dataset name, description, tags, size, split list
- Enrichable: column statistics, sample rows, schema comparison, quality scores
- Expensive: full dataset download, cross-dataset joins, similarity analysis

### Where It Doesn't Fit

**1. No natural paywall.**
HF Hub data is free. The DataFetch thesis explicitly requires paywalled data to
demonstrate the explore-before-commit model. If the underlying data is free, what
does `purchase()` unlock?

Possible answers:
- **Compute, not data.** `purchase()` pays for expensive analysis (cross-dataset
  comparison, quality scoring, embedding-based similarity) that requires significant
  compute. The data is free; the intelligence is not.
- **Curated intelligence.** Pre-computed quality scores, freshness assessments,
  schema compatibility matrices. Value-add on top of free data.
- **But this weakens the thesis.** The product design doc says "paywalled data +
  MPP payment is essential. Value is in reducing asymmetry through better interfaces
  + free exploration." If the raw data is free, the asymmetry being reduced is
  different (compute/analysis asymmetry, not data asymmetry).

**2. Less cross-referencing depth than UK business data.**
UK business data has natural joins: company -> directors -> other companies ->
properties -> financial filings. HF Hub datasets are more independent. The
cross-referencing that makes intent-shaped interfaces shine is weaker.

**3. HuggingFace could ship this themselves.**
HF already has an MCP server, a datasets skill, and semantic search. Adding
intent-shaped exploration is a natural next step for them. Building on their
platform means competing with the platform owner.

**4. The domain doesn't demonstrate governance.**
UK business data has natural governance needs (spend caps on paid enrichments,
rate limits on sensitive data). HF Hub data is all public. The governance layer
(vitest invariants, spend caps) has less to enforce.

**5. Less domain complexity.**
The product design doc chose UK business data because it "rewards the environment
model over flat REST calls." HF Hub's API is already relatively well-structured.
The gap between "current API" and "intent-shaped interface" is smaller than for
Companies House.

---

## Proposed Intent Interfaces (If HF Hub Is Chosen)

```typescript
interface DatasetDiscovery {
  // Find datasets matching criteria (absorbs tag search, metadata filtering,
  // semantic similarity, and download-count ranking into one intent)
  findDatasets(criteria: {
    task?: string | string[];
    language?: string | string[];
    modality?: 'text' | 'image' | 'audio' | 'tabular' | 'multimodal';
    minRows?: number;
    maxRows?: number;
    hasLabels?: boolean;
    license?: string[];
    query?: string; // semantic search
  }): Promise<DatasetSet>;

  // Compare multiple datasets across dimensions
  compareDatasets(
    datasets: DatasetSet,
    dimensions: ('schema' | 'size' | 'label_distribution' | 'quality' | 'freshness')[]
  ): Promise<DatasetComparison>;

  // Rank datasets by suitability for a specific use case
  rankBySuitability(
    datasets: DatasetSet,
    useCase: {
      task: string;
      targetSize: 'small' | 'medium' | 'large';
      prioritize: ('quality' | 'size' | 'diversity' | 'freshness')[];
    }
  ): Promise<RankedDatasetSet>;
}

interface DatasetExploration {
  // Get schema with column types, null rates, and sample values
  inspectSchema(dataset: DatasetRef): Promise<SchemaReport>;

  // Sample rows with optional stratification
  sampleRows(
    dataset: DatasetRef,
    options: { n: number; stratifyBy?: string; split?: string }
  ): Promise<SampleResult>;

  // Compute quality metrics (completeness, consistency, distribution stats)
  assessQuality(dataset: DatasetRef): Enrichable<QualityReport>;

  // Find similar datasets by schema or content
  findSimilar(dataset: DatasetRef): Enrichable<DatasetSet>;
}
```

The key insight: `findDatasets` absorbs what today requires 3-4 separate API calls
(tag search + metadata fetch + size check + stats check) into a single typed intent.
`compareDatasets` does something that HF Hub literally cannot do today.

---

## Alternative: HF Hub as a SECONDARY Domain

Rather than replacing UK business data, HF Hub could be the **second PoC** mentioned
in the product design doc (Phase 3). The product design doc says the second PoC should
be "execution-based" to validate governance. But there's a third option:

**HF Hub as a data-domain PoC that validates generality.**

Phase 1: UK business data (proves thesis with paywalled, complex, cross-referenceable data)
Phase 2: envkit extraction
Phase 3: HF Hub datasets (proves the same folder interface works for a completely
different domain, audience, and data shape)

This is compelling because:
- Different data character (metadata-heavy vs. record-heavy)
- Different access patterns (discovery vs. lookup)
- Same intent-shaped interface pattern
- Same explore/purchase model (even if purchase = compute, not data)
- Validates that envkit generalizes

---

## Competitive Landscape: Who Else Solves HF Discovery?

| Tool | Approach | Limitation |
|------|----------|------------|
| **HF Hub search** | Tag + keyword filtering | No semantic search, no cross-dataset comparison |
| **HF MCP Server** | Agent access to Hub search + Gradio tools | Still uses the same limited search under the hood |
| **HF Datasets Skill** | Teaches agent the Dataset Viewer API | Agent still calls APIs one-by-one, no composition |
| **Semantic Search MCP** | Embedding-based similarity search | Discovery only, no exploration or comparison |
| **Activeloop Deep Lake** | Vector DB for datasets with versioning | Different product category (storage, not discovery) |
| **Croissant/MLCommons** | Standardized dataset metadata format | Metadata standard, not a tool |

Nobody offers intent-shaped dataset exploration today. The gap is real.

- Source: [HF MCP Server](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/agents-mcp)
- Source: [Semantic search MCP](https://playbooks.com/mcp/davanstrien-huggingface-hub-search)

---

## HF Hub API Technical Details for Implementation

### What You'd Cache for Mock Data

```bash
# 1. Top 1000 datasets by downloads
curl "https://huggingface.co/api/datasets?sort=downloads&direction=-1&limit=1000"

# 2. For each dataset, get size info
curl "https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/size?dataset={namespace}/{repo}"

# 3. For each dataset, get split info
curl "https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/splits?dataset={namespace}/{repo}"

# 4. For each dataset, get column statistics (per split)
curl "https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/statistics?dataset={ns}/{repo}&config={config}&split={split}"

# 5. For each dataset, get first rows (for schema inference + samples)
curl "https://datasets-server.huggingface.co/first-rows?dataset={ns}/{repo}&config={config}&split={split}"
```

This gives you: name, description, tags, downloads, likes, size (rows + bytes),
schema (column names + types), statistics (distributions, means, null rates),
and sample rows. Sufficient for rich mock data.

### Rate Limits

HF Hub rate limits are not publicly documented in the API spec. The docs say
"subject to HF-wide rate limits" with an option to upgrade. In practice, for
authenticated users, the limits are generous enough for caching 1000 datasets
(a few thousand requests total).

### SQL Access Pattern

The HF Datasets Skill documents a powerful pattern: get parquet shard URLs via
`/parquet`, then query them with `npx parquetlens` using DuckDB SQL. This could
be what `purchase()` wraps: the agent writes SQL against the actual dataset, and
the environment handles parquet download + query execution.

```typescript
// Inside the environment, purchase() could enable:
const result = await purchase({
  intent: "query",
  dataset: "stanfordnlp/imdb",
  sql: "SELECT label, COUNT(*) FROM data GROUP BY label",
  maxUsd: 0.10
});
// Environment downloads parquet shards, runs SQL, returns results
```

---

## Key Takeaways

**1. HF Hub has a genuine discovery/exploration problem that intent-shaped interfaces
could solve.** Cross-dataset comparison, quality assessment, and suitability ranking
are completely unserved. The gap between "current API" and "environment interface"
is meaningful.

**2. The paywall problem is real.** DataFetch's thesis requires paid data to prove
explore-before-commit. HF Hub data is free. You'd be selling compute/analysis, not
data access. This changes the value proposition from "reduce information asymmetry"
to "reduce analysis friction." Still valid, but different.

**3. Best as a second domain, not a replacement.** UK business data remains a stronger
first PoC because it has natural paywalls, deep cross-referencing, and governance needs.
HF Hub is a compelling second domain that proves envkit generalizes to metadata-heavy,
discovery-oriented use cases.

**4. The audience overlap is perfect.** Every Claude Code and OpenClaw user who works
with ML datasets would immediately understand the value. No domain explanation needed.

**5. HuggingFace could ship this.** They have the data, the MCP server, the skills
infrastructure, and the engineering team. Building this as a DataFetch domain means
competing with the platform owner. The defense: HF optimizes for breadth (models +
datasets + Spaces + papers), DataFetch optimizes for depth (the environment interaction
model). But it's a risk.

**6. Implementation effort is low.** Caching 1000 datasets of metadata takes hours,
not days. The mock data is trivially derivable. The intent interfaces are clean.
If you wanted a fast way to validate the environment thesis with a friendly audience,
this is it.

---

# HuggingFace Hub as DataFetch PoC Domain: R&D Scouting Brief

> Research date: 2026-03-31
> Source: https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api, https://github.com/huggingface/skills
> Category: platform
> Context: Evaluating HF Hub datasets as an alternative PoC domain for DataFetch's
> environment-first interaction model (see kb/product_design.md)

---

## Overview

HuggingFace Hub is the dominant repository for ML models and datasets, hosting 2M+
models and 500K+ datasets. It exposes a comprehensive REST API, a Dataset Viewer API
for row-level access, and client libraries in Python and JS. The question is whether
wrapping HF Hub's dataset discovery and exploration behind DataFetch's typed folder
interfaces would demonstrate the environment-first thesis better than (or alongside)
the UK business data domain.

## The Idea

Instead of UK Companies House data, use HuggingFace Hub datasets as the domain:
- Agent enters a DataFetch environment folder with typed interfaces for dataset
  discovery, exploration, comparison, and download
- Mock data: cached metadata for ~1000 popular datasets (sizes, schemas, tags, stats)
- Intent interfaces: `findDatasets`, `compareSchemas`, `sampleRows`, `assessQuality`
- `explore()` returns dataset metadata, column statistics, sample rows (free)
- `purchase()` downloads full dataset slices or runs compute-heavy analysis (paid)

## How HF Hub Works Today

### Two API Surfaces

**1. Hub REST API** (huggingface.co/api/*)
- `GET /api/datasets` -- list/search datasets with filters (tags, author, sort)
- `GET /api/datasets/{ns}/{repo}` -- dataset metadata
- `GET /api/datasets/{ns}/{repo}/tree/{rev}/` -- browse files
- `GET /datasets/{ns}/{repo}/resolve/{rev}/{path}` -- download specific files
- `GET /api/trending?type=dataset` -- trending datasets
- `GET /api/quicksearch?q=...&type=dataset` -- cross-type search
- `GET /api/datasets-tags-by-type` -- available filter tags
- Full OpenAPI spec at `huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.json`
- Markdown version for agents at `huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.md`

**2. Dataset Viewer API** (datasets-server.huggingface.co/*)
- `/is-valid` -- check if dataset is viewable
- `/splits` -- list configs and splits
- `/first-rows` -- preview first 100 rows
- `/rows` -- paginate rows (max 100 per page)
- `/search` -- text search within columns
- `/filter` -- predicate-based row filtering with sort
- `/parquet` -- get parquet shard URLs for direct download
- `/size` -- row counts and byte sizes per split
- `/statistics` -- column-level stats (distribution, mean, median)
- `/croissant` -- ML-specific metadata in Croissant format

All endpoints are free, unauthenticated for public datasets. Gated datasets require
a Bearer token.

- Source: [HF Hub API docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/api)
- Source: [Dataset Viewer docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/dataset-viewer/index)
- Source: [OpenAPI spec (markdown)](https://huggingface.co/.well-known/openapi.md)

### Existing Agent Tooling

**HF MCP Server:** Official MCP server that gives Claude/Codex/Cursor access to search
models, datasets, Spaces, and papers from within the editor. Exposes Gradio-based tools.

**HF Datasets Skill:** A SKILL.md file (for OpenClaw-style agents) that teaches the
agent the Dataset Viewer API workflow: validate, resolve splits, preview rows, paginate,
search, filter, get parquet URLs, query via SQL with `npx parquetlens`.

**Semantic Search MCP:** Community-built server enabling embedding-based similarity
search over HF models and datasets (intent-based, not keyword).

- Source: [HF MCP Server docs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/agents-mcp)
- Source: [HF Datasets Skill](https://github.com/huggingface/skills/blob/main/skills/huggingface-datasets/SKILL.md)

### Known Pain Points

| Problem | Detail |
|---------|--------|
| **Discovery is broken at scale** | 500K+ datasets, basic tag filtering only. No domain-specific vocabulary, no free-form topics (GitHub-style). Finding the right dataset for a task is genuinely hard. |
| **Tag/metadata quality is inconsistent** | Many datasets have no tags, wrong tags, or missing metadata. No quality enforcement. |
| **No cross-dataset comparison** | Want to compare 3 NER datasets? You must manually fetch each, parse schemas, compare. No built-in tooling. |
| **No quality signals** | No freshness scores, no completeness metrics, no "this dataset is better than that one" signals beyond download count. |
| **Pagination is clunky for agents** | 100 rows max per request. Agent must loop, track offsets, handle partial flags. Token-expensive. |
| **No composition** | Can't join or cross-reference datasets. Each is an island. |
| **SQL access requires extra tooling** | `npx parquetlens` works but is a separate tool the agent must discover and learn. |

- Source: [GitHub issue #4702: domain-specific discovery](https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/issues/4702)
- Source: [HF criticisms search](https://www.allaboutai.com/ai-reviews/hugging-face/)

---

## F

**Bottom line on the HF Hub idea:**

**Strong fit for thesis validation**, but **better as a second domain, not a replacement** for UK business data. Here's why:

**What works:**
- HF Hub has a genuine, painful discovery problem. Nobody offers cross-dataset comparison, quality scoring, or suitability ranking today. Intent-shaped interfaces like `findDatasets({ task: "NER", language: "en", minRows: 10000 })` would be meaningfully better than current tag search.
- The audience (Claude Code/OpenClaw/Codex ML users) is exactly your target. Zero domain explanation needed.
- Mock data is trivial to generate -- cache metadata for 1000 datasets in a few hours.
- Implementation effort is the lowest of any domain you've considered.

**What doesn't work as a primary PoC:**
- **No natural paywall.** The data is free. `purchase()` would buy compute/analysis, not data. This changes the thesis from "reduce information asymmetry" to "reduce analysis friction." Still valid, but different from what the product design doc specifies.
- **Less cross-referencing depth.** UK business data has company -> directors -> properties -> financials. HF datasets are more independent islands.
- **HuggingFace could ship this themselves.** They already have the MCP server and skills infrastructure.

**Recommended path:** Keep UK business data for Phase 1 (proves thesis with paywalled, complex data). Use HF Hub as the Phase 3 second domain (proves envkit generalizes to metadata-heavy discovery use cases with a different audience).

1→# Proof of Concept: agent-browser as Governed Environment
     2→
     3→**Target**: Target 5 (agent-browser) from [Target Prototypes](target_prototypes.md)
     4→
     5→> **Scope**: Concrete build plan for proving envrun's key concepts using agent-browser as the base environment and per-web-application environments as the primary test surface. Maps each build stage to the falsifiable thesis spine from [Product Design](product_design.md). For the full spec, see [Spec](spec.md). For market context, see [Market Thesis](market_thesis.md).
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## The Idea
    10→
    11→agent-browser exposes every browser action as a discrete CLI command (`open`, `snapshot`, `click @e2`, `fill @e3 "value"`, `batch [...]`). We wrap those commands into typed TypeScript modules, creating a **base environment** that any agent can navigate as a codebase.
    12→
    13→On top of that base, we create **application environments** per web application. Each application environment derives higher-level intent interfaces from the underlying browser primitives. The interface the agent sees is not "click sidebar, select analytics, download CSV." It is `getAnalytics({ period: '7d', metric: 'impressions' })`.
    14→
    15→Those intent-level interfaces are built through the same trajectory commit mechanism the spec describes: the agent explores, discovers a reliable path, commits it as a reusable function, and progressively compresses it. Eventually, popular trajectories compress so far that the browser is not even involved: historical data is cached locally, the differential is fetched only when needed, and the response resolves from a database query rather than a browser session. That is convergence. The trajectory has compiled into deterministic software.
    16→
    17→---
    18→
    19→## Why This Example
    20→
    21→The Twitter analytics workflow is a strong POC vehicle because it exercises every layer of the thesis in a progression that is concrete, measurable, and easy to demonstrate.
    22→
    23→### The Progression
    24→
    25→```
    26→Stage 0: Raw CLI
    27→  Agent calls agent-browser CLI commands directly.
    28→  12+ tool calls per task. High token cost. Brittle.
    29→
    30→Stage 1: Base environment (agent-browser as typed modules)
    31→  Agent writes TypeScript against navigation.ts, interaction.ts, observation.ts.
    32→  Same 12 actions, but composed in code, with type safety and context pruning.
    33→
    34→Stage 2: Application environment (Twitter)
    35→  Agent builds twitter/analytics.ts with intent-level interfaces.
    36→  "Download my analytics CSV" = 1 function call wrapping the 12-action trajectory.
    37→
    38→Stage 3: Convergent interface
    39→  Agent derives getAnalytics({ period, metric }) on top of the CSV download.
    40→  Parses CSV, extracts the specific figure, returns structured data.
    41→
    42→Stage 4: Full convergence
    43→  Popular trajectories are optimized. Historical analytics are cached in the
    44→  data layer. The agent fetches only the differential. The browser is invoked
    45→  only when new data is needed. Most requests resolve from the local database.
    46→  The trajectory has compiled into deterministic software.
    47→```
    48→
    49→### Concept Coverage
    50→
    51→| Concept | Where it appears | What we measure |
    52→|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
    53→| **Code mode > tool calling** (L0) | Stage 0 → Stage 1 | Token cost, completion rate, time: typed modules vs raw CLI |
    54→| **Codebase shape as discovery** (L1) | Stage 1 | Time-to-first-successful-action for an agent dropped into the environment cold |
    55→| **Governance safety delta** (L2) | Stage 2 | Domain allowlists prevent navigation to wrong sites, PII detection blocks filling sensitive forms, rate limits throttle rapid-fire submissions |
    56→| **Branchable state** (L3) | Stage 2-3 | Agent branches to try two navigation strategies in parallel (e.g., sidebar path vs direct URL), picks the one that works, commits it |
    57→| **Trajectory convergence** (L4) | Stage 3 → Stage 4 | Token cost per task over 50 runs. Must show a declining curve. |
    58→| **Marketplace delegation** (L5) | Multiple app environments | Agent routes "get my Twitter analytics" to the Twitter environment, "check my Shopify orders" to the Shopify environment. Routing is based on AppBench scores. |
    59→| **Extensions/committed trajectories** | Stage 2-3 | Agent commits `downloadAnalyticsCSV()` as a reusable function with escalation boundary |
    60→| **Escalation boundaries** | Stage 3 | Escalation fires when Twitter changes UI layout, otherwise deterministic |
    61→| **Hub aggregation** | Stage 4 | Multiple users' trajectories reveal common patterns (analytics download), provider promotes to native interface |
    62→| **Simulation boundary** | All stages | Every browser action has real side effects. The environment must declare this honestly. |
    63→| **Authorization as governance** | Stage 2 | Governance rules ARE the authorization: "this agent cannot navigate to account settings," "this agent cannot post tweets" |
    64→
    65→---
    66→
    67→## Architecture: Three Layers
    68→
    69→### Layer 1: Base Environment (agent-browser)
    70→
    71→The base environment wraps agent-browser's CLI into typed modules.
    72→
    73→```
    74→agent-browser.env/
    75→  env.manifest.yaml
    76→  CLAUDE.md
    77→  modules/
    78→    navigation.ts       # open, goto, back, forward, reload
    79→    interaction.ts      # click, fill, select, hover, drag, scroll
    80→    observation.ts      # snapshot, screenshot, pdf, source
    81→    state.ts            # cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, profiles
    82→    network.ts          # HAR recording, route interception
    83→    sessions.ts         # create, list, restore, named sessions
    84→  governance/
    85→    invariants/
    86→      session-isolation.test.ts    # Sessions cannot access each other's state
    87→      navigation-timeout.test.ts   # Navigation must complete within budget
    88→    verifiers/
    89→      accessibility-refs.test.ts   # Actions reference valid element refs
    90→  skills/
    91→    runtime/
    92→      cdp-lifecycle.md             # How to connect to the browser daemon
    93→    environment/
    94→      snapshot-before-act.md       # Always snapshot before mutating
    95→    application/
    96→      web-research.md              # Common web research patterns
    97→  traces/
    98→  data/                            # Session traces, HAR archives, screenshots
    99→```
   100→
   101→**What this proves**: Layer 0 (code mode) and Layer 1 (codebase shape). The agent writes `await navigation.goto('https://x.com')` instead of calling `agent-browser goto https://x.com` as a tool. We measure the token and completion delta.
   102→
   103→### Layer 2: Application Environment (Twitter)
   104→
   105→An application environment is a derivative environment that imports the base and adds domain-specific modules, governance, and data.
   106→
   107→```
   108→twitter.env/
   109→  env.manifest.yaml
   110→  CLAUDE.md
   111→  modules/
   112→    auth.ts              # Login flow, session restore, cookie management
   113→    analytics.ts         # getAnalytics(period, metric), downloadCSV()
   114→    profile.ts           # getProfile(), getFollowerCount()
   115→    timeline.ts          # getTweets(filter), getEngagement(tweetId)
   116→  governance/

1→# Proof of Concept: agent-browser as Governed Environment
     2→
     3→**Target**: Target 5 (agent-browser) from [Target Prototypes](target_prototypes.md)
     4→
     5→> **Scope**: Concrete build plan for proving envrun's key concepts using agent-browser as the base environment and per-web-application environments as the primary test surface. Maps each build stage to the falsifiable thesis spine from [Product Design](product_design.md). For the full spec, see [Spec](spec.md). For market context, see [Market Thesis](market_thesis.md).
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## The Idea
    10→
    11→agent-browser exposes every browser action as a discrete CLI command (`open`, `snapshot`, `click @e2`, `fill @e3 "value"`, `batch [...]`). We wrap those commands into typed TypeScript modules, creating a **base environment** that any agent can navigate as a codebase.
    12→
    13→On top of that base, we create **application environments** per web application. Each application environment derives higher-level intent interfaces from the underlying browser primitives. The interface the agent sees is not "click sidebar, select analytics, download CSV." It is `getAnalytics({ period: '7d', metric: 'impressions' })`.
    14→
    15→Those intent-level interfaces are built through the same trajectory commit mechanism the spec describes: the agent explores, discovers a reliable path, commits it as a reusable function, and progressively compresses it. Eventually, popular trajectories compress so far that the browser is not even involved: historical data is cached locally, the differential is fetched only when needed, and the response resolves from a database query rather than a browser session. That is convergence. The trajectory has compiled into deterministic software.
    16→
    17→---
    18→
    19→## Why This Example
    20→
    21→The Twitter analytics workflow is a strong POC vehicle because it exercises every layer of the thesis in a progression that is concrete, measurable, and easy to demonstrate.
    22→
    23→### The Progression
    24→
    25→```
    26→Stage 0: Raw CLI
    27→  Agent calls agent-browser CLI commands directly.
    28→  12+ tool calls per task. High token cost. Brittle.
    29→
    30→Stage 1: Base environment (agent-browser as typed modules)
    31→  Agent writes TypeScript against navigation.ts, interaction.ts, observation.ts.
    32→  Same 12 actions, but composed in code, with type safety and context pruning.
    33→
    34→Stage 2: Application environment (Twitter)
    35→  Agent builds twitter/analytics.ts with intent-level interfaces.
    36→  "Download my analytics CSV" = 1 function call wrapping the 12-action trajectory.
    37→
    38→Stage 3: Convergent interface
    39→  Agent derives getAnalytics({ period, metric }) on top of the CSV download.
    40→  Parses CSV, extracts the specific figure, returns structured data.
    41→
    42→Stage 4: Full convergence
    43→  Popular trajectories are optimized. Historical analytics are cached in the
    44→  data layer. The agent fetches only the differential. The browser is invoked
    45→  only when new data is needed. Most requests resolve from the local database.
    46→  The trajectory has compiled into deterministic software.
    47→```
    48→
    49→### Concept Coverage
    50→
    51→| Concept | Where it appears | What we measure |
    52→|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
    53→| **Code mode > tool calling** (L0) | Stage 0 → Stage 1 | Token cost, completion rate, time: typed modules vs raw CLI |
    54→| **Codebase shape as discovery** (L1) | Stage 1 | Time-to-first-successful-action for an agent dropped into the environment cold |
    55→| **Governance safety delta** (L2) | Stage 2 | Domain allowlists prevent navigation to wrong sites, PII detection blocks filling sensitive forms, rate limits throttle rapid-fire submissions |
    56→| **Branchable state** (L3) | Stage 2-3 | Agent branches to try two navigation strategies in parallel (e.g., sidebar path vs direct URL), picks the one that works, commits it |
    57→| **Trajectory convergence** (L4) | Stage 3 → Stage 4 | Token cost per task over 50 runs. Must show a declining curve. |
    58→| **Marketplace delegation** (L5) | Multiple app environments | Agent routes "get my Twitter analytics" to the Twitter environment, "check my Shopify orders" to the Shopify environment. Routing is based on AppBench scores. |
    59→| **Extensions/committed trajectories** | Stage 2-3 | Agent commits `downloadAnalyticsCSV()` as a reusable function with escalation boundary |
    60→| **Escalation boundaries** | Stage 3 | Escalation fires when Twitter changes UI layout, otherwise deterministic |
    61→| **Hub aggregation** | Stage 4 | Multiple users' trajectories reveal common patterns (analytics download), provider promotes to native interface |
    62→| **Simulation boundary** | All stages | Every browser action has real side effects. The environment must declare this hone

   142→### Layer 3: Convergent Interface
   143→
   144→The convergent interface is not a separate artifact. It is the result of the extension layer compounding over time.
   145→
   146→```typescript
   147→// extensions/services/analytics-cache.ts
   148→// Deployed as persistent worker on merge. Callable via HTTP. Runs on cron.
   149→
   150→import { downloadAnalyticsCSV } from '../workflows/download-analytics-csv';
   151→import { db } from '../../data/analytics.db';
   152→
   153→/**
   154→ * Fetch analytics for a given period and metric.
   155→ * Resolves from cache when possible. Fetches differential via browser only when
   156→ * cached data is stale (older than 24h or missing the requested period).
   157→ *
   158→ * Convergence: 50 runs showed token cost declining from ~8,400 to ~200 as
   159→ * cache coverage increased. After 30 runs, 90% of requests resolve without
   160→ * touching the browser.
   161→ */
   162→export async function getAnalytics(
   163→  params: { period: '7d' | '30d' | '90d'; metric: 'impressions' | 'engagement' | 'followers' }
   164→): Promise<AnalyticsResult> {
   165→  const cached = await db.query(params);
   166→  if (cached && !isStale(cached)) return cached;
   167→
   168→  // Cache miss or stale: fetch via browser trajectory
   169→  const csv = await downloadAnalyticsCSV();
   170→  const parsed = parseAnalyticsCSV(csv);
   171→  await db.upsert(parsed);  // Store for future cache hits
   172→
   173→  return extractMetric(parsed, params);
   174→}
   175→```
   176→
   177→**What this proves**: Layer 4 (convergence). The trajectory compiles into deterministic software. The browser is a fallback, not the primary path. Token cost per task declines measurably over time.

I think this is a genuinely interesting reframing. Let me lay out what I see, both the upside and the problems.

**What you're describing:**
An envrun-powered marketplace where each "environment" wraps an existing free API (HF Hub, Companies House, etc.) with intent-shaped interfaces. Agents pay a small fee not for the data, but for the interface quality. Over time, the marketplace observes natural language intents from agents, and the environments autonomously improve their interfaces by converging agent trajectories into better typed functions.

**What's compelling about this:**

1. **It resolves the paywall problem from brief 16.** You're not charging for data (which is free). You're charging for *interface intelligence*, the gap between "12 API calls with offset tracking and schema parsing" and `findDatasets({ task: "NER", language: "en" })`. That's a real service.

2. **Trajectory convergence becomes the product moat.** This is the key envrun concept (poc.md Stage 3-4): popular agent workflows compile into deterministic software. Applied to data APIs, it means the marketplace gets *better* with usage. The 100th agent to search HF datasets benefits from the 99 before it. That's a compounding advantage no static API wrapper has.

3. **The marketplace framing solves the "HuggingFace could ship this" problem.** If you're wrapping *one* API, the platform owner can replicate. If you're a marketplace wrapping *hundreds* of APIs with cross-cutting intent convergence, no single platform owner can replicate the whole thing.

4. **Natural language intent -> converged interface is the envrun thesis applied commercially.** Agent says "find me a good NER dataset." First time, the environment interprets this via LLM, makes 8 API calls, returns results. After 50 agents ask similar things, the trajectory compiles into `findDatasets({ task: "NER" })` and resolves in milliseconds. That *is* the convergence curve from poc.md.

**What's problematic:**

1. **You now have two PoCs competing for attention.** The envrun poc.md is about agent-browser wrapping Twitter. DataFetch is about UK business data. This marketplace idea is a third thing. It uses envrun concepts, but it's not the same PoC. You risk spreading thin across three prototypes without proving any single thesis.

2. **The fee model is fragile at the bottom.** If the underlying API is free and your wrapper costs $0.02 per call, the agent (or its operator) can just call the API directly. The value of the intent interface has to exceed the markup on every single call. For simple lookups, it won't. For complex multi-step workflows, it will. That means you need to find domains where the complexity gap is wide enough to justify the fee.

3. **"Autonomously improve interfaces" is the hardest part of envrun, not the easiest.** poc.md puts trajectory convergence at Stage 3-4, after proving code mode (Stage 1), governance (Stage 2), and committed trajectories (Stage 2-3). Building the marketplace *before* proving convergence works is building the distribution before the product.

4. **Intent disambiguation is expensive.** When an agent says "find me datasets about sentiment," do they mean sentiment analysis datasets? Datasets with sentiment labels? Datasets about public opinion? The LLM interpretation step costs tokens and adds latency. Until convergence kicks in (after many similar queries), every request is expensive to serve. Your margin on early queries might be negative.

**My honest take:**

The marketplace vision is the right *endgame* for envrun applied to data. But it's not the right *first step*. Here's what I'd suggest:

**Build one environment well first.** Pick HF Hub (easiest mock data, perfect audience) or UK business data (strongest thesis proof). Build the envrun environment for it. Prove convergence works on a single domain. Then the marketplace is "we did this for HF datasets, and the same envkit lets anyone wrap any API." That's a launch story.

If you try to build the marketplace abstraction first, you'll end up designing the platform without having built the thing the platform enables. That's the same trap the product design doc warns about: "SDK-first is platform drift."

**The order matters:**
1. Single environment proves convergence (poc.md Stage 1-4)
2. Second environment proves envkit generalizes (DataFetch Phase 3)
3. Marketplace proves the network effect (many environments, cross-intent learning)

Want me to sketch how HF Hub or UK business data would look as the first environment using the envrun architecture from poc.md? That would be the concrete next step.

Here's a slightly more up-to-date idea that we could take this product towards. We start by reframing the mission, which is to gaolbreak data from vertical applications so they can be consumed by agents natively. No more agent browsers, no more API interfaces. Application environments that the agents can traverse and build custom harnesses against to achieve the reliability they need and an on-screen application from it.
Now here's the question that we need to discuss: What data sets are we missing today to unlock the agency for downstream applications? Take for example:
- travel
- flight information
- train information
- car rental information
- hotel information
These are all spread out across several applications and data sets and might benefit from being agent-natively consolidated under an environment and the way we described end-to-end. We can use the techniques that we just listed here to, for now, just give them away for free and test the concept. I imagine there are also other categories of information where you can build answering applications, for example entertainment, even development. If I want to find the latest GitHub, all of these corporate networks that are somewhat closed, we can just gather public information and make it programmatically accessible through an environment interface.
Can you think it through and help me flesh out if this is something we could tackle?

This is a fundamentally different framing and I think it's stronger. Let me think through it honestly.

**The reframe:** Instead of "better interfaces for existing APIs," you're saying "liberate data trapped in vertical apps so agents can consume it natively." The environment isn't a wrapper around an API -- it's a *replacement* for the app. The agent doesn't need to browser-automate Skyscanner. It navigates a flight environment with typed interfaces, mock data for exploration, and real data on commit.

**Why this is stronger than the previous versions:**

The DataFetch product design was about proving "folders > APIs." The Merit/StableEnrich research showed "payment-as-auth for agent data access." But both assumed the data already existed in API form somewhere. Your new framing targets data that *doesn't* have good API access -- it's locked inside vertical web apps, behind login walls, in fragmented databases, or only accessible via browser automation.

That's a real gap. Let me map out where it exists.

---

**Category analysis: Where is agent-consumable data missing?**

**Travel** is the strongest category because the data is:
- High-value (people make expensive decisions based on it)
- Deeply fragmented (flights on 20+ carriers, hotels on 10+ OTAs, trains on national operators)
- Time-sensitive (prices change hourly)
- Poorly accessible (most "APIs" are B2B-only with minimum commitments, or scraping-dependent)

| Sub-domain | Current state | Why agents can't consume it |
|------------|--------------|---------------------------|
| **Flights** | Google Flights has no public API. Skyscanner/Kiwi have B2B APIs with approval gates. Amadeus GDS API exists but requires certification + deposit. | No free, agent-accessible flight search. Period. Every agent that "searches flights" is either browser-automating or using an expensive B2B integration. |
| **Trains** | UK: National Rail has Darwin API (free, XML, painful). EU: No unified API. Trainline has no public API. Deutsche Bahn has an unofficial one. | Fragmented by country, no unified schema, most require scraping. |
| **Hotels** | Booking.com affiliate API (approval required). Google Hotels no API. Airbnb no public API. | Same pattern: data exists on websites, not in agent-consumable form. |
| **Car rental** | No major provider has a public API. Enterprise, Hertz, Avis -- all website-only. | Pure browser-automation territory. |
| **Events/entertainment** | Ticketmaster has an API (free, rate-limited). Eventbrite has one. But venues, local events, restaurant bookings -- fragmented. | Partial coverage from a few providers, massive long tail with no API. |

**Development/tech info** is interesting but weaker:

| Sub-domain | Current state | Gap |
|------------|--------------|-----|
| **GitHub activity** | GitHub API is excellent, free, well-documented | Small gap -- mostly solved. MCP servers exist. |
| **Package ecosystems** | npm, PyPI, crates.io all have APIs | Solved. Discovery/comparison could be better (like the HF Hub brief found). |
| **Stack Overflow/forums** | SO API exists. Reddit API exists but restricted. | Moderate gap -- rate limits and auth friction, not data absence. |
| **Corporate networks** (LinkedIn, Glassdoor) | No public APIs. Anti-scraping enforcement. | Large gap but legally risky territory. |

**Other strong categories:**

| Category | Why it's strong | Example intents |
|----------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Government services** | Public data, terrible interfaces, no APIs | "What permits do I need to open a restaurant in Brooklyn?" "What's the status of my visa application?" |
| **Real estate** (beyond UK) | Zillow API killed in 2021. Redfin, Realtor.com -- no public APIs. MLS data locked behind broker access. | "Find 3-bed homes under $500K within 30min commute of downtown Austin" |
| **Healthcare** | Provider directories, insurance coverage, drug pricing -- all fragmented, mostly website-only | "Which dermatologists near me accept Aetna and have availability this week?" |
| **Local services** | Plumbers, electricians, cleaners -- Yelp API is limited, Google Maps API is expensive | "Find a licensed electrician available Saturday in my area" |
| **Education** | University course catalogs, admission requirements, scholarship databases | "Which UK universities offer part-time MSc in data science under GBP 15K?" |

---

**Now, the hard questions:**

**1. Where does the data come from?**

This is the make-or-break question. You have three options:

- **Public datasets + periodic scraping.** Aggregate publicly available data (government sources, open datasets, cached web data) into a structured environment. Legal, but freshness is limited. Works well for: government services, real estate (Land Registry-style data), education.

- **Browser-automation-as-backend.** The environment's `purchase()` call triggers a real browser session that scrapes the live site. The envrun environment is the clean interface; the backend is agent-browser doing the dirty work. This is what you built the agent-browser PoC for. Works for: travel, entertainment, local services. But it's legally gray and brittle (sites change layouts).

- **Data partnerships / aggregator APIs.** Partner with or pay for B2B data feeds (Amadeus for flights, aggregator APIs for hotels). The environment wraps these into intent-shaped interfaces. More reliable, but adds cost and business complexity.

The honest answer: you probably need all three, and the mix varies by domain. Travel is mostly option 2 or 3. Government is mostly option 1. Real estate is a mix.

**2. What's the legal exposure?**

Scraping commercial sites (airlines, hotels, rental agencies) to repackage their data is legally contested territory. Ryanair sued Kiwi.com. LinkedIn sued HiQ. The CFAA and EU Database Directive create real risk. 

For a "give it away free and test the concept" phase, the risk is low (no commercial harm argument). But scaling means addressing this. The safest domains are: government/public data (OGL, FOIA equivalents), educational institutions (public catalogs), and open datasets.

**3. What's the MVP that tests the thesis?**

You said "give them away for free and test the concept." The concept to test is: **agents performing complex tasks across fragmented data sources work better inside a typed environment than calling APIs or browser-automating.**

The MVP needs:
- One domain with genuinely fragmented data
- An environment with intent-shaped interfaces
- Mock data for exploration, real data on commit
- A benchmark: environment vs. browser-automation vs. raw API for the same task

**Travel is the flashiest but hardest** (live pricing, legal risk, data freshness). **UK government/business data is the most defensible** (OGL, static-ish, already researched). **Education is an interesting middle ground** (public catalogs, moderate freshness needs, clear intent interfaces like "find programs matching X criteria").

**4. How does convergence apply here?**

This is where the envrun thesis makes the idea special vs. just "another data aggregator."

Take travel: The first agent that searches for "cheap flights London to Barcelona next weekend" triggers 8 API calls / scraping sessions. The trajectory gets committed as `searchFlights({ from, to, dates, budget })`. After 100 agents search similar routes, the system has cached route/price patterns, knows which sources return fastest, and can answer most queries from a local database with differential updates. The browser/API backend fires only for fresh pricing.

That's the Stage 0 -> Stage 4 progression from poc.md, applied to data. The environment gets cheaper and faster to operate with every query. That's the moat.

---

**My recommendation:**

Pick **one domain** where:
- The data is genuinely hard for agents to access today (not already solved by good APIs)
- The legal/ethical position is clean
- The intent interfaces are obviously better than the status quo
- You can build mock data quickly

**Travel** is the most exciting but most risky. **UK business + property** (your original DataFetch domain) is the most defensible and already researched. **Education** is underexplored and clean.

If you want to go bold: build a travel environment with cached/aggregated flight data (not live scraping) as the free tier, browser-automation for live pricing as the paid tier. The intent interface is `searchFlights()` / `compareRoutes()` / `buildItinerary()`. Agents explore cached data for free, pay (via MPP) for live pricing. That directly demonstrates every layer of the envrun thesis.

If you want to go safe: stick with UK business data, but reframe it under this new "jailbreak data from vertical apps" mission. Companies House website is a vertical app. Your environment jailbreaks its data into agent-native form. Same thesis, proven territory.

Want me to flesh out the travel environment as a concrete architecture, or would you rather map out multiple domains side by side to pick the strongest first target?
would you be able to form a deep research task where we go and find for these areas?

# Research Question

For each of the following vertical categories, identify: (1) what data exists that agents need but cannot easily access today, (2) what APIs/datasets are available vs locked behind vertical apps, (3) what the gap looks like between "current agent access" and "native programmatic access via an environment," and (4) how viable each category is as a first target for an "environment that jailbreaks data from vertical apps for agent-native consumption."

## Categories to investigate:

### 1. Travel & Transport
- Flight search and pricing (Google Flights, Skyscanner, Kiwi, Amadeus GDS, airline direct)
- Train information (National Rail UK, Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trainline, Amtrak)
- Car rental (Enterprise, Hertz, Avis, Sixt -- any public APIs?)
- Hotel/accommodation (Booking.com, Airbnb, Hotels.com, Google Hotels)
- Multi-modal trip planning (combining flights + trains + hotels + car rental)

### 2. Entertainment & Events
- Event discovery (Ticketmaster, Eventbrite, local venue listings, festivals)
- Restaurant/dining (OpenTable, Resy, Google Maps, Yelp, TheFork)
- Cinema/theater (showtimes, ticket availability)
- Sports (fixtures, tickets, live scores)
- Music/concerts (Bandsintown, Songkick, Spotify events)

### 3. Real Estate & Property (beyond UK)
- US property data (Zillow killed their API, Redfin, Realtor.com, MLS access)
- EU property data (Rightmove, Zoopla for UK; country-specific elsewhere)
- Commercial real estate (CoStar, LoopNet -- notoriously closed)
- Rental markets (Apartments.com, Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace)

### 4. Government & Public Services
- Permit and licensing information
- Court records, legal filings
- Immigration/visa status
- Benefits eligibility
- Public procurement / tenders

### 5. Healthcare
- Provider directories (who accepts what insurance, availability)
- Drug pricing (GoodRx, pharmacy comparison)
- Insurance coverage details
- Clinical trial discovery (ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO registry)

### 6. Education
- University course catalogs and admission requirements
- Scholarship databases
- School ratings and comparison
- Online course aggregation (Coursera, edX, Udemy)

### 7. Developer & Tech Ecosystem
- GitHub activity and repository intelligence (beyond basic API)
- Package ecosystem intelligence (npm, PyPI, crates.io -- cross-ecosystem)
- Documentation quality and freshness
- Stack Overflow / forum knowledge extraction
- Corporate developer platforms (Jira, Confluence, internal tools)

### 8. Local Services & Commerce
- Service provider discovery (plumbers, electricians, cleaners)
- Price comparison for physical goods
- Grocery/food delivery pricing
- Automotive (used car pricing, service history, parts availability)

For each category, assess:
- **Data availability**: What's freely available? What's API-gated? What's locked in apps?
- **Legal position**: Can this data be aggregated legally? OGL/public domain vs scraping risk?
- **Agent demand**: How often do agents actually need this data today?
- **Complexity gap**: How much better would an intent-shaped environment be vs current access?
- **Freshness requirements**: Is the data static (update monthly) or real-time (prices change hourly)?
- **Mock data feasibility**: How easy is it to build realistic mock data for the benchmark?
- **Competitive landscape**: Who else is trying to solve this for agents?

Conclude with a ranked recommendation of the top 3 domains for a first environment build, with justification.

Context: This research supports the product at /Users/06506792/src/tries/2026-03-21-datafetch. The vision is to "jailbreak data from vertical applications so they can be consumed by agents natively" using typed folder environments (see kb/product_design.md). The environments use intent-shaped TypeScript interfaces, mock-then-commit exploration, and trajectory convergence. We want to find the domain where this interaction model creates the most value vs the status quo.

# Deep Research

<!-- STATIC CONTEXT BLOCK START - Optimized for prompt caching -->
<!-- All static instructions, methodology, and templates below this line -->
<!-- Dynamic content (user queries, results) added after this block -->

## Core System Instructions

**Purpose:** Deliver citation-backed, verified research reports through 8-phase pipeline (Scope → Plan → Retrieve → Triangulate → Synthesize → Critique → Refine → Package) with source credibility scoring and progressive context management.

**Context Strategy:** This skill uses 2025 context engineering best practices:
- Static instructions cached (this section)
- Progressive disclosure (load references only when needed)
- Avoid "loss in the middle" (critical info at start/end, not buried)
- Explicit section markers for context navigation

---

## Decision Tree (Execute First)

```
Request Analysis
├─ Simple lookup? → STOP: Use WebSearch, not this skill
├─ Debugging? → STOP: Use standard tools, not this skill
└─ Complex analysis needed? → CONTINUE

Mode Selection
├─ Initial exploration? → quick (3 phases, 2-5 min)
├─ Standard research? → standard (6 phases, 5-10 min) [DEFAULT]
├─ Critical decision? → deep (8 phases, 10-20 min)
└─ Comprehensive review? → ultradeep (8+ phases, 20-45 min)

Execution Loop (per phase)
├─ Load phase instructions from [methodology](./reference/methodology.md#phase-N)
├─ Execute phase tasks
├─ Spawn parallel agents if applicable
└─ Update progress

Validation Gate
├─ Run `python scripts/validate_report.py --report [path]`
├─ Pass? → Deliver
└─ Fail? → Fix (max 2 attempts) → Still fails? → Escalate
```

---

## Workflow (Clarify → Plan → Act → Verify → Report)

**AUTONOMY PRINCIPLE:** This skill operates independently. Infer assumptions from query context. Only stop for critical errors or incomprehensible queries.

### 1. Clarify (Rarely Needed - Prefer Autonomy)

**DEFAULT: Proceed autonomously. Derive assumptions from query signals.**

**ONLY ask if CRITICALLY ambiguous:**
- Query is incomprehensible (e.g., "research the thing")
- Contradictory requirements (e.g., "quick 50-source ultradeep analysis")

**When in doubt: PROCEED with standard mode. User will redirect if incorrect.**

**Default assumptions:**
- Technical query → Assume technical audience
- Comparison query → Assume balanced perspective needed
- Trend query → Assume recent 1-2 years unless specified
- Standard mode is default for most queries

### 1.5. Report Folder Selection (ALWAYS - Before Research Begins)

**ALWAYS ask the user for the report folder name before starting research.**

**Prompt the user:**
> "What folder name should I save this report under? (This will be saved to `experiments/reports/[your-folder-name]/` in the current directory.)"

**Folder resolution:**
- Base path: `[cwd]/experiments/reports/`
- User provides folder name (e.g., "psilocybin-trials", "ai-safety-q1")
- Full path becomes: `[cwd]/experiments/reports/[folder-name]/`

**Reuse logic (supports multiple researchers sharing a folder):**
- If `[cwd]/experiments/reports/[folder-name]/` already exists, use it as-is (do NOT create a new one)
- If it does not exist, create it with `mkdir -p`
- This allows multiple research runs to accumulate reports in the same folder

**Set the resolved path as `REPORT_DIR` for all subsequent steps.**


---

### 2. Plan

**Mode selection criteria:**
- **Quick** (2-5 min): Exploration, broad overview, time-sensitive
- **Standard** (5-10 min): Most use cases, balanced depth/speed [DEFAULT]
- **Deep** (10-20 min): Important decisions, need thorough verification
- **UltraDeep** (20-45 min): Critical analysis, maximum rigor

**Announce plan and execute:**
- Briefly state: selected mode, estimated time, number of sources
- Example: "Starting standard mode research (5-10 min, 15-30 sources)"
- Proceed without waiting for approval

---

### 3. Act (Phase Execution)

**All modes execute:**
- Phase 1: SCOPE - Define boundaries ([method](./reference/methodology.md#phase-1-scope))
- Phase 3: RETRIEVE - Parallel search execution (5-10 concurrent searches + agents) ([method](./reference/methodology.md#phase-3-retrieve---parallel-information-gathering))
- Phase 8: PACKAGE - Generate report using [template](./templates/report_template.md)

**Standard/Deep/UltraDeep execute:**
- Phase 2: PLAN - Strategy formulation
- Phase 4: TRIANGULATE - Verify 3+ sources per claim
- Phase 4.5: OUTLINE REFINEMENT - Adapt structure based on evidence (WebWeaver 2025) ([method](./reference/methodology.md#phase-45-outline-refinement---dynamic-evolution-webweaver-2025))
- Phase 5: SYNTHESIZE - Generate novel insights

**Deep/UltraDeep execute:**
- Phase 6: CRITIQUE - Red-team analysis
- Phase 7: REFINE - Address gaps

**Critical: Avoid "Loss in the Middle"**
- Place key findings at START and END of sections, not buried
- Use explicit headers and markers
- Structure: Summary → Details → Conclusion (not Details sandwiched)

**Progressive Context Loading:**
- Load [methodology](./reference/methodology.md) sections on-demand
- Load [template](./templates/report_template.md) only for Phase 8
- Do not inline everything - reference external files

**Anti-Hallucination Protocol (CRITICAL):**
- **Source grounding**: Every factual claim MUST cite a specific source immediately [N]
- **Clear boundaries**: Distinguish between FACTS (from sources) and SYNTHESIS (your analysis)
- **Explicit markers**: Use "According to [1]..." or "[1] reports..." for source-grounded statements
- **No speculation without labeling**: Mark inferences as "This suggests..." not "Research shows..."
- **Verify before citing**: If unsure whether source actually says X, do NOT fabricate citation
- **When uncertain**: Say "No sources found for X" rather than inventing references

**Writing Standards:**

**Bullet Point Policy (Anti-Fatigue Enforcement):**
- Use bullets SPARINGLY: Only for distinct lists (product names, company roster, enumerated steps)
- NEVER use bullets as primary content delivery - they fragment thinking
- Each findings section requires substantive prose paragraphs (3-5+ paragraphs minimum)
- Example: Instead of "• Market size: kg/background-research.4B" write "The global market reached kg/background-research.4 billion in 2023, driven by increasing consumer demand and regulatory tailwinds [1]."

**Anti-Fatigue Quality Check (Apply to EVERY Section):**
Before considering a section complete, verify:
- [ ] **Paragraph count**: ≥3 paragraphs for major sections (## headings)
- [ ] **Prose-first**: <20% of content is bullet points (≥80% must be flowing prose)
- [ ] **No placeholders**: Zero instances of "Content continues", "Due to length", "[Sections X-Y]"
- [ ] **Evidence-rich**: Specific data points, statistics, quotes (not vague statements)
- [ ] **Citation density**: Major claims cited within same sentence

**If ANY check fails:** Regenerate the section before moving to next.

**Source Attribution Standards (Critical for Preventing Fabrication):**
- **Immediate citation**: Every factual claim followed by [N] citation in same sentence
- **Quote sources directly**: Use "According to [1]..." or "[1] reports..." for factual statements
- **Distinguish fact from synthesis**:
  - ✅ GOOD: "Mortality decreased 23% (p<0.01) in the treatment group [1]."
  - ❌ BAD: "Studies show mortality improved significantly."
- **No vague attributions**:
  - ❌ NEVER: "Research suggests...", "Studies show...", "Experts believe..."
  - ✅ ALWAYS: "Smith et al. (2024) found..." [1], "According to FDA data..." [2]
- **Label speculation explicitly**:
  - ✅ GOOD: "This suggests a potential mechanism..." (analysis, not fact)
  - ❌ BAD: "The mechanism is..." (presented as fact without citation)
- **Admit uncertainty**:
  - ✅ GOOD: "No sources found addressing X directly."
  - ❌ BAD: Fabricating a citation to fill the gap
- **Template pattern**: "[Specific claim with numbers/data] [Citation]. [Analysis/implication]."

## Output Contract

**Format:** Comprehensive markdown report following [template](./templates/report_template.md) EXACTLY

**Required sections (all must be detailed):**
- Executive Summary (2-3 concise paragraphs, 50-250 words)
- Introduction (2-3 paragraphs: question, scope, methodology, assumptions)
- Main Analysis (4-8 findings, each 300-500 words with citations [1], [2], [3])
- Synthesis & Insights (500-1000 words: patterns, novel insights, implications)
- Limitations & Caveats (2-3 paragraphs: gaps, assumptions, uncertainties)
- Recommendations (3-5 immediate actions, 3-5 next steps, 3-5 further research)
- **Bibliography (CRITICAL - see rules below)**
- Methodology Appendix (2-3 paragraphs: process, sources, verification)

**Bibliography Requirements (ZERO TOLERANCE - Report is UNUSABLE without complete bibliography):**
- ✅ MUST include EVERY citation [N] used in report body (if report has [1]-[50], write all 50 entries)
- ✅ Format: [N] Author/Org (Year). "Title". Publication. URL (Retrieved: Date)
- ✅ Each entry on its own line, complete with all metadata
- ❌ NO placeholders: NEVER use "[8-75] Additional citations", "...continue...", "etc.", "[Continue with sources...]"
- ❌ NO ranges: Write [3], [4], [5]... individually, NOT "[3-50]"
- ❌ NO truncation: If 30 sources cited, write all 30 entries in full
- ⚠️ Validation WILL FAIL if bibliography contains placeholders or missing citations
- ⚠️ Report is GARBAGE without complete bibliography - no way to verify claims

**Strictly Prohibited:**
- Placeholder text (TBD, TODO, [citation needed])
- Uncited major claims
- Broken links
- Missing required sections
- **Short summaries instead of detailed analysis**
- **Vague statements without specific evidence**

**Writing Standards (Critical):**
- **Narrative-driven**: Write in flowing prose with complete sentences that build understanding progressively
- **Precision**: Choose each word deliberately - every word must carry intention
- **Economy**: Eliminate fluff, unnecessary adjectives, fancy grammar
- **Clarity**: Use precise technical terms, avoid ambiguity. Embed exact numbers in sentences, not bullets
- **Directness**: State findings clearly without embellishment
- **Signal-to-noise**: High information density, respect reader's time
- **Bullet discipline**: Use bullets only for distinct lists (products, companies, steps). Default to prose paragraphs
- **Examples of precision**:
  - Bad: "significantly improved outcomes" → Good: "reduced mortality 23% (p<0.01)"
  - Bad: "several studies suggest" → Good: "5 RCTs (n=1,847) show"
  - Bad: "potentially beneficial" → Good: "increased biomarker X by 15%"
  - Bad: "• Market: kg/background-research.4B" → Good: "The market reached kg/background-research.4 billion in 2023, driven by consumer demand [1]."

**Quality gates (enforced by validator):**
- Minimum 2,000 words (standard mode)
- Average credibility score >60/100
- 3+ sources per major claim
- Clear facts vs. analysis distinction
- All sections present and detailed

---

## 🏠 US Real Estate APIs: Zillow, Redfin, MLS & More (2025–2026)

### **Zillow**
Zillow Group offers a collection of brands providing a wide range of APIs and data sets — with close to **20 APIs** available, covering various aspects of real estate. These span Mortgage, MLS, Public Data, Zestimates, and Transactions, available to both the public and partners.

However, many developers supplement Zillow's official API with scraping techniques and other Zillow scraping APIs to overcome restrictions and access richer data, as Zillow's API access policies require careful navigation. Specifically, Zillow API access is limited, and regional MLS restrictions may affect comprehensiveness.

---

### **Redfin**
Redfin offers data on property listings, sales, and market trends. While its API access is limited, it provides useful data for certain use cases such as market analysis and property metadata.

Redfin is considered friendlier to data extraction than Zillow — they offer CSV downloads for search results and have a less aggressive bot detection system. Redfin's search API (`redfin.com/stingray/api/gis`) returns JSON with listing details including listing price, sold price, HOA, lot size, year built, listing/sold dates, and Redfin Estimate.

---

### **Realtor.com / MLS**
Realtor.com pulls directly from MLS data, making it the most accurate source for active listings. Their internal GraphQL API (`realtor.com/api/v1/hulk`) serves structured listing data. The data quality is excellent — you get MLS numbers, listing office details, and open house schedules that other sites don't expose.

MLS data is the backbone of real estate listings in the US, but is fragmented across many regional systems. The Bridge Listing Output platform (via Zillow Group) allows brokers and developers to access MLS listing data via a modern RESTful API, with data returned normalized to the RESO data dictionary standard. All data access is at the discretion of individual MLS partners in the US and Canada.

---

### **Access for Agents & Brokers**
For brokers and agents, the recommended approach is to contact your local MLS for RESO Web API or RETS credentials, and for developers building a product, to start vendor approval with the MLS and consider partnering with a RESO-certified aggregator to speed access.

Access typically comes with membership fees, per-API or vendor fees, and possible per-listing or per-call charges. Contracts will include strict use/display rules, data retention and deletion requirements, branding/attribution, and audit rights — and noncompliant use risks termination, fines, and legal action.

---

### **Third-Party Unified APIs**

- **RealtyAPI**: Provides access to property, rental, and market data from Zillow, Redfin, Realtor, Airbnb, Apartments.com, and StreetEasy through a single, high-performance API. It does not serve cached data — every request fetches live data directly from the source.

- **Apify (Multi-Source Scraper)**: Provides deduplicated US property listings with cross-source price comparison, unified schema (30+ fields), and agent contact data — for sale, for rent, or recently sold. It extracts price, MLS, agent contacts, AVM valuations, photos, and open houses, covering all 50 states with 7 listing types and 50+ fields per property.

- **Mashvisor**: Offers nationwide MLS coverage with active and inactive listings and bulk ingestion for large-scale applications. It delivers investment metrics such as cash flow, cap rate, and cash-on-cash return — not available in Zillow or AirDNA APIs — and updates data daily for STR metrics and in real time for MLS metrics.

- **BatchData**: An enterprise-grade API offering everything from assessor and recorder data, to MLS listings data and permits, to AVMs and involuntary liens, suitable for powering search applications at scale.

- **CoreLogic**: CoreLogic API solutions plug in its massive property, mortgage, and risk datasets for property details, valuations, market insights, and portfolio analytics — enterprise-grade APIs aimed at lenders, insurers, and large proptech players needing highly curated data.

- **Realtors Property Resource (RPR)**: RPR is the U.S. REALTORS®-only national property database, offering APIs and integrations that surface tax records, MLS data, demographics, and market analytics. Access is tied to NAR membership and MLS/vendor partnerships, making it a strong option for REALTOR-centric workflows.

---

### **Key Use Cases in 2025–2026**
Top use cases include investment analysis (comparing price-per-sqft across zip codes, tracking days-on-market trends), market research (monitoring inventory levels and price reductions at scale), competitive intelligence, lead generation (FSBO or expired listings), and rental yield modeling.

---

**Summary**: The real estate API landscape in 2025–2026 is rich but fragmented. Official APIs from Zillow and Redfin have limitations, while MLS access requires membership/vendor approval. Third-party aggregators like RealtyAPI, Mashvisor, BatchData, and Apify offer more flexible, unified data access for developers and agents alike.

Here is a comprehensive summary of the search results on **healthcare provider directory APIs, insurance drug pricing, and GoodRx programmatic access**:

---

## 💊 GoodRx API — Drug Pricing Programmatic Access (2025)

### Overview
The GoodRx V2 API suite enables developers to access real-time prescription pricing and discount information from the GoodRx platform. Through its endpoints, developers can compare medication prices across pharmacies, retrieve available coupon and membership savings, and obtain key adjudication details to support seamless integration with healthcare, pharmacy, or patient-facing applications.

---

### Key API Endpoints

1. **Price Compare API**
   The Price Compare API (`GET /v2/price/compare`) returns the lowest available cash and coupon prices for a given drug, including details like dosage, form, quantity, manufacturer type, and pharmacy information. It matches drug names or NDCs to common forms and quantities, and includes both brand and generic equivalents when applicable.

2. **Coupon API**
   The Coupon API (`POST /v2/coupon`) provides full coupon adjudication details for offers retrieved from the Price Compare endpoint. It allows clients to retrieve coupon adjudication info for a particular drug, request contact info for customers and pharmacists, and obtain the URL to the GoodRx coupon in HTML or PDF format.

3. **Drug Search API**
   The Drug Search API allows clients to query the GoodRx drug database with strings to retrieve the best match possible. It can be used to correct user misspellings or to differentiate between different drug spellings.

4. **Fair Price API** *(Deprecated — use V2 Price Compare)*
   The Fair Price API allows clients to retrieve the maximum price that a consumer, with or without insurance, should pay for this drug at a local pharmacy. One caveat is that you cannot define the quantity desired, since GoodRx only calculates the Fair Price for the most common quantity prescribed (usually a 30-day supply).

5. **Low Price API** *(Deprecated — use V2 Price Compare)*
   The Low Price API allows clients to retrieve the lowest available price for a prescription medication from a predefined set of national chains and mail order pharmacies. The API uses its extensive dataset to select the most common forms and quantities if not provided, and includes generic or brand equivalents.

---

### Coverage & Integrations
GoodRx APIs power platforms such as prescription adherence apps, drug information resources, EHR and practice management software, digital health platforms, and medical reference apps. Nationwide pharmacy chains covered include Walmart, CVS, Walgreens, and RiteAid. In total, GoodRx covers 80% of US retail drug purchases.

---

### Provider Mode & Insurance Integration
GoodRx has added insurance coverage information to its drug cost estimation platform for providers (Provider Mode), making it the only platform for clinicians to compare insurance prices, cash prices, and manufacturer savings programs in one place.

When providers search for a drug on GoodRx's platform and verify their identity using their National Provider Identifier (NPI), they're prompted to enter the patient's name, date of birth, gender, and zip code. GoodRx has partnered with specialty pharmacy workflow company AssistRx on the benefits check, which pings its network of insurers and pharmacy benefit managers to find that patient's coverage information. The provider can then see how much that patient will pay for that drug under their insurance and compare it to other options.

---

### Rate Limiting & Authentication
The GoodRx API by default does not impose rate limiting on accounts. However, API usage is tracked and any abuse of the system will result in an account suspension and an inquiry into the high activity. The GoodRx API expects HTTP URL request parameters and returns JSON responses. All requests must include your API Key and the parameters must be signed using the provided shared private key.

---

### GoodRx & Medicare Part D (2025)
In 2025, Medicare Part D introduced key changes like a new $2,000 annual out-of-pocket cap and the elimination of the "donut hole." While GoodRx can still provide additional savings by offering lower drug prices at participating pharmacies, these discounts do not count toward your Medicare Part D spending threshold.

---

**🔗 To apply for a GoodRx API key**, visit [goodrx.com/developer/apply](https://www.goodrx.com/developer/apply). For full V2 documentation, see [goodrx.com/developer/v2-documentation](https://www.goodrx.com/developer/v2-documentation).
