     9→
    10→## Land Registry
    11→- Price Paid Data: free bulk CSV, every residential transaction since 1995, OGL
    12→- CCOD: ~3.5M corporate-owned titles, free, OGL, includes CH company numbers
    13→- OCOD: ~100K overseas-owned titles, free, OGL
    14→- Individual title registers: GBP 3/title, NO bulk redistribution allowed
    15→- National Polygon Dataset: GBP 4,500+/yr, restricted licence
    16→- Key enrichment: AVM, corporate portfolio mapping, area analytics
    17→
    18→## EPC Register
    19→- Free bulk download, ~20M certificates
    20→- Energy rating (A-G), floor area, wall type, heating, estimated costs
    21→- OGL, commercially redistributable
    22→- Cross-references with property transactions by address matching
    23→
    24→## Weather/Climate
    25→- Met Office DataPoint: free API, OGL, UK forecasts and observations
    26→- Met Office MIDAS Open: historic observations, free via CEDA archive
    27→- ERA5/Copernicus: free, global reanalysis 1940-present, hourly, commercial OK
    28→- NOAA: free, public domain (US government), global datasets
    29→- Open-Meteo: free for non-commercial, paid for commercial (from ~EUR 15/mo)
    30→- Key enrichment: location-specific interpolation, climate risk scoring
    31→
    32→## Other Valuable Sources (all OGL unless noted)
    33→- The Gazette: insolvency notices, winding-up petitions (OGL)
    34→- ICO Register: data controller registrations
    35→- FCA Register: regulated firms and individuals (API)
    36→- Charity Commission: ~170K charities, trustees, financials (API + bulk)
    37→- Ofsted: school/nursery ratings (API + bulk)
    38→- CQC: ~30K health/social care providers (API + bulk)
    39→- FHRS: ~500K food business ratings (API)
    40→- Census 2021: demographics down to output area (~300 people)
    41→- ONS Nomis: labour market data (API)
    42→- police.uk: crime data by location (API)
    43→- HMRC Trade: imports/exports by commodity/country
    44→- Planning applications: per-council, no national aggregation (scraping needed)
    45→- TfL/BODS: transport data (APIs, OGL)
    46→
    47→## Legal Framework
    48→- OGL v3 covers most UK government data, explicitly permits commercial use
    49→- GDPR applies to director/PSC personal data, use legitimate interest basis
    50→- UK database right (sui generis): cannot bulk-extract "substantial part" of someone else's DB
    51→- Building your own enriched database from primary sources is fine
    52→- Computer Misuse Act applies to unauthorized access, but public web pages generally OK
    53→- No specific UK anti-scraping statute

1→# Market Thesis: DataFetch (datafetch.ai)
     2→
     3→## Core Hypothesis
     4→
     5→AI agents are becoming the primary consumers of structured data APIs. The Machine Payments Protocol (mpp.dev) enables frictionless per-query purchasing without signup, API keys, or billing accounts. The first data providers to offer enriched public data via MPP will capture the emerging agent economy's data spend.
     6→
     7→The deeper thesis: REST endpoints are a transitional interface. The endgame is **intent-centric data environments**, where agents don't call APIs but write TypeScript programs against typed, intent-shaped interfaces, explore strategies for free against mock data, and commit to paid execution. This creates a fundamentally different relationship (the agent *works within* DataFetch, not *calls* DataFetch) and a compounding moat via the trajectory library.
     8→
     9→## The Opportunity
    10→
    11→### Supply Side: Free Public Data, Expensive to Use
    12→- UK government publishes vast datasets under OGL v3 (Open Government Licence), freely commercially redistributable
    13→- Raw data is free but fragmented across dozens of sources, inconsistent formats, no cross-referencing
    14→- Existing providers (Endole, Creditsafe, Beauhurst) package this data behind enterprise subscriptions ($5K-$100K/yr)
    15→- No existing provider offers per-query, agent-payable access
    16→
    17→### Demand Side: Agents Need Data Mid-Workflow
    18→- AI agents performing due diligence, lead qualification, property research, compliance checks need data on-the-fly
    19→- Current model: human signs up for subscription, configures API key, agent uses it. Friction-heavy, limits agent autonomy
    20→- MPP model: agent discovers endpoint via llms.txt, pays per-query via HTTP 402, gets data. Zero onboarding
    21→- The agent economy is growing rapidly, every major AI lab is shipping agent frameworks (Claude Computer Use, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK)
    22→
    23→### Why Now
    24→- MPP launched March 2026, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs
    25→- Submitted to IETF as formal internet standard (paymentauth.org)
    26→- Stripe integration means card payments work alongside crypto, same dashboard/settlement
    27→- Sub-cent transactions viable on Tempo chain ($0.001 tx fees, 0.5s finality)
    28→- First-mover window: mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed
    29→- UK OGL data is uniquely well-suited: permissive licensing, rich datasets, global demand for UK company/property data
    30→
    31→## Market Sizing
    32→
    33→### UK Business Data Market
    34→- Creditsafe (essentially a Companies House reseller at core): hundreds of millions GBP revenue
    35→- Dun & Bradstreet UK operations: substantial
    36→- Total UK business data market: estimated GBP 1-2 billion annually
    37→- Even niche vertical products (e.g., construction sector financial health): GBP 1-10M ARR
    38→
    39→### UK Property Data Market
    40→- UK proptech market: GBP 6+ billion
    41→- Property data specifically: multi-hundred-million-pound market
    42→- Landmark Information Group, LonRes, Dataloft, Hometrack all operate here
    43→
    44→### Adjacent Markets
    45→- Global weather data market: USD 3-4 billion
    46→- Sales intelligence (ZoomInfo, Apollo): USD 3+ billion
    47→- Location intelligence: USD 15+ billion globally
    48→
    49→### Our Addressable Slice
    50→- We're not replacing Creditsafe or ZoomInfo. We're serving the agent economy's per-query needs
    51→- Target: the long tail of queries that don't justify a subscription
    52→- If 1M agent queries/month at average $0.25/query = $250K MRR = $3M ARR
    53→- If 10M queries/month = $30M ARR
    54→- These are aspirational but directionally plausible given agent growth trajectory
    55→- Environment tier unlocks higher ARPU: complex analytical intents at $2-5 each, vs $0.05-1.00 for REST. An agent doing competitive analysis might spend $5 per intent but get $500 worth of analytical work done in one shot
    56→
    57→### The Trajectory Library (Compounding Moat)
    58→- Every agent that uses the environment tier contributes (anonymized) query patterns
    59→- Common patterns crystallize into optimized curated interfaces (cheaper, faster)
    60→- Over time, the most common analytical intents become deterministic workflows, near-zero marginal token spend
    61→- DataFetch evolves from "data API" to "library of proven analytical intelligence"
    62→- This is a data network effect: more agent usage -> better interfaces -> more agent usage
    63→- The trajectory library is time-based defensibility, a new entrant with the same idea starts with zero accumulated patterns
    64→
    65→## Competitive Landscape
    66→
    67→| Player | Model | Weakness for Agent Economy |
    68→|--------|-------|---------------------------|
    69→| Endole | Credit-based, GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Requires signup, API key, manual billing |
    70→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | $10K+ minimum, human sales process |
    71→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription $5K+ | Targets VCs/government, not agents |
    72→| OpenCorporates | API from $500/mo | Subscription-only, no per-query |
    73→| Companies House API | Free, rate-limited | Raw data only, no enrichment, 600 req/5 min |
    74→
    75→**Gap**: No one offers enriched UK public data with MPP-native per-query payment. The protocol is weeks old.
    76→
    77→**Deeper gap**: No data provider offers an intent-centric environment where agents can explore query strategies for free before paying. Every existing service charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. The mock-then-commit model (validated by PySyft in production at UN/national stats agencies) aligns cost with value in a way no competitor currently does.
    78→
    79→| Player | Could copy REST + MPP? | Could copy intent environment? |
    80→|--------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
    81→| Endole | Yes, if MPP grows | No, requires new interface paradigm + mock data infrastructure |
    82→| Creditsafe | Yes, but cultural mismatch | No, enterprise DNA incompatible with agent-native exploration |
    83→| OpenCorporates | Possible | Unlikely, data-only, no enrichment layer to power intent resolution |
    84→| LLM providers | Could build generic data agents | Lack domain-specific enrichment + trajectory library |
    85→| Snowflake/Databricks | Could build intent layers over warehouses | Sell infrastructure, not data products |
    86→
    87→## Key Assumptions (to be stress-tested)
    88→
    89→1. Agent data consumption will grow significantly in 2026-2027
    90→2. Per-query pricing is viable at $0.05-$2.00 for enriched public data
    91→3. Enrichment (scoring, cross-referencing, entity resolution) creates enough value to justify markup over free raw data
    92→4. MPP adoption will grow beyond early adopters
    93→5. First-mover advantage in the mpp.dev directory matters
    94→6. UK OGL data licensing permits our commercial model without legal risk
    95→7. A small team can build and maintain the data pipeline at acceptable cost
    96→8. The data refresh cadence we can achieve (daily/weekly) is sufficient for buyers
    97→9. Code-writing agents (Claude, Codex) will become the dominant agent archetype, making the TypeScript environment tier the primary interface within 12-18 months
    98→10. The mock-then-commit exploration model is sufficiently compelling to change agent data consumption patterns (validated by PySyft in adjacent domain, but untested for commercial data APIs)
    99→11. Intent-shaped interfaces (encoding domain knowledge) create meaningful value over schema-mirror typed APIs
   100→12. The trajectory library will compound fast enough to create defensibility before competitors can replicate the architecture
   101→
   102→## Risks
   103→
   104→- **MPP adoption risk**: Protocol is brand new, may not gain traction. Mitigation: also offer traditional API key access
   105→- **Data quality risk**: Enrichment algorithms may produce unreliable scores. Mitigation: start with simple, verifiable enrichments
   106→- **Competition risk**: Established players could add MPP support quickly. Mitigation: move fast, build data quality moat
   107→- **Regulatory risk**: GDPR for director personal data, database rights. Mitigation: legitimate interest basis, DPIA, suppression mechanism
   108→- **Unit economics risk**: Per-query revenue may not cover infrastructure costs at low volume. Mitigation: lean architecture (Cloudflare Workers, serverless)
   109→- **Environment adoption risk**: Code-writing agents may not adopt the TypeScript environment tier if REST is "good enough." Mitigation: REST remains Tier 1, environment is additive. The token economics argument (orders of magnitude cheaper for complex queries) creates strong pull for sophisticated agents
   110→- **Interface authoring risk**: Intent-shaped interfaces require deep domain knowledge to author well. Bad interfaces produce bad agent experiences. Mitigation: start with DataFetch-authored interfaces (Phase 1), evolve to community-proposed + AI-generated as usage patterns emerge
   111→- **Mock data fidelity risk**: If mock data distributions don't match real data well enough, agents' exploration results won't predict real execution outcomes. Mitigation: generate mocks from actual data distributions (not random), validate mock-to-real fidelity systematically
   112→

1→# Product Design: DataFetch, envrun.ai's First Proof-of-Concept Environment
     2→
     3→Status: APPROVED
     4→Generated by /office-hours + /autoplan on 2026-03-23
     5→
     6→## Vision
     7→
     8→DataFetch is the first proof-of-concept environment for envrun.ai. It demonstrates that agents performing complex data tasks inside a **repo-shaped environment** (typed folder of interfaces, tests, governance, mock data) outperform the same agents using CLIs or REST APIs.
     9→
    10→The innovation is not the data. It is the interaction model: agents work *within* DataFetch rather than *calling* it. Instead of teaching an agent a new CLI with unique verbs and flags, you mount a virtual folder of typed TypeScript interfaces. The agent navigates it like a local codebase, which is what it already knows how to do.
    11→
    12→DataFetch uses UK business and property intelligence as its domain, chosen for permissive licensing (OGL v3), rich cross-referenceable datasets, and complexity that rewards the environment model over flat REST calls.
    13→
    14→### Core Thesis
    15→
    16→Code agents navigating typed folder interfaces outperform the same agents using CLIs/APIs for complex data acquisition tasks. **This must be proven by benchmark before committing to build.**
    17→
    18→### Relationship to envrun.ai
    19→
    20→DataFetch is not a standalone product. It is the first environment built with envkit (envrun.ai's SDK), demonstrating the platform's value proposition with a real domain. The second PoC (an execution-based environment with workflow invariants) validates that the SDK generalizes beyond data.
    21→
    22→| DataFetch Concept | envrun.ai Equivalent |
    23→|---|---|
    24→| TypeScript intent-shaped interfaces | Module interfaces (outer rim) |
    25→| Mock-then-commit exploration | Branching + simulation |
    26→| Real execution (paid via MPP) | Merge to production with governance |
    27→| Governance (cost caps, rate limits) | Invariants + soft verifiers |
    28→| Trajectory convergence | Committed extensions/workflows |
    29→| Enrichable\<T\> (resolve on demand) | Inner rim opt-in access |
    30→| Provenance receipts | Traces |
    31→
    32→## Problem Statement
    33→
    34→Code agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) are excellent at navigating codebases: reading files, writing code, branching, testing. But when they need external services, they fall back to CLIs and APIs, each a unique DSL. `stripe customers list --limit 10` is different from `gh pr list --state open` is different from `kubectl get pods`. The agent has to learn each one. Error handling, output parsing, and state management differ for every tool.
    35→
    36→The workaround costs:
    37→- Agents spend tokens learning each CLI's syntax
    38→- Multi-step workflows require extensive glue code between tools
    39→- No free exploration of paywalled data (every API call costs money)
    40→- No branching (can't try 3 approaches in parallel)
    41→- No trajectory reuse (same glue code gets rewritten every session)
    42→
    43→### Demand Evidence
    44→
    45→First-principles thesis. No direct demand from external users.
    46→
    47→Founder observation from using OpenClaw: "Whenever agents have access to folder interfaces and can treat the project as local, even if they're not touching the core logic but they just understand the interfaces, they just seem to perform better than just giving them CLIs and MCPs or APIs."
    48→
    49→Supporting structural evidence:
    50→- Cloudflare demonstrated 99.9% token reduction with code-mode (Mar 2026)
    51→- Anthropic demonstrated 98.7% token reduction independently (Mar 2026)
    52→- Both converged on the same pattern: agents writing code against typed interfaces instead of calling tools one-at-a-time
    53→
    54→## The Interaction Model
    55→
    56→### Three Access Tiers (Long-Term Vision)
    57→
    58→Every data domain on DataFetch is accessible through three tiers. The PoC focuses on Tier 3 (environment-first), with Tier 1 endpoints as a secondary access path. Tier 2 is deferred.
    59→
    60→| Tier | Interface | Agent Requirement | Price Model |
    61→|------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
    62→| Tier 1: REST API | Standard endpoints (`GET /entity/:id/enriched`) | Any HTTP-capable agent | Per-endpoint MPP |
    63→| Tier 2: Natural Language Intent | Agent describes query in English, DataFetch translates | Any agent | Per-intent MPP (deferred) |
    64→| Tier 3: Code Environment | Agent navigates folder of typed interfaces, explores mock data, commits to paid execution | Code-writing agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) | Compute-based MPP (explore free, execute paid) |
    65→
    66→**PoC priority:** Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary (compatibility). Tier 2 deferred.
    67→
    68→### Intent-Shaped Interfaces
    69→
    70→Interfaces encode **domain intelligence**, not data schemas. The agent describes *what* it wants to know. The environment resolves *how*.
    71→
    72→**Bad (schema-mirror):**
    73→```typescript
    74→interface CompaniesTable {
    75→  getById(number: string): Company;
    76→  search(query: { name?: string; sic?: string[] }): Company[];
    77→}
    78→```
    79→
    80→**Good (intent-shaped):**
    81→```typescript
    82→interface MarketIntelligence {
    83→  findCompetitors(criteria: {
    84→    sector: string | string[];
    85→    backed_by?: string;
    86→    vintage?: { from?: number; to?: number };
    87→  }): Promise<CompanySet>;
    88→
    89→  enrichWithTeam(
    90→    companies: CompanySet,
    91→    dimensions: ('headcount' | 'leadership' | 'location_breakdown')[]
    92→  ): Promise<EnrichedCompanySet>;
    93→
    94→  rankBy(
    95→    companies: EnrichedCompanySet,
    96→    metric: 'growth_rate' | 'financial_health' | 'hiring_velocity'
    97→  ): Promise<RankedCompanySet>;
    98→}
    99→```
   100→
   101→The agent doesn't need to know that "data enrichment" maps to SIC codes 6201, 6202, 6311, or that "backed by Y Combinator" requires joining an investor table. The intent interface absorbs domain complexity.
   102→
   103→Over time, the agents' glue code (novel compositions of explore/purchase calls) gets mined to produce simpler, more intent-centric curated interfaces. The interface layer evolves from agent usage, not just author design.
   104→
   105→### The `Enrichable<T>` Abstraction
   106→
   107→Not all data dimensions are materialized upfront. Some are expensive to compute, some require cross-referencing, some are proprietary. The agent sees the full type surface and cost of each dimension, composes its intent without triggering resolution, and resolution happens only at purchase time.
   108→
   109→```typescript
   110→// Enrichable<T>: a dimension that exists but is not materialized.
   111→// The agent sees the type surface and cost, but resolution requires purchase().
   112→type Enrichable<T> = {
   113→  available: true;
   114→  cost: { usd: number; description: string };
   115→  resolve: () => Promise<T>;  // Only callable inside purchase() context
   116→};
   117→
   118→type Company = {
   119→  number: string;
   120→  name: string;
   121→  status: 'active' | 'dissolved' | 'liquidation';
   122→  sic_codes: string[];
   123→  incorporated: Date;
   124→  // Always available (free via explore):
   125→  officers_count: number;
   126→  // Enrichable (costs money, resolved via purchase):
   127→  financials?: Enrichable<FinancialProfile>;
   128→  risk_score?: Enrichable<number>;
   129→  director_network?: Enrichable<DirectorGraph>;
   130→};
   131→```
   132→
   133→In envrun.ai terms, always-available fields are the **outer rim** (public interface). Enrichable dimensions are the **inner rim** (opt-in, paid access). Governance controls which enrichments an agent can request and at what cost.
   134→
   135→### Mock-Then-Commit: Explore Before You Pay
   136→
   137→Every other data API charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. DataFetch inverts this:
   138→
   139→1. Agent enters the environment folder, reads TypeScript interfaces and AGENTS.md
   140→2. Mock data has identical schemas, realistic distributions, but synthetic values
   141→3. Agent branches (`git branch`) to try different query compositions in parallel (free, instant)
   142→4. Agent compares result shape and cardinality across branches
   143→5. Agent commits the winning approach via `purchase()` for real execution (paid via MPP)
   144→6. Real data returned + provenance receipt
   145→
   146→This pattern maps directly to envrun.ai's branching + simulation model: branch = isolated copy of state, merge = governance-checked commit to production.
   147→
   148→### Provenance: The Trust Layer
   149→
   150→Every real execution (purchase) returns a provenance receipt:
   151→- What data sources were used (named, versioned)
   152→- What filters and joins were applied
   153→- Row counts before and after filtering
   154→- Whether the result is reproducible (and until when)
   155→- Drill-down availability and cost for underlying data
   156→- Itemized pricing breakdown
   157→
   158→The agent (or its human principal) can verify the result came from real, identified data and that the computation is auditable. In envrun.ai terms, this is the **trace** for the committed trajectory.
   159→
   160→### The Convergence Play (Future Vision)
   161→
   162→LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time:
   163→
   164→1. First time an agent needs a particular analytical pattern, it writes the intent from scratch
   165→2. That trajectory gets saved as a reusable function (envrun.ai: committed extension)
   166→3. Next time any agent needs similar intelligence, the trajectory runs deterministically
   167→4. Over time, common intents become optimized curated interfaces, near-zero marginal token s

1→# Product Design: DataFetch, envrun.ai's First Proof-of-Concept Environment
     2→
     3→Status: APPROVED
     4→Generated by /office-hours + /autoplan on 2026-03-23
     5→
     6→## Vision
     7→
     8→DataFetch is the first proof-of-concept environment for envrun.ai. It demonstrates that agents performing complex data tasks inside a **repo-shaped environment** (typed folder of interfaces, tests, governance, mock data) outperform the same agents using CLIs or REST APIs.
     9→
    10→The innovation is not the data. It is the interaction model: agents work *within* DataFetch rather than *calling* it. Instead of teaching an agent a new CLI with unique verbs and flags, you mount a virtual folder of typed TypeScript interfaces. The agent navigates it like a local codebase, which is what it already knows how to do.
    11→
    12→DataFetch uses UK business and property intelligence as its domain, chosen for permissive licensing (OGL v3), rich cross-referenceable datasets, and complexity that rewards the environment model over flat REST calls.
    13→
    14→### Core Thesis
    15→
    16→Code agents navigating typed folder interfaces outperform the same agents using CLIs/APIs for complex data acquisition tasks. **This must be proven by benchmark before committing to build.**
    17→
    18→### Relationship to envrun.ai
    19→
    20→DataFetch is not a standalone product. It is the first environment built with envkit (envrun.ai's SDK), demonstrating the platform's value proposition with a real domain. The second PoC (an execution-based environment with workflow invariants) validates that the SDK generalizes beyond data.
    21→
    22→| DataFetch Concept | envrun.ai Equivalent |
    23→|---|---|
    24→| TypeScript intent-shaped interfaces | Module interfaces (outer rim) |
    25→| Mock-then-commit exploration | Branching + simulation |
    26→| Real execution (paid via MPP) | Merge to production with governance |
    27→| Governance (cost caps, rate limits) | Invariants + soft verifiers |
    28→| Trajectory convergence | Committed extensions/workflows |
    29→| Enrichable\<T\> (resolve on demand) | Inner rim opt-in access |
    30→| Provenance receipts | Traces |
    31→
    32→## Problem Statement
    33→
    34→Code agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) are excellent at navigating codebases: reading files, writing code, branching, testing. But when they need external services, they fall back to CLIs and APIs, each a unique DSL. `stripe customers list --limit 10` is different from `gh pr list --state open` is different from `kubectl get pods`. The agent has to learn each one. Error handling, output parsing, and state management differ for every tool.
    35→
    36→The workaround costs:
    37→- Agents spend tokens learning each CLI's syntax
    38→- Multi-step workflows require extensive glue code between tools
    39→- No free exploration of paywalled data (every API call costs money)
    40→- No branching (can't try 3 approaches in parallel)
    41→- No trajectory reuse (same glue code gets rewritten every session)
    42→
    43→### Demand Evidence
    44→
    45→First-principles thesis. No direct demand from external users.
    46→
    47→Founder observation from using OpenClaw: "Whenever agents have access to folder interfaces and can treat the project as local, even if they're not touching the core logic but they just understand the interfaces, they just seem to perform better than just giving them CLIs and MCPs or APIs."
    48→
    49→Supporting structural evidence:
    50→- Cloudflare demonstrated 99.9% token reduction with code-mode (Mar 2026)
    51→- Anthropic demonstrated 98.7% token reduction independently (Mar 2026)
    52→- Both converged on the same pattern: agents writing code against typed interfaces instead of calling tools one-at-a-time
    53→
    54→## The Interaction Model
    55→
    56→### Three Access Tiers (Long-Term Vision)
    57→
    58→Every data domain on DataFetch is accessible through three tiers. The PoC focuses on Tier 3 (environment-first), with Tier 1 endpoints as a secondary access path. Tier 2 is deferred.
    59→
    60→| Tier | Interface | Agent Requirement | Price Model |
    61→|------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
    62→| Tier 1: REST API | Standard endpoints (`GET /entity/:id/enriched`) | Any HTTP-capable agent | Per-endpoint MPP |
    63→| Tier 2: Natural Language Intent | Agent describes query in English, DataFetch translates | Any agent | Per-intent MPP (deferred) |
    64→| Tier 3: Code Environment | Agent navigates folder of typed interfaces, explores mock data, commits to paid execution | Code-writing agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) | Compute-based MPP (explore free, execute paid) |
    65→
    66→**PoC priority:** Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary (compatibility). Tier 2 deferred.
    67→
    68→### Intent-Shaped Interfaces
    69→
    70→Interfaces encode **domain intelligence**, not data schemas

    81→
    82→Both layers share the same data ingestion, enrichment pipeline, and production store. The environment layer adds: TypeScript interface modules, mock data generation, intent solver, and provenance receipt generation.
    83→
    84→## Data Ingestion
    85→
    86→### Companies House
    87→
    88→**Bulk Data (daily):**
    89→- Source: Companies House bulk data product (CSV/JSON)
    90→- Contains: ~5M active companies, officers, PSCs, charges, filing history
    91→- Refresh: Daily snapshot download via Companies House data products page
    92→- Storage: Raw files to S3, parsed records to PostgreSQL
    93→
    94→**Streaming API (near-realtime):**
    95→- Source: Companies House streaming API
    96→- Events: New filings, company updates, officer appointments/resignations
    97→- Consumer: Long-running process that applies deltas to production DB
    98→- Latency: Minutes from filing to availability
    99→
   100→**Accounts Data (iXBRL):**
   101→- Source: Companies House document API
   102→- Format: iXBRL (inline XBRL tagged HTML)
   103→- Extraction: Parse XBRL tags to extract: revenue, profit/loss, total assets, total liabilities, net assets, employee count
   104→- Challenge: Not all companies file digitally. Micro-entities file minimal data. Only ~40% of companies file accounts with useful financial detail
   105→- Storage: Extracted financial metrics in dedicated table, linked to company record
   106→
   107→### Land Registry
   108→
   109→**Price Paid Data (monthly):**
   110→- Source: gov.uk bulk download (CSV)
   111→- Contains: Every residential transaction in England & Wales since 1995 (~28M records)
   112→- Fields: Price, date, postcode, property type, tenure, new/old, address
   113→- Refresh: Monthly update file (incremental)
   114→
   115→**CCOD/OCOD (quarterly):**
   116→- Source: gov.uk bulk download
   117→- CCOD: ~3.5M titles owned by UK companies (title number, tenure, address, company, CH number, price paid)
   118→- OCOD: ~100K titles owned by overseas entities
   119→- Cross-reference: CCOD company numbers link directly to Companies House
   120→
   121→**EPC Register (monthly):**
   122→- Source: Open Data Communities bulk download
   123→- Contains: Energy Performance Certificates for ~20M properties
   124→- Fields: Address, EPC rating (A-G), floor area, wall type, heating type, estimated energy cost
   125→- Cross-reference: Address matching to Land Registry records
   126→
   127→### Additional Sources
   128→
   129→| Source | Format | Refresh | Records |
   130→|--------|--------|---------|---------|
   131→| The Gazette | RSS/API | Daily | Insolvency notices, winding-up petitions |
   132→| ICO Register | Bulk download | Monthly | Data controller registrations |
   133→| FCA Register | API | Daily | Regulated firms and individuals |
   134→| Charity Commission | API + bulk | Monthly | ~170K registered charities |
   135→| Ofsted | API + bulk | Monthly | School/nursery inspection ratings |
   136→| FHRS | API | Daily | ~500K food business ratings |
   137→| Census 2021 | Bulk download | Static | Demographics by output area |
   138→| ONS Nomis | API | Monthly | Employment, earnings by area |
   139→| police.uk | API | Monthly | Crime data by location |
   140→
   141→## Enrichment Pipeline
   142→
   143→### Entity Resolution
   144→
   145→**Company matching:**
   146→- Primary key: Companies House number (deterministic)
   147→- Fuzzy matching for sources without CH number: company name + postcode + SIC code
   148→
   149→**Director matching (cross-company):**
   150→- Match on: surname + partial DOB (month/year) + forename initial
   151→- Confirm with: nationality, country of residence, co-director patterns
   152→- Output: Director ID that links across all their appointments
   153→- Challenge: Common names produce false positives. Conservative matching preferred (miss some links rather than create false ones)
   154→
   155→**Address matching (property to company):**
   156→- Normalize addresses using OS AddressBase (if licensed) or PAF-free alternatives
   157→- Match Land Registry addresses to Companies House registered addresses and EPC addresses
   158→- Challenge: Address formatting varies wildly across sources. "Flat 2, 10 High St" vs "10 HIGH STREET FLAT 2" vs "Second Floor, 10 High Street"
   159→

   161→
   162→**Financial Health Score (0-100):**
   163→
   164→Inputs:
   165→- Latest accounts: current ratio, debt/equity, net assets trend, revenue growth (where available)
   166→- Filing behaviour: days late on average, overdue filings count
   167→- Charges: active charges count, recent charge activity
   168→- Gazette: proximity to insolvency notices, winding-up petitions
   169→- Company age and status
   170→
   171→Weighting: Accounts data (40%), filing behaviour (25%), charges (15%), gazette (15%), age (5%)

   173→Where accounts data is unavailable (micro-entities, dormant companies), score shifts to filing behaviour and age-based model.

   176→- Flag: Director of recently dissolved company (within 5 years) now directing a new company
   177→- Additional signals: Same registered address, similar SIC code, similar company name
   178→- Scoring: Number of dissolved company links, recency, similarity of new com

1→# Appendix: Reference Data & Market Context
     2→
     3→## A. MPP Protocol Reference
     4→
     5→### What is MPP?
     6→Machine Payments Protocol, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs (March 2026). An HTTP authentication scheme that standardizes the 402 Payment Required status code.
     7→
     8→### Core Flow
     9→1. Client requests resource -> `GET /endpoint`
    10→2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)
    11→3. Client pays (signs blockchain tx, provides card token, etc.)
    12→4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
    13→5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header
    14→
    15→### Transaction Modes
    16→- **Charge (one-time):** Immediate settlement per request. Good for discrete API calls
    17→- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency
    18→
    19→### SDKs
    20→| Language | Package | Install |
    21→|----------|---------|---------|
    22→| TypeScript | mppx | npm install mppx |
    23→| Python | pympp | pip install pympp |
    24→| Rust | mpp-rs | cargo add mpp |
    25→
    26→### Key Resources
    27→- Protocol overview: mpp.dev/overview
    28→- Server quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/server
    29→- Agent quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/agent
    30→- IETF spec: paymentauth.org
    31→- Stripe blog: stripe.com/blog/machine-payments-protocol
    32→
    33→## B. UK Open Government Licence (OGL v3) Summary
    34→
    35→**Permits:** Copy, publish, distribute, transmit, adapt, exploit commercially and non-commercially
    36→**Requires:** Acknowledge the source, provide link to licence
    37→**Does NOT require:** Payment, registration, or permission
    38→
    39→### OGL-Covered Datasets Used
    40→- Companies House basic company data
    41→- Land Registry Price Paid Data
    42→- Land Registry CCOD/OCOD
    43→- EPC Register
    44→- Charity Commission register
    45→- CQC provider data
    46→- FHRS food hygiene ratings
    47→- Ofsted inspection data
    48→- Census / ONS statistical data
    49→- The Gazette (insolvency notices)
    50→- Met Office DataPoint
    51→- police.uk crime data
    52→- HMRC trade statistics
    53→
    54→### NOT OGL (require separate licensing)
    55→- Ordnance Survey premium products (AddressBase, MasterMap)
    56→- Royal Mail PAF (postcode/address data)
    57→- Land Registry National Polygon Dataset (GBP 4,500+/yr)
    58→- Individual Land Registry title registers (GBP 3/title, no bulk redistribution)
    59→
    60→## C. Competitor Pricing Reference
    61→
    62→### UK Company Data
    63→
    64→| Provider | Model | Price Point | Enrichment Level |

Here is the complete audit.

---

## Research Audit: Background Briefs vs. Core Documents

### GAPS

**GAP-1: MPP security concerns not addressed anywhere in core docs**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (01-mpp-protocol.md, line 47): "Security concerns: prompt injection could cause misleading purchases"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (Rate Limiting & Abuse Prevention section, line 258-263) and `product_design.md` (Error Handling section, line 363-368)
- **Issue:** The core docs discuss rate limiting and error codes but never address the prompt injection attack vector, where a malicious data response or injected content could trick an agent into making purchases it did not intend. For a product whose entire model is autonomous agent spending, this is a critical gap.
- **Suggestion:** Add a "Security Considerations" section to `spec.md` covering: prompt injection mitigation (e.g., sandboxed payment confirmation, human-in-the-loop approval above thresholds), and reference the concern raised in HN reception of MPP.

**GAP-2: MPP missing B2B primitives (invoices, refunds, bills of lading)**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (line 48): "Missing B2B primitives: no invoices, refunds, or bills of lading"
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (Risks section, line 102-111) and `product_design.md` (Payment Flow, line 247-257)
- **Issue:** None of the core docs acknowledge that MPP currently lacks refund or invoicing mechanisms. For compliance/due-diligence agents (Persona 4) operating in regulated environments, the inability to issue refunds or generate invoices is a real limitation. The product design's error handling notes "500: no charge" but never addresses what happens if payment succeeds and the data returned is wrong or incomplete.
- **Suggestion:** Add to Risks in `market_thesis.md`: "MPP protocol maturity risk: MPP currently lacks B2B primitives (invoices, refunds). Enterprise/compliance buyers may require these. Mitigation: implement application-level credit/refund mechanism, generate invoices from payment receipts."

**GAP-3: Regulation E / consumer banking concerns unmentioned**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (line 49): "Open question on consumer banking regulation (Regulation E)"
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (Risks section) and `appendix.md` (GDPR Compliance Plan, section F)
- **Issue:** The appendix has a thorough GDPR section but nothing on payment regulation. If agents spend on behalf of consumers (or even businesses), Regulation E and its UK equivalents (PSR 2017) could apply. This is especially relevant given the "no accounts, no signup" model.
- **Suggestion:** Add a brief note under Risks or a new Appendix section on payment regulation considerations.

**GAP-4: Competing/adjacent payment protocols not discussed**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (lines 52-55): x402 (blockchain payments), L402 (Bitcoin Lightning), ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol, also from Stripe)
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (entire doc) and `appendix.md` (Section A, MPP Protocol Reference)
- **Issue:** The core docs treat MPP as the only protocol. ACP is particularly notable since it is also from Stripe and could compete for the same agent commerce space. The market thesis should acknowledge protocol risk more concretely by naming alternatives.
- **Suggestion:** In `market_thesis.md` Risks section, expand "MPP adoption risk" to mention x402, L402, and ACP by name. In `appendix.md` Section A, add a brief "Adjacent Protocols" subsection.

**GAP-5: MPP Pull vs Push submission modes not reflected in spec**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (lines 21-24): Pull mode (client signs, server broadcasts) vs Push mode (client broadcasts, sends tx hash)
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (MPP Integration section, lines 204-236)
- **Issue:** The spec shows a single integration pattern but does not discuss which submission mode DataFetch will use, or whether to support both. This has implications for latency, security, and transaction finality.
- **Suggestion:** Add a brief note to `spec.md` MPP Integration section specifying that DataFetch uses Pull mode (simpler, server controls broadcast) with a note on future Push mode support.

**GAP-6: Land Registry individual title register restrictions**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 14): "Individual title registers: GBP 3/title, NO bulk redistribution allowed"
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Tier 1 Endpoints, line 280: `GET /property/address/:id` at GBP 0.50) and `appendix.md` (Section B, line 57-58 mentions it but only in the "NOT OGL" list)
- **Issue:** The product design prices property address lookups at GBP 0.50 and includes "ownership type" in the response. If this data comes from individual title registers, the "no bulk redistribution" restriction means DataFetch cannot pre-fetch and cache these. Each lookup would cost GBP 3 from Land Registry alone, making GBP 0.50 pricing a loss. The property corporate portfolio endpoint (GBP 1.00) using CCOD is fine (OGL), but individual residential titles are legally distinct.
- **Suggestion:** In `product_design.md`, add a footnote to the `/property/address/:id` endpoint clarifying which data sources it uses and confirming it does NOT rely on individual title registers (or adjust pricing if it does). In `spec.md`, address this in the Data Ingestion section.

**GAP-7: National Polygon Dataset licensing cost**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 15): "National Polygon Dataset: GBP 4,500+/yr, restricted licence"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (Infrastructure Cost Estimate, lines 265-276)
- **Issue:** If any property intelligence features require polygon/boundary data, the GBP 4,500+/yr licensing cost is not reflected in infrastructure estimates. The current estimate is $60-220/month.
- **Suggestion:** Add a note in `spec.md` cost estimate that polygon/boundary data would require separate licensing at GBP 4,500+/yr if needed for area profile features.

**GAP-8: Weather and climate data sources entirely absent from core docs**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (lines 25-30): Met Office DataPoint, ERA5/Copernicus, NOAA, Open-Meteo
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (Adjacent Markets, line 45: "Global weather data market: USD 3-4 billion") and `product_design.md` (Future Domains, line 303: "Climate & ESG Risk")
- **Issue:** The market thesis mentions the weather data market as an adjacent opportunity and the product design lists "Climate & ESG Risk" as a future domain, but no core doc incorporates the specific free weather/climate data sources identified in the research. The appendix lists "Met Office DataPoint" under OGL datasets but the spec has no weather data ingestion plan.
- **Suggestion:** When the Climate & ESG domain is developed, the spec should reference the specific sources from Brief 02. For now, add a brief note to the Future Domains table in `product_design.md` mentioning the available free sources (Met Office, ERA5, NOAA).

**GAP-9: Planning application data gap acknowledged in research but not in spec**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 44): "Planning applications: per-council, no national aggregation (scraping needed)"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (Data Ingestion, Additional Sources table, lines 129-139) and `product_design.md` (Data Sources, line 292)
- **Issue:** The spec lists data sources like The Gazette and FCA Register but omits planning applications entirely. The product design mentions nothing about it. Yet the appendix expansion path (Section G, line 214) lists "Planning Pipeline" as a Phase 3 addition. The research brief flags this requires scraping individual council sites, which is significantly harder than the other data sources.
- **Suggestion:** Add planning applications to the spec's Additional Sources table with a note: "Per-council, no national API, requires scraping. Deferred to Phase 3+." This manages expectations about the Phase 3 expansion path.

**GAP-10: HMRC Trade data mentioned in research but absent from spec**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 43): "HMRC Trade: imports/exports by commodity/country"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (Data Ingestion section) and `appendix.md` (Section B, line 52 mentions it in the OGL list)
- **Issue:** The appendix acknowledges HMRC trade data as OGL-covered but the spec has no ingestion plan for it. This is relevant to the "Global Trade Intelligence" future domain listed in `product_design.md`.

**GAP-11: TfL/BODS transport data absent from core docs**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 45): "TfL/BODS: transport data (APIs, OGL)"
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Data Sources, line 291-295) and `spec.md` (Additional Sources)
- **Issue:** Transport data could enrich area profiles (the `/area/:postcode/profile` endpoint promises "transport" data per `product_design.md` line 282) but no transport data source is listed in the spec's ingestion plan.
- **Suggestion:** Add TfL/BODS to the spec's Additional Sources table, or remove "transport" from the area profile endpoint description if it is not planned.

**GAP-12: UK database right (sui generis) not addressed**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (lines 50-51): "UK database right: cannot bulk-extract 'substantial part' of someone else's DB. Building your own enriched database from primary sources is fine."
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (Risks, line 107: only mentions GDPR and "database rights" without specifics) and `appendix.md` (Section F: GDPR only)
- **Issue:** The market thesis mentions "database rights" in passing but never explains the sui generis database right or why DataFetch's approach (building from primary government sources) is legally safe. This is an important legal distinction, the research brief explicitly clarifies that building your own enriched database from primary sources is fine.
- **Suggestion:** Add to `appendix.md` Section F (or new Section H): "UK Database Right: The sui generis database right prevents bulk extraction of a 'substantial part' of another party's database. DataFetch builds its own database from primary government sources (Companies House, Land Registry, etc.), which is legally permissible. We do not extract from competitors' databases."

---

### CONTRADICTIONS

**CONTRADICTION-1: Spec Phase numbering vs Product Design Phase numbering**
- **Source:** `spec.md` line 5: "Phase 1: REST API Layer" and line 305: "Phase 4: Intent-Centric Environment Layer"
- **vs.** `product_design.md` lines 175-218: Phase 1 = Thesis Validation (benchmark), Phase 2 = DataFetch PoC + SDK, Phase 3 = Second PoC
- **Issue:** The spec describes four phases where Phase 1 is REST and Phase 4 is the environment layer. The product design describes three phases where Phase 1 is a benchmark with the environment folder. These are fundamentally different roadmaps. The product design explicitly says "PoC priority: Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary" (line 66), while the spec's architecture leads with REST as Phase 1.
- **Suggestion:** Align the spec to the product design's phasing, since the product design is marked "APPROVED" and was generated more recently. The spec's Phase 1 (REST) should be relabeled or reordered to match the product design's environment-first approach.

**CONTRADICTION-2: Payment method specificity**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (line 15): MPP is "Payment-method agnostic: stablecoins (Tempo), cards (Stripe), Lightning"
- **vs.** `spec.md` lines 206-221: The MPP integration code only configures Tempo (stablecoin) as the payment method
- **Issue:** The spec implementation shows only `tempo()` as the payment method, but the market thesis (line 27) says "Stripe integration means card payments work alongside crypto." The spec should at minimum note that Stripe card payments will be supported, not just Tempo stablecoins.
- **Suggestion:** Update the spec's MPP integration example to show multiple payment methods, or add a comment noting that card payments via Stripe will be added.

**CONTRADICTION-3: Companies House rate limit**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 4): "Free REST API (600 req/5 min)"
- **vs.** `market_thesis.md` (line 73): "600 req/5 min" (correct)
- **Note:** These actually agree. No contradiction here, just confirming consistency.

---

### STALE INFO

**STALE-1: "Protocol is weeks old" may need updating**
- **Source:** `market_thesis.md` (line 75): "The protocol is weeks old"
- **Context:** Brief 01 (line 5): MPP launched March 2026. The product design header says the date is 2026-03-23.
- **Issue:** If these documents are maintained over time, this phrase will become inaccurate. It is currently accurate (launched early March, current date late March), but it is phrased in a way that will rot.
- **Suggestion:** Replace with "The protocol launched in March 2026" for durability.

**STALE-2: mpp.dev services directory description**
- **Source:** `market_thesis.md` (line 28): "mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed"
- **Context:** Brief 01 (lines 37-41) lists at least 5 services already on MPP (Browserbase, PostalForm, Stripe Climate, Quick Intel, plus DataFetch would be added). The directory is growing.
- **Issue:** "Nearly empty" and "handful" are time-sensitive claims. As the directory grows, this characterization will become misleading.
- **Suggestion:** Change to "mpp.dev/services directory has fewer than 10 services listed as of March 2026" for precision.

---

### MISSED OPPORTUNITIES

**MISSED-1: MPP Session mode for streaming use cases**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (lines 18-19): "Session: streaming payment channel, sub-cent costs"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (MPP Integration) and `product_design.md` (Payment Flow)
- **Opportunity:** The core docs only discuss the "Charge" (one-time) transaction mode. The "Session" mode enables streaming payment channels with sub-cent costs, which could be ideal for the environment tier. An agent exploring and purchasing multiple enrichments in a single analytical session could use a Session channel instead of paying per-Charge for each `purchase()` call. This would reduce payment overhead and enable true sub-cent micro-transactions for individual enrichment dimensions.
- **Suggestion:** Add Session mode as a future optimization for the environment tier in `product_design.md` Pricing Philosophy or `spec.md` MPP Integration.

**MISSED-2: MCP transport support for agent discoverability**
- **Source:** Brief 01 (line 34): "MCP transport support for JSON-RPC tool calls"
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Agent Discoverability, lines 323-351)
- **Opportunity:** The product design mentions llms.txt and mpp.dev directory for discoverability but omits MCP (Model Context Protocol) as a transport. Given that Claude Code, OpenClaw, and other code agents already use MCP for tool discovery, exposing DataFetch as an MCP tool server would be a natural discoverability path alongside llms.txt. This is especially relevant since the product design targets exactly these agents.
- **Suggestion:** Add MCP server as a third discoverability mechanism in the Agent Discoverability section.

**MISSED-3: Competitor enrichment specifics from research brief**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 8): "Key enrichment: financial scoring from iXBRL, director networks, filing risk signals, UBO chains, phoenix detection"
- **Affected doc:** `market_thesis.md` (Competitive Landscape, lines 66-84)
- **Opportunity:** The market thesis lists competitors and their weaknesses for agents but does not detail what enrichments competitors actually offer. The research brief identifies the specific enrichments that make companies like Endole and Creditsafe valuable. The competitive landscape table could be strengthened by noting which enrichments DataFetch matches or exceeds.
- **Suggestion:** Add an "Enrichment Parity" column to the competitive landscape table showing which enrichments each competitor offers vs. DataFetch.

**MISSED-4: EPC data as a differentiator for property intelligence**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (lines 18-22): ~20M EPC certificates with energy rating, floor area, wall type, heating, estimated costs, commercially redistributable
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Tier 1 Endpoints, line 280: `/property/address/:id` returns "EPC rating")
- **Opportunity:** EPC data is mentioned briefly but undervalued. With growing ESG/climate regulation, EPC ratings are increasingly required for property transactions, mortgage lending decisions, and corporate portfolio assessment. The product design could call out EPC-based enrichment as a specific differentiator, especially for the Climate & ESG Risk future domain. Cross-referencing EPC with CCOD (corporate-owned properties) could reveal corporate portfolio energy efficiency scores, a novel enrichment no competitor offers.
- **Suggestion:** Add a "Corporate Portfolio Energy Score" enrichment to the property intelligence tier, computed from EPC ratings across a company's CCOD-listed properties.

**MISSED-5: The Gazette for real-time risk signals**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 33): "The Gazette: insolvency notices, winding-up petitions (OGL)"
- **Affected doc:** `spec.md` (Financial Health Score Methodology uses Gazette data, lines 159-163) but `product_design.md` (Tier 1 Endpoints) does not surface Gazette signals directly
- **Opportunity:** Gazette data is used as an input to the financial health score but is not exposed as a standalone signal. A real-time "Gazette Alert" enrichment (has this company appeared in The Gazette in the last 30/90/365 days, and for what?) would be valuable for compliance agents (Persona 4) who need to know about winding-up petitions immediately, not mediated through a composite score.
- **Suggestion:** Consider adding a `gazette_alerts` field to the enriched company endpoint or as an `Enrichable<T>` dimension.

**MISSED-6: FCA Register for regulated entity verification**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 35): "FCA Register: regulated firms and individuals (API)"
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Data Sources, line 293 lists it) and `spec.md` (Additional Sources, line 133)
- **Opportunity:** The FCA Register is listed as a data source but not surfaced in any specific endpoint or enrichment. For compliance agents (Persona 4), knowing whether a company or its directors are FCA-regulated is a critical check. This could be a high-value `Enrichable<T>` dimension: "Is this company or any of its directors FCA-registered? What permissions do they hold?"
- **Suggestion:** Add FCA regulation status as an enrichment dimension on the company risk report endpoint.

**MISSED-7: Open-Meteo commercial pricing model as a template**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (line 29): "Open-Meteo: free for non-commercial, paid for commercial (from ~EUR 15/mo)"
- **Affected doc:** `product_design.md` (Pricing Philosophy, lines 353-358)
- **Opportunity:** Open-Meteo's model (free for non-commercial, paid for commercial) is an interesting precedent for the DataFetch pricing philosophy. While DataFetch uses per-query MPP pricing, offering a free tier for non-commercial/research use could drive adoption and trajectory library growth. Agents in development/testing would generate usage patterns without payment, feeding the convergence play.
- **Suggestion:** Consider whether a free tier for non-commercial agents (limited queries, watermarked data) could accelerate trajectory library growth. Note this in the Pricing Philosophy section as a future consideration.

**MISSED-8: Computer Misuse Act and scraping legal clarity**
- **Source:** Brief 02 (lines 52-53): "Computer Misuse Act applies to unauthorized access, but public web pages generally OK. No specific UK anti-scraping statute."
- **Affected doc:** `appendix.md` (Section F, GDPR only) and `spec.md` (Data Ingestion mentions "Scrapers (planning portals)" at line 13)
- **Opportunity:** The spec explicitly mentions scraping planning portals but the legal appendix says nothing about scraping legality. The research brief provides the legal framework (Computer Misuse Act, no anti-scraping statute, public pages generally OK). This should be documented to derisk the planned scraping work.
- **Suggestion:** Add scraping legal considerations to `appendix.md`, referencing the Computer Misuse Act and noting that public web page scraping for planning data is legally permissible under current UK law.

     2→
     3→## Successful Companies Built on Public Data
     4→
     5→### Company/Business Data
     6→- Clearbit (acquired by HubSpot ~$150M): email/domain enrichment, $0.05-0.25/record
     7→- ZoomInfo ($6B+ revenue): contact + company data, enterprise $15K-100K+/yr
     8→- Apollo.io: aggressive freemium, $0.01-0.05/record, disrupted ZoomInfo pricing
     9→- OpenCorporates: 200+ registries normalized, API from $500/mo
    10→
    11→### UK-Specific
    12→- Endole: Companies House enrichment, GBP 0.25-0.80/report, pay-as-you-go
    13→- DueDil (acquired by Creditsafe): compliance/KYB, GBP 0.50-2.00/check
    14→- Beauhurst: high-growth company intelligence, GBP 5K-30K/yr subscriptions
    15→- Creditsafe: enterprise credit scoring, hundreds of millions GBP revenue
    16→
    17→### Other Verticals
    18→- BuiltWith: tech stack detection, $295-995/mo, ~$0.10-0.50/lead
    19→- SimilarWeb (~$200M ARR): web traffic estimation, $125+/mo
    20→- Crunchbase: startup/funding data, $49/mo to $49K/yr API
    21→
    22→## Pricing Models That Work
    23→
    24→### Per-Query Pricing Bands
    25→| Price | Use Case | Examples |
    26→|-------|----------|---------|
    27→| $0.001-0.01 | High-volume, low-enrichment | Email validation, basic lookups |
    28→| $0.01-0.10 | Medium enrichment | Company profiles, basic financials |
    29→| $0.10-0.50 | Rich enrichment | Full reports, multi-source |
    30→| $0.50-2.00 | Compliance/regulatory | KYB, AML screening |
    31→| $2.00-10.00 | Deep investigative | Full director history, risk analysis |
    32→
    33→### Credit-Based Systems
    34→- Most common for data products
    35→- Psychological benefit: spending "5 credits" vs "$0.50"
    36→- Variable pricing per endpoint without complex billing
    37→- Pre-purchase drives upfront revenue
    38→- Expiry (30-365 days) drives recurring purchases
    39→
    40→### Key Pricing Principle
    41→Price on decision value, not production cost. A GBP 0.50 risk score preventing a GBP 50K bad debt is trivially justified. Same data sold as "public records lookup" only commands GBP 0.05.
    42→
    43→## High-Value Enrichment Patterns
    44→
    45→1. **Cross-referencing**: Combining 3-5 public datasets creates proprietary insights. Each additional source adds disproportionate value
    46→2. **Entity resolution**: Linking "J Smith" across companies. Hardest and most valuable enrichment
    47→3. **Scoring/classification**: Financial health, risk, growth signals. The defensible moat
    48→4. **Historical tracking**: Change detection, trend analysis. Best as monitoring subscriptions
    49→5. **NLP extraction**: Structured data from unstructured filings (PDFs, iXBRL). Transforms free PDFs into valuable structured data
    50→6. **Geocoding/spatial**: Address normalization, proximity analysis, area profiling
    51→
    52→## Competitive Moat
    53→- The data is public, so raw data is not the moat
    54→- Moat is: enrichment quality + freshness + cross-referencing + API convenience + MPP-native access
    55→- Network effects possible via monitoring (more customers = better signal on what data to prioritize refreshing)
    56→
    57→## Unit Economics Sweet Spot
    58→- GBP 0.10-1.00 per enriched record for UK company data
    59→- Below 0.05: hard to sustain unless billions of queries
    60→- 0.10-0.30: basic enrichment over free Companies House data
    61→- 0.30-1.00: multi-source enrichment
    62→- 1.00-5.00: compliance/regulated use cases
    63→- Above 5.00: needs to be a "report" with significant analysis
    64→

1→# Data Peers: MCP Registries, Skills Registries & API Data Services
     2→
     3→> Research date: 2026-03-22
     4→> Mode: ultradeep
     5→> Sources: 40+
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Executive Summary
    10→
    11→The landscape of how AI agents discover and consume tools, data, and capabilities has crystallized around three complementary layers in 2026: **MCP registries** (protocol-level tool discovery), **skills registries** (procedural knowledge distribution), and **API data services** (structured data delivery). MCP, originally introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, has become the de facto standard for agent-tool connectivity, now governed by the Linux Foundation with adoption from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. The ecosystem has grown explosively from ~100 servers at launch to nearly 19,000 listed on community directories. Meanwhile, the Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io) has emerged as the cross-platform format for distributing procedural knowledge, with 89,000+ skills tracked on skills.sh. API data services are rapidly evolving from traditional developer tools into AI-native infrastructure, with MCP servers and structured schemas becoming key differentiators.
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## 1. MCP Registries
    16→
    17→### 1.1 The Official MCP Registry
    18→
    19→**URL:** https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io
    20→**Operator:** MCP project (Linux Foundation, community-driven)
    21→**Launched:** September 8, 2025 (preview)
    22→**API Version:** v0.1 (frozen October 2025, no breaking changes)
    23→
    24→The canonical upstream registry for publicly available MCP servers. It is intentionally minimal, providing a REST API and basic search but no polished browsing UI. Third-party registries (Smithery, Glama, MCP.so) layer discovery UX on top of it.
    25→
    26→**Technical Details:**
    27→- **API Base:** `https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/`
    28→- **Key Endpoints:**
    29→  - `GET /v0/servers` - List/search servers (supports `search`, `limit` max 100, `cursor`, `offset`)
    30→  - `GET /v0/servers/{name}/versions/{version}` - Single server detail
    31→  - `GET /v0/version` - Registry version
    32→- **Data Model:** Each server entry contains name (GitHub-style namespace like `io.github.owner/repo`), description, version, repository URL, packages (npm/pypi/docker), transport type (stdio/sse/streamable-http), and metadata (status, publish date, latest flag)
    33→- **Namespace Auth:** Server names follow reverse-DNS tied to verified GitHub accounts. An `mcpName` field in `package.json` must match, preventing impersonation
    34→- **Publishing:** Via `mcp-publisher` CLI (`brew install mcp-publisher` on macOS), supports `init`, `login github`, `publish` commands
    35→- **Moderation:** Community members can flag servers for spam/malicious code. Maintainers can denylist entries
    36→- **Health Checks:** All servers pinged every 5 seconds for liveness
    37→- **Schema:** JSON Schema 2020-12, versioned at `https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/2025-09-29/server.schema.json`
    38→- **No auth required for reads** (public GET endpoints)
    39→
    40→**Governance:** Community-owned, backed by Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, Microsoft. The registry itself is open-source and supports sub-registries, allowing organizations to create opinionated downstream catalogs.
    41→
    42→**2026 Roadmap Items:**
    43→- **MCP Server Cards:** A `.well-known` URL standard for exposing structured server metadata, enabling discovery by browsers/crawlers/registries without connecting
    44→- **Stateless transport:** Evolving Streamable HTTP for load-balanced, multi-instance deployments
    45→- **Governance WG:** Contributor ladder (participant -> contributor -> facilitator -> lead -> core maintainer), delegation model for WGs, quarterly charter reviews
    46→
    47→[Source: registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, Nordic APIs, MCP Blog]
    48→
    49→---
    50→
    51→### 1.2 MCP.so
    52→
    53→**URL:** https://mcp.so
    54→**Operator:** Third-party community
    55→**Server Count:** ~18,871 (as of March 2026)
    56→
    57→The largest community-driven MCP directory. Tracks explosive growth from ~100 servers at MCP's November 2024 launch to nearly 19,000. Features include a call-volume leaderboard, filters (Featured, Latest, Official, Hosted), and tag/category browsing. Submission is via GitHub issues.
    58→
    59→[Source: mcp.so, Nordic APIs]
    60→
    61→---
    62→
    63→### 1.3 Glama.ai
    64→
    65→**URL:** https://glama.ai/mcp/servers
    66→**Operator:** Glama
    67→**Server Count:** ~9,000+ production-ready
    68→
    69→Takes an editorial stance, filtering out duplicates, demos, and low-quality entries. Uses Firecracker VM isolation for enterprise-grade security. Provides AI chat for discovery and extensive category/status filters. Also hosts and runs MCP servers for users (not just metadata).
    70→
    71→[Source: Composio comparison, Nordic APIs, Glama blog]
    72→
    73→---
    74→
    75→### 1.4 Smithery
    76→
    77→**URL:** https://smithery.ai
    78→**Operator:** Third-party
    79→**Server Count:** 2,800+ verified
    80→
    81→Positioned as the "Docker Hub for MCP." Cloud platform for deploying MCP agents with CLI and Docker options. Free tier for basic hosting, paid plans for more tools and security. Best for experimentation, discovery, and prototyping, not enterprise-grade gateway use.
    82→
    83→[Source: Composio comparison]
    84→
    85→---
    86→
    87→### 1.5 OpenTools Registry
    88→
    89→**URL:** https://opentools.com/registry
    90→**Operator:** OpenTools
    91→**Tagline:** "One API to use any LLM with every MCP tool"
    92→
    93→A unified API layer for LLM tool use. OpenAI SDK-compatible API (`api.opentools.com` as base URL) that lets developers pass MCP tools directly in the `tools` parameter when calling any supported LLM. Task-centric discovery curated to exclude duplicates and abandoned projects. Authentication via Clerk.
    94→
    95→**API Example:**
    96→```python
    97→from openai import OpenAI
    98→client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.opentools.com", api_key="<KEY>")
    99→completion = client.chat.completions.create(
   100→    model="anthropic/claude-3.7-sonnet",
   101→    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Compare top 5 EVs"}],
   102→    tools=[{"type": "mcp", "ref": "firecrawl"}]
   103→)
   104→```
   105→
   106→[Source: opentools.com, Nordic APIs]
   107→
   108→---
   109→
   110→### 1.6 GitHub MCP Registry
   111→
   112→**URL:** https://github.com/mcp
   113→**Operator:** GitHub/MCP community
   114→
   115→Showcases reference servers and community contributions. Hosts servers for NuGet, Azure services, Azure DevOps, Stripe, Elasticsearch, and Microsoft documentation. Visibility influenced by stars, forks, and repo activity.
   116→
   117→[Source: GitHub, Nordic APIs]
   118→
   119→---
   120→
   121→### 1.7 Composio
   122→
   123→**URL:** https://composio.dev
   124→**Operator:** Composio
   125→**Integrations:** 500+ pre-built (Slack, GitHub, Notion, Stripe, etc.)
   126→
   127→An agentic integration platform providing a single unified MCP Gateway endpoint. Key differentiator: provides **working integrations** with managed auth (full OAuth, RBAC, PII redaction), not just discovery. Enterprise-grade with OpenTelemetry observability, rate limiting, and governance. Works with Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and any MCP-compatible client.
   128→
   129→[Source: Composio blog, comparison pages]
   130→
   131→---
   132→
   133→### 1.8 guMCP (Gumloop)
   134→
   135→**URL:** https://gumloop.com/mcp
   136→**Operator:** Gumloop
   137→**License:** GPL-3.0
   138→
   139→Free, open-source hosted MCP servers. Aims to build the largest MCP server collection with a unified backend. Dual transport (stdio + SSE). SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, HIPAA compliant. No monetization intent ("Use it, have fun"). New servers added almost daily.
   140→
   141→[Source: Gumloop blog, GitHub]
   142→
   143→---
   144→
   145→### 1.9 MCP-Get
   146→
   147→**URL:** https://mcp-get.com
   148→**Operator:** Third-party
   149→
   150→Functions as both registry and monitoring service. Real-time server status/activity monitoring with uptime insights. Useful for developers who need operational reliability data on servers they depend on.
   151→
   152→[Source: Nordic APIs]
   153→
   154→---
   155→
   156→### 1.10 Mastra MCP Registry Registry
   157→
   158→**URL:** https://mastra.ai/mcp-registry-registry
   159→**Operator:** Mastra
   160→
   161→A meta-registry that catalogs other registries rather than servers directly. "Registry of registries" providing a cross-ecosystem view. Also available as an MCP server (`@mastra/mcp-registry-registry`) for programmatic querying.
   162→
   163→[Source: Mastra blog, Nordic APIs]
   164→
   165→---
   166→
   167→### Registry Comparison Table
   168→
   169→| Registry | Server Count | Type | Best For | Auth/Security |
   170→|----------|-------------|------|----------|---------------|
   171→| **Official MCP** | Unknown (canonical) | Metadata catalog | Upstream truth, API consumption | Namespace auth via GitHub |
   172→| **MCP.so** | ~18,871 | Community directory | Broadest discovery | Community moderation |
   173→| **Glama** | ~9,000+ | Curated + hosted | Enterprise exploration | Firecracker VM isolation |
   174→| **Smithery** | 2,800+ | Marketplace | Prototyping, discovery | Basic |
   175→| **OpenTools** | N/A | Unified API proxy | Direct LLM integration | API key (Clerk) |
   176→| **Composio** | 500+ managed | Integration platform | Production, enterprise | OAuth, RBAC, PII redaction |
   177→| **guMCP** | Growing daily | Free hosted | Democratized access | SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA |
   178→| **MCP-Get** | N/A | Registry + monitoring | Uptime tracking | N/A |
   179→| **Mastra** | Meta-aggregator | Registry of registries | Ecosystem overview | N/

     5→> Sources: 40+

     8→
     9→## Executive Summary
    10→
    11→The landscape of how AI agents discover and consume tools, data, and capabilities has crystallized around three complementary layers in 2026: **MCP registries** (protocol-level tool discovery), **skills registries** (procedural knowledge distribution), and **API data services** (structured data delivery). MCP, originally introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, has become the de facto standard for agent-tool connectivity, now governed by the Linux Foundation with adoption from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. The ecosystem has grown explosively from ~100 servers at launch to nearly 19,000 listed on community directories. Meanwhile, the Agent Skills standard (agentskills.io) has emerged as the cross-platform format for distributing procedural knowledge, with 89,000+ skills tracked on skills.sh. API data services are rapidly evolving from traditional developer tools into AI-native infrastructure, with MCP servers and structured schemas becoming key differentiators.
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## 1. MCP Registries
    16→
    17→### 1.1 The Official MCP Registry
    18→
    19→**URL:** https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io
    20→**Operator:** MCP project (Linux Foundation, community-driven)
    21→**Launched:** September 8, 2025 (preview)
    22→**API Version:** v0.1 (frozen October 2025, no breaking changes)
    23→
    24→The canonical upstream registry for publicly available MCP servers. It is intentionally minimal, providing a REST API and basic search but no polished browsing UI. Third-party registries (Smithery, Glama, MCP.so) layer discovery UX on top of it.
    25→
    26→**Technical Details:**
    27→- **API Base:** `https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io/v0/`
    28→- **Key Endpoints:**
    29→  - `GET /v0/servers` - List/search servers (supports `search`, `limit` max 100, `cursor`, `offset`)
    30→  - `GET /v0/servers/{name}/versions/{version}` - Single server detail
    31→  - `GET /v0/version` - Registry version
    32→- **Data Model:** Each server entry contains name (GitHub-style namespace like `io.github.owner/repo`), description, version, repository URL, packages (npm/pypi/docker), transport type (stdio/sse/streamable-http), and metadata (status, publish date, latest flag)
    33→- **Namespace Auth:** Server names follow reverse-DNS tied to verified GitHub accounts. An `mcpName` field in `package.json` must match, preventing impersonation
    34→- **Publishing:** Via `mcp-publisher` CLI (`brew install mcp-publisher` on macOS), supports `init`, `login github`, `publish` commands
    35→- **Moderation:** Community members can flag servers for spam/malicious code. Maintainers can denylist entries
    36→- **Health Checks:** All servers pinged every 5 seconds for liveness
    37→- **Schema:** JSON Schema 2020-12, versioned at `https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/2025-09-29/server.schema.json`
    38→- **No auth required for reads** (public GET endpoints)
    39→
    40→**Governance:** Community-owned, backed by Anthropic, GitHub, PulseMCP, Microsoft. The registry itself is open-source and supports sub-registries, allowing organizations to create opinionated downstream catalogs.
    41→
    42→**2026 Roadmap Items:**
    43→- **MCP Server Cards:** A `.well-known` URL standard for exposing structured server metadata, enabling discovery by browsers/crawlers/registries without connecting
    44→- **Stateless transport:** Evolving Streamable HTTP for load-balanced, multi-instance deployments
    45→- **Governance WG:** Contributor ladder (participant -> contributor -> facilitator -> lead -> core maintainer), delegation model for WGs, quarterly charter reviews
    46→
    47→[Source: registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, Nordic APIs, MCP Blog]
    48→

    50→
    51→### 1.2 MCP.so
    52→
    53→**URL:** https://mcp.so
    54→**Operator:** Third-party community
    55→**Server Count:** ~18,871 (as of March 2026)
    56→
    57→The largest community-driven MCP directory. Tracks explosive growth from ~100 servers at MCP's November 2024 launch to nearly 19,000. Features include a call-volume leaderboard, filters (Featured, Latest, Official, Hosted), and tag/category browsing. Submission is via GitHub issues.
    58→
    59→[Source: mcp.so, Nordic APIs]

    64→
    65→**URL:** https://glama.ai/mcp/servers
    66→**Operator:** Glama
    67→**Server Count:** ~9,000+ production-ready
    68→
    69→Takes an editorial stance, filtering out duplicates, demos, and low-quality entries. Uses Firecracker VM isolation for enterprise-grade security. Provides AI chat for discovery and extensive category/status filters. Also hosts and runs MCP servers for users (not just metadata).
