    47→Founder observation from using OpenClaw: "Whenever agents have access to folder interfaces and can treat the project as local, even if they're not touching the core logic but they just understand the interfaces, they just seem to perform better than just giving them CLIs and MCPs or APIs."
    48→
    49→Supporting structural evidence:
    50→- Cloudflare demonstrated 99.9% token reduction with code-mode (Mar 2026)
    51→- Anthropic demonstrated 98.7% token reduction independently (Mar 2026)
    52→- Both converged on the same pattern: agents writing code against typed interfaces instead of calling tools one-at-a-time
    53→
    54→## The Interaction Model
    55→
    56→### Three Access Tiers (Long-Term Vision)
    57→
    58→Every data domain on DataFetch is accessible through three tiers. The PoC focuses on Tier 3 (environment-first), with Tier 1 endpoints as a secondary access path. Tier 2 is deferred.
    59→
    60→| Tier | Interface | Agent Requirement | Price Model |
    61→|------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
    62→| Tier 1: REST API | Standard endpoints (`GET /entity/:id/enriched`) | Any HTTP-capable agent | Per-endpoint MPP |
    63→| Tier 2: Natural Language Intent | Agent describes query in English, DataFetch translates | Any agent | Per-intent MPP (deferred) |
    64→| Tier 3: Code Environment | Agent navigates folder of typed interfaces, explores mock data, commits to paid execution | Code-writing agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) | Compute-based MPP (explore free, execute paid) |
    65→
    66→**PoC priority:** Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary (compatibility). Tier 2 deferred.
    67→
    68→### Intent-Shaped Interfaces
    69→
    70→Interfaces encode **domain intelligence**, not data schemas

    95→- Source: Companies House streaming API
    96→- Events: New filings, company updates, officer appointments/resignations
    97→- Consumer: Long-running process that applies deltas to production DB
    98→- Latency: Minutes from filing to availability
    99→
   100→**Accounts Data (iXBRL):**
   101→- Source: Companies House document API
   102→- Format: iXBRL (inline XBRL tagged HTML)
   103→- Extraction: Parse XBRL tags to extract: revenue, profit/loss, total assets, total liabilities, net assets, employee count
   104→- Challenge: Not all companies file digitally. Micro-entities file minimal data. Only ~40% of companies file accounts with useful financial detail
   105→- Storage: Extracted financial metrics in dedicated table, linked to company record
   106→
   107→### Land Registry
   108→
   109→**Price Paid Data (monthly):**
   110→- Source: gov.uk bulk download (CSV)
   111→- Contains: Every residential transaction in England & Wales since 1995 (~28M records)
   112→- Fields: Price, date, postcode, property type, tenure, new/old, address
   113→- Refresh: Monthly update file (incremental)
   114→
   115→**CCOD/OCOD (quarterly):**
   116→- Source: gov.uk bulk download
   117→- CCOD: ~3.5M titles owned by UK companies (title number, tenure, address, company, CH number, price paid)
   118→- OCOD: ~100K titles owned by overseas entities
   119→- Cross-reference: CCOD company numbers link directly to Companies House
   120→
   121→**EPC Register (monthly):**
   122→- Source: Open Data Communities bulk download
   123→- Contains: Energy Performance Certificates for ~20M properties
   124→- Fields: Address, EPC rating (A-G), floor area, wall type, heating type, estimated energy cost
   125→- Cross-reference: Address matching to Land Registry records
   126→
   127→### Additional Sources

   132→| ICO Register | Bulk download | Monthly | Data controller registrations |

   134→| Charity Commission | API + bulk | Monthly | ~170K registered charities |

   137→| Census 2021 | Bulk download | Static | Demographics by output area |

   139→| police.uk | API | Monthly | Crime data by location |

   142→
   143→### Entity Resolution
   144→
   145→**Company matching:**
   146→- Primary key: Companies House number (deterministic)
   147→- Fuzzy matching for sources without CH number: company name + postcode + SIC code
   148→
   149→**Director matching (cross-company):**
   150→- Match on: surname + partial DOB (month/year) + forename initial
   151→- Confirm with: nationality, country of residence, co-director patterns
   152→- Output: Director ID that links across all their appointments
   153→- Challenge: Common names produce false positives. Conservative matching preferred (miss some links rather than create false ones)
   154→
   155→**Address matching (property to company):**
   156→- Normalize addresses using OS AddressBase (if licensed) or PAF-free alternatives
   157→- Match Land Registry addresses to Companies House registered addresses and EPC addresses
   158→- Challenge: Address formatting varies wildly across sources. "Flat 2, 10 High St" vs "10 HIGH STREET FLAT 2" vs "Second Floor, 10 High Street"

   161→
   162→**Financial Health Score (0-100):**
   163→
   164→Inputs:
   165→- Latest accounts: current ratio, debt/equity, net assets trend, revenue growth (where available)
   166→- Filing behaviour: days late on average, overdue filings count
   167→- Charges: active charges count, recent charge activity
   168→- Gazette: proximity to insolvency notices, winding-up petitions
   169→- Company age and status
   170→
   171→Weighting: Accounts data (40%), filing behaviour (25%), charges (15%), gazette (15%), age (5%)
   172→
   173→Where accounts data is unavailable (micro-entities, dormant companies), score shifts to filing behaviour and age-based model.

   176→- Flag: Director of recently dissolved company (within 5 years) now directing a new company
   177→- Additional signals: Same registered address, similar SIC code, similar company name

1→# Appendix: Reference Data & Market Context
     2→
     3→## A. MPP Protocol Reference
     4→
     5→### What is MPP?
     6→Machine Payments Protocol, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs (March 2026). An HTTP authentication scheme that standardizes the 402 Payment Required status code.
     7→
     8→### Core Flow
     9→1. Client requests resource -> `GET /endpoint`
    10→2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)
    11→3. Client pays (signs blockchain tx, provides card token, etc.)
    12→4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
    13→5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header
    14→
    15→### Transaction Modes
    16→- **Charge (one-time):** Immediate settlement per request. Good for discrete API calls
    17→- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency
    18→
    19→### SDKs
    20→| Language | Package | Install |
    21→|----------|---------|---------|
    22→| TypeScript | mppx | npm install mppx |
    23→| Python | pympp | pip install pympp |
    24→| Rust | mpp-rs | cargo add mpp |
    25→
    26→### Key Resources
    27→- Protocol overview: mpp.dev/overview
    28→- Server quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/server
    29→- Agent quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/agent
    30→- IETF spec: paymentauth.org
    31→- Stripe blog: stripe.com/blog/machine-payments-protocol
    32→
    33→## B. UK Open Government Licence (OGL v3) Summary
    34→
    35→**Permits:** Copy, publish, distribute, transmit, adapt, exploit commercially and non-commercially
    36→**Requires:** Acknowledge the source, provide link to licence
    37→**Does NOT require:** Payment, registration, or permission
    38→
    39→### OGL-Covered Datasets Used
    40→- Companies House basic company data
    41→- Land Registry Price Paid Data
    42→- Land Registry CCOD/OCOD
    43→- EPC Register
    44→- Charity Commission register
    45→- CQC provider data
    46→- FHRS food hygiene ratings
    47→- Ofsted inspection data
    48→- Census / ONS statistical data
    49→- The Gazette (insolvency notices)
    50→- Met Office DataPoint
    51→- police.uk crime data
    52→- HMRC trade statistics
    53→
    54→### NOT OGL (require separate licensing)
    55→- Ordnance Survey premium products (AddressBase, MasterMap)
    56→- Royal Mail PAF (postcode/address data)
    57→- Land Registry National Polygon Dataset (GBP 4,500+/yr)
    58→- Individual Land Registry title registers (GBP 3/title, no bulk redistribution)
    59→
    60→## C. Competitor Pricing Reference
    61→
    62→### UK Company Data
    63→
    64→| Provider | Model | Price Point | Enrichment Level |
    65→|----------|-------|-------------|------------------|
    66→| Companies House API | Free | 0 (rate-limited) | Raw data only |
    67→| Endole | Pay-as-you-go | GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Scored, basic network |
    68→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | GBP 10K+/yr minimum | Full credit scoring |
    69→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription | GBP 5K-30K/yr | Growth/innovation signals |
    70→| OpenCorporates | API subscription | $500+/mo | Cross-jurisdiction, no scoring |
    71→| DueDil (now Creditsafe) | API credits | GBP 0.50-2.00/check | Compliance/KYB focused |
    72→
    73→### Our Proposed Positioning
    74→- Below Endole on basic lookups (GBP 0.05 vs 0.25)
    75→- Comparable to Endole on enriched (GBP 0.25)
    76→- Below DueDil on compliance checks (GBP 1.00 vs 1.50+)
    77→- Zero friction: no signup, no subscription, no API key
    78→
    79→### International Data Products (for comparison)
    80→
    81→| Provider | Data Type | Per-Query Price |
    82→|----------|-----------|-----------------|
    83→| Clearbit | Company enrichment | $0.05-0.25 |
    84→| Apollo.io | Contact + company | $0.01-0.05 |
    85→| BuiltWith | Technology profiles | $0.10-0.50 |
    86→| SimilarWeb | Traffic data | $0.01-0.10 |
    87→| Crunchbase | Startup/funding | $0.05-0.20 |
    88→
    89→## D. Companies House Data Schema (Key Fields)
    90→
    91→### Company Profile
    92→- company_number (PK)
    93→- company_name
    94→- company_status (active, dissolved, liquidation, etc.)
    95→- company_type (ltd, plc, llp, etc.)
    96→- date_of_creation
    97→- date_of_cessation
    98→- registered_office_address (premises, address_line_1, address_line_2, locality, region, postal_code, country)
    99→- sic_codes (array of 5-digit codes)
   100→- accounts.next_due, accounts.last_made_up_to
   101→- confirmation_statement.next_due, confirmation_statement.last_made_up_to
   102→- has_charges, has_insolvency_history
   103→- jurisdiction
   104→
   105→### Officer (Director/Secretary)
   106→- officer_id
   107→- company_number (FK)
   108→- name (surname, forename)
   109→- officer_role (director, secretary, llp-member, etc.)
   110→- appointed_on, resigned_on
   111→- date_of_birth (month, year only)
   112→- nationality
   113→- country_of_residence
   114→- occupation
   115→- address (correspondence address, not residential)
   116→
   117→### PSC (Person of Significant Control)
   118→- psc_id
   119→- company_number (FK)
   120→- name or corporate_name
   121→- natures_of_control (array: ownership-of-shares-25-to-50-percent, voting-rights-75-to-100-percent, etc.)
   122→- nationality, country_of_residence
   123→- date_of_birth (month, year)
   124→- address
   125→- ceased_on (if no longer a PSC)
   126→- For corporate PSCs: identification.legal_authority, identification.place_registered, identification.registration_number
   127→
   128→### Charges
   129→- charge_id
   130→- company_number (FK)
   131→- status (outstanding, fully-satisfied, part-satisfied)
   132→- created_on, delivered_on, satisfied_on
   133→- persons_entitled (lender names)
   134→- particulars (description of charged property)
   135→- classification (nature-of-charge, etc.)
   136→
   137→## E. Financial Health Score Methodology (Draft)
   138→
   139→### Input Variables
   140→
   141→**From Accounts (40% weight):**
   142→- Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (target: > 1.5)
   143→- Debt to equity = total liabilities / net assets (target: < 2.0)
   144→- Net assets trend (increasing = positive signal)
   145→- Revenue growth YoY (where available)
   146→- Profit margin (where available)
   147→
   148→**From Filing Behaviour (25% weight):**
   149→- Average days late (0 = perfect, >30 = concerning)
   150→- Percentage of filings late
   151→- Currently overdue filings count
   152→- Trend: improving or worsening
   153→
   154→**From Charges (15% weight):**
   155→- Active charges count
   156→- Recent charge activity (new charges in last 12 months)
   157→- Charge satisfaction rate
   158→
   159→**From Gazette/Insolvency (15% weight):**
   160→- Winding-up petitions (severe negative signal)
   161→- Strike-off action (moderate negative)
   162→- Administrative receiver appointed (severe)
   163→
   164→**From Company Age/Status (5% weight):**
   165→- Companies < 2 years old get a slight penalty (less track record)
   166→- Dormant companies scored separately
   167→
   168→### Score Bands
   169→- 80-100: Strong financial position
   170→- 60-79: Adequate, no immediate concerns
   171→- 40-59: Caution, some risk indicators
   172→- 20-39: Significant risk, multiple negative signals
   173→- 0-19: Severe risk, active insolvency indicators
   174→
   175→### Known Limitations
   176→- ~60% of UK companies file micro-entity or abbreviated accounts with minimal financial detail
   177→- Score for these companies relies heavily on filing behaviour and charges (lower confidence)
   178→- Financial data can be up to 21 months old at time of filing (9 month filing deadline + 12 month accounting period)
   179→- Score should always be accompanied by confidence indicator and data freshness
   180→
   181→## F. GDPR Compliance Plan
   182→
   183→### Personal Data Processed
   184→- Director/secretary names
   185→- Director date of birth (month/year only)
   186→- Director correspondence addresses (not residential)
   187→- PSC names, nationality, country of residence
   188→
   189→### Lawful Basis
   190→- Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f))
   191→- Data is published by Companies House under statutory authority
   192→- Processing serves legitimate business interests (credit checking, due diligence, compliance)
   193→- Balanced against individual rights: data is already public, we add enrichment not new personal data
   194→
   195→### Required Actions
   196→1. Privacy policy explaining processing activities
   197→2. Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) documented
   198→3. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for systematic profiling
   199→4. Right to object mechanism (suppression list)
   200→5. Data subject access request (DSAR) process
   201→6. Respect Companies House residential address suppression
   202→7. Do not attempt to derive full dates of birth
   203→8. Consider ICO registration if not already registered
   204→
   205→## G. Potential Product Expansion Path
   206→
   207→```
   208→Phase 1 (Months 1-2): Company Intelligence API
   209→  |
   210→  v
   211→Phase 2 (Months 2-4): + Property Intelligence
   212→  |
   213→  v
   214→Phase 3 (Months 4-6): + Planning Pipeline + Trade Intelligence
   215→  |
   216→  v
   217→Phase 4 (Months 6-12): + Climate Risk + Tech/Hiring Signals
   218→  |
   219→  v
   220→Phase 5 (Year 2): + Niche products (Care, Charity, Food, Hyperlocal)
   221→  |
   222→  v
   223→Phase 6 (Year 2+): International expansion (US SEC, EU company registries)
   224→```

    10→2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)

    12→4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
    13→5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header

    17→- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency

1→# Research Report: Niche Data Businesses You Could Build, Inspired by YC W26 Patterns
     2→
     3→## Executive Summary
     4→
     5→- **The Agent Economy Needs Data Infrastructure:** 56 of 198 YC W26 companies are building AI agents, yet most lack access to domain-specific, high-quality data. The picks-and-shovels opportunity is in supplying the data layer these agents consume, not building agents themselves [1][2].
     6→- **Domain-Specific Datasets Command Premium Pricing:** As foundation models commoditize, the scarcity shifts from models to data. Companies building proprietary, vertical datasets are setting the fastest records from zero to $100M in revenue, per a16z's 2025 analysis [3].
     7→- **The AI Training Dataset Market Is Exploding:** Valued at $3.59B in 2025, projected to reach $23.18B by 2034 (22.9% CAGR). Synthetic data generation alone grew 36% in adoption and is on track for $3.4B by 2030 [4][5].
     8→- **Agent Memory and Context Infrastructure Is the New Database Layer:** Startups like Mem0 ($24M Series A), Letta, and Zep are building the memory/knowledge graph layer agents need. This is foundational infrastructure with massive TAM [6].
     9→- **Underserved Verticals Present the Highest-Margin Opportunities:** Healthcare ($164B AI market by 2030), legal ($32.5B legal tech by 2026), construction ($2.1T industry with analog workflows), and supply chain ($50B AI market by 2031) all have massive data gaps that solo founders or small teams can exploit [7][8][9][10].
    10→
    11→**Primary Recommendation:** Build a niche data business that curates, structures, or generates domain-specific datasets for one underserved vertical, then compound your data moat through a flywheel of agent usage and feedback.
    12→
    13→**Confidence Level:** High, based on convergent signals across 40+ sources spanning market research, VC analysis, and startup funding data.
    14→
    15→---
    16→
    17→## Introduction
    18→
    19→### Research Question
    20→What niche data businesses could you build, informed by the patterns visible in YC's W26 batch, where 85% of companies are AI-first, a third are building agents, and the dominant playbook is "vertical AI coding agent for [industry]"?
    21→
    22→This question matters because the article reveals a structural shift: the copilot era lasted 18 months, and we are now in the replacement era. Every $50K-$150K/yr knowledge worker role is getting an AI agent pointed at it. But agents need data to function, and most industries lack the structured, high-quality, domain-specific datasets these agents require. The infrastructure layer beneath the agent wave is where durable, defensible businesses can be built.
    23→
    24→### Scope & Methodology
    25→This research investigated niche data business opportunities across 12 dimensions: AI training datasets, synthetic data generation, data-as-a-service, agent memory/context infrastructure, domain-specific datasets, data labeling/annotation, compliance data, geospatial data, real-time data feeds, agent payment/exchange protocols, web scraping/collection, and data moat strategies. The analysis focused on identifying gaps where data businesses could serve the emerging agent economy described in the YC W26 batch.
    26→
    27→Research was conducted using 15 parallel web searches across industry reports, VC analyses, market research firms (Grand View Research, Precedence Research, Mordor Intelligence), tech publications (TechCrunch, VentureBeat), and startup databases (Crunchbase, Tracxn, SeedTable). Over 40 unique sources were consulted, covering the period from 2024 through March 2026, with emphasis on 2025-2026 data.
    28→
    29→### Key Assumptions
    30→- The agent economy trend visible in YC W26 represents a durable structural shift, not a temporary hype cycle
    31→- Data businesses can be built by solo founders or small teams, given current AI tooling
    32→- The shift from general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific models will accelerate demand for curated vertical datasets
    33→- Compliance and regulatory requirements will tighten, increasing the value of clean, governed data
    34→- The reader is evaluating business ideas they could personally build, favoring capital-efficient approaches
    35→
    36→---
    37→
    38→## Main Analysis
    39→
    40→### Finding 1: Agent Memory and Context Infrastructure Is the Most Underbuilt Layer
    41→
    42→The entire YC W26 batch is building agents, but agents are stateless by default. Traditional LLMs start each interaction without context or memory. This creates a massive infrastructure gap: autonomy without memory does not scale [6].
    43→
    44→Three startups currently dominate this nascent space. Mem0 raised a $24M Series A in October 2025 and was selected as AWS's exclusive memory provider. It uses a hybrid datastore combining vector, key-value, and graph stores. Letta (formerly MemGPT) implements an OS-inspired memory hierarchy with "sleep-time compute," where background agents reorganize memory during idle periods. Zep (Graphiti) stores memory as a temporal knowledge graph that tracks how facts change over time [6].
    45→
    46→The broader context layer is evolving rapidly. IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent in March 2026 specifically to make "real-time data the engine of enterprise AI and agents" [11]. Nimble raised $47M in February 2026 to give AI agents access to real-time web data, with their CEO noting that "trusted live web data is increasingly becoming a prerequisite for AI agents performing critical business decisions" [11].
    47→
    48→Gartner recently classified Knowledge Graphs as a "Critical Enabler" with immediate impact on generative AI, and the convergence of GraphRAG (retrieval-augmented generation powered by knowledge graphs) with agent architectures is creating what practitioners call an "AI-ready knowledge fabric" [6].
    49→
    50→The niche data business opportunity here is not building another Mem0, but rather building the domain-specific memory and context layers that vertical agents need. A construction agent needs memory structured around projects, permits, schedules, and subcontractors. A legal agent needs memory structured around cases, precedents, statutes, and deadlines. These vertical memory schemas are intensely domain-specific and represent defensible data businesses that horizontal memory platforms will not build.
    51→
    52→**Sources:** [6], [11]
    53→
    54→---
    55→
    56→### Finding 2: Domain-Specific Training Datasets Are the New Gold
    57→
    58→The AI training dataset market was valued at $3.59B in 2025 and is projected to reach $23.18B by 2034, with a 22.9% CAGR [4]. But the real story is the shift from volume to specificity. As foundation model capabilities commoditize, a16z's January 2025 report explicitly identifies proprietary data models as the foundation of durable AI moats [3].
    59→
    60→The rise of Small Language Models (SLMs) is accelerating this shift dramatically. Niche industries are moving toward SLMs with fewer than 30B parameters, which require hyper-specific, curated datasets rather than general internet crawls [12]. Domain-specific models like Diabetica-7B (for diabetes) and PatentBERT (for IP research) demonstrate that focused datasets produce superior performance within their domains [12].
    61→
    62→The business model is straightforward: curate, clean, and structure datasets for underserved verticals, then sell them as fine-tuning packages or API-accessible data products. The top 8 players in the training dataset market hold only 43% market share, indicating significant room for specialized entrants [4]. Scale AI's revenue climbed to $870M in 2024 and is tracking $2B in 2025, while Meta invested $15B for a 49% stake in the company at a $29B+ valuation, confirming that proprietary training data is an irreplaceable AI asset [13].
    63→
    64→The highest-margin opportunity is in regulated verticals where data is scarce, hard to access, and requires domain expertise to structure. Healthcare AI datasets alone are expected to surpass $2.5B by 2026 [13]. Automotive OEMs processing more than 3 million labels per month for Level 4 autonomy represent another concentrated demand pool [13].
    65→
    66→**Sources:** [3], [4], [12], [13]
    67→
    68→---
    69→
    70→### Finding 3: Synthetic Data for Regulated Industries Is a $3.4B Opportunity
    71→
    72→The synthetic data generation market was estimated at $576M in 2024 and is projected to reach $3.4B by 2030, growing at a 34.43% CAGR, one of the fastest-growing segments in AI infrastructure [5]. NVIDIA's acquisition of Gretel in March 2025 validated the strategic importance of this category [5].
    73→
    74→The opportunity is sharpest in regulated industries where real data is expensive, legally constrained, or ethically problematic to collect. In healthcare, MDClone partners with hospitals to generate synthetic health data, Syntegra builds synthetic data engines purpose-built for healthcare, and Octopize MD provides synthetic medical data for research [5]. In finance, Synthera AI generates realistic yield curves, stock prices, and FX rates [5]. In automotive, Waymo supplements millions of miles of real driving with billions of miles of simulated scenarios [5].
    75→
    76→The regulatory tailwind is powerful: 72% of enterprises report data privacy constraints limiting access to production datasets, which is increasing demand for synthetic data by 40% in pilot deployments [5]. GDPR, CCPA, and the 2026 EU AI Act are all pushing organizations toward synthetic alternatives.
    77→
    78→For a solo founder or small team, the play is building a synthetic data generation service for one specific vertical. Healthcare synthetic data is particularly attractive because HIPAA constraints make real data nearly impossible to share, yet AI model development requires massive, diverse data

200→### Patterns Identified
   201→
   202→**Pattern 1: The Data Layer Beneath Every Agent Category**
   203→Every YC W26 agent company, whether in healthcare, legal, finance, or construction, has an implicit data dependency that most have not solved. The AI sales rep needs prospect data. The AI SRE needs incident pattern data. The AI accountant needs chart-of-accounts schemas and payer rules. Each vertical agent category creates a corresponding vertical data business opportunity. The pattern is consistent: agent companies focus on workflow and UX, leaving the data layer as an externality they would prefer to buy rather than build.
   204→
   205→**Pattern 2: Compliance as Moat Accelerator**
   206→In every vertical examined, regulatory complexity increases the value of structured data. HIPAA makes healthcare data scarce. GDPR makes European consumer data expensive. The EU AI Act creates new documentation requirements. SOC 2 gates enterprise sales. Rather than viewing compliance as a cost, the most defensible data businesses treat it as the barrier that prevents commodity competitors from entering. The harder it is to collect, structure, and govern data in a given domain, the more valuable a clean data product becomes.
   207→
   208→**Pattern 3: The Flywheel from Data Product to Data Moat**
   209→The strongest data businesses are those where product usage generates more data, which improves the product, which attracts more users. A labeling service that also trains models on labeled data gets better at pre-labeling, reducing costs and improving quality. A legal dataset that tracks which predictions were accurate improves its prediction accuracy. A synthetic data generator that gets feedback on model performance generates more realistic synthetics. This flywheel dynamic, visible in companies from Abridge to Scale AI, is the key to building durable competitive advantage.
   210→
   211→### Novel Insights
   212→
   213→**Insight 1: The "Agent Schema" Business**
   214→No single source explicitly described this, but the convergence of agent memory infrastructure (Finding 1), domain-specific datasets (Finding 2), and underserved verticals (Findings 5-8) points to a new category: the "agent schema" business. This is a company that defines and maintains the canonical data structures an AI agent needs to operate in a specific industry. For construction, this means the schema for projects, permits, materials, labor, and inspections. For healthcare, the schema for encounters, diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes. The company that owns the schema owns the interoperability layer, similar to how HL7/FHIR became the backbone of health data exchange.
   215→
   216→**Insight 2: Data Businesses Have Higher Capital Efficiency Than Agent Businesses**
   217→The YC W26 batch is dominated by agent companies that will compete fiercely on UX, model capability, and go-to-market speed. Data businesses, by contrast, face less direct competition and require less capital to start. A curated dataset can be built by one person with domain expertise. A synthetic data service needs one engineer and one domain expert. A labeling service needs a network of vetted annotators. These are $0-$50K to launch versus $500K-$5M for an agent company. Yet data businesses can achieve similar or higher margins because data is resold repeatedly with near-zero marginal cost.
   218→
   219→### Implications
   220→
   221→**For You:**
   222→The optimal strategy is to pick one vertical from the YC W26 batch, deeply understand its data gaps, and build a focused data product. Healthcare and legal have the highest margins due to regulatory barriers. Construction and supply chain have the lowest competition. Agent infrastructure (memory, context, evaluation) has the highest upside but requires more technical depth. The choice depends on your domain expertise and appetite for regulatory complexity.
   223→
   224→**Broader Implications:**
   225→The agent economy will create a parallel "data economy" worth tens of billions within 5 years. The companies that build the data substrate for agents will be as foundational as AWS was for cloud computing. Early movers who establish domain-specific data products now will compound their advantage as agent adoption scales.
   226→
   227→**Second-Order Effects:**
   228→As agents consume more structured data, the value of unstructured data decreases. Data businesses that structure, annotate, and govern data will capture value from data businesses that merely collect and store it. The web scraping era gives way to the data curation era.
   229→
   230→---
   231→
   232→## Limitations & Caveats
   233→
   234→### Counterevidence Register
   235→
   236→**Contradictory Finding 1: Data Moats May Be Eroding**
   237→Some analysts argue that increasingly powerful foundation models reduce the need for proprietary data, as models can "learn" domain specifics from smaller fine-tuning sets or even zero-shot [3]. However, the weight of evidence from a16z, venture funding data, and Meta's $15B Scale AI investment suggests data moats are strengthening, not weakening, for domain-specific applications [3][13].
   238→
   239→**Contradictory Finding 2: 40% of Agentic AI Deployments May Be Canceled**
   240→Gartner predicts that 40% of agentic AI deployments will be canceled by 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, or poor risk controls [6]. If agent adoption stalls, the data businesses serving agents would face reduced demand. This risk is mitigated by the breadth of agent adoption (168 of 198 YC W26 companies are AI-first) and by the fact that data products can serve both agent and human consumers.
   241→
   242→### Known Gaps
   243→- Revenue data for domain-specific data businesses is scarce, as most are private and early-stage
   244→- The research focused primarily on US/English-language markets, potentially underweighting opportunities in Asia-Pacific and Europe
   245→- Long-term defensibility of specific data moats remains theoretical until proven by multi-year market data
   246→
   247→### Areas of Uncertainty
   248→- How quickly agent-to-agent protocols (ACP, AP2, x402) will achieve meaningful transaction volume
   249→- Whether AI model capabilities will advance fast enough to reduce the need for domain-specific training data
   250→- The pace and specifics of regulatory enforcement (EU AI Act, state-level AI laws) that would accelerate compliance data demand
   251→
   252→---
   253→
   254→## Recommendations
   255→
   256→### Immediate Actions
   257→
   258→1. **Pick One Vertical and Map Its Data Gaps**
   259→   - What: Choose one industry from the YC W26 batch (healthcare, legal, construction, supply chain) and create a comprehensive map of what data agents in that vertical need but cannot easily access
   260→   - Why: Findings 1-11 all converge on domain specificity as the highest-value strategy
   261→   - How: Interview 10-20 builders in that vertical, analyze existing data products, identify gaps
   262→   - Timeline: 2-4 weeks
   263→
   264→2. **Build a Minimum Viable Data Product**
   265→   - What: Create a small, curated dataset or data API that addresses one specific gap identified in step 1
   266→   - Why: Data businesses can be validated with minimal capital, a $50K dataset that 10 companies would pay $5K for is a $50K business with 100% margins
   267→   - How: Combine web collection, public records, and domain expertise to structure data that is currently unstructured or scattered
   268→   - Timeline: 4-8 weeks after gap identification
   269→
   270→3. **Establish Compliance Foundations Early**
   271→   - What: If targeting a regulated vertical, set up data governance, privacy policies, and compliance documentation from day one
   272→   - Why: Compliance is the moat (Finding 4). Starting compliant is 10x easier than retrofitting compliance later
   273→   - How: Use tools like Comp AI (open source) or Vanta for baseline compliance
   274→   - Timeline: Concurrent with product development
   275→
   276→### Next Steps
   277→
   278→1. **Design the Flywheel**
   279→   - Identify how product usage can generate more data, improving the product
   280→   - Plan the progression from static dataset to dynamic data service to platform
   281→
   282→2. **Test Pricing with Pre-Sales**
   283→   - Before building the full product, approach 5-10 potential customers with a description and pricing
   284→   - Validate willingness to pay and optimal price point
   285→
   286→3. **Monitor Agent Protocol Adoption**
   287→   - Track ACP, AP2, and x402 adoption rates for timing on agent payment data opportunities
   288→   - The transaction intelligence category (Finding 7) has high upside but requires market maturation
   289→
   290→### Further Research Needs
   291→
   292→1. **Competitive Landscape Mapping for Specific Verticals**
   293→   - What: For your chosen vertical, map every existing data product, its pricing, and its gaps
   294→   - Why: The 40+ source overview here identifies opportunity categories but not specific competitive dynamics within each
   295→
   296→2. **Data Acquisition Cost Analysis**
   297→   - What: For your chosen data product, estimate the cost per record of data collection, cleaning, and structuring
   298→   - Why: Unit economics determine whether the business is viable for a solo founder versus requiring VC funding
   299→
   300→3. **Regulatory Deep Dive for Target Vertical**
   301→   - What: Map specific regulatory requirements (HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, industry-specific) that affect data collection, storage, and sale in your chosen vertical
   302→   - Why: Compliance determines both cost structure and competitive moat depth
   303→
   304→---
   305→
   306→## Bibliography
   307→
   308→[1] YC W26 Batch Analysis (2026). "I analyzed all YC W26 companies: Here's what it tells us about the future." Original source article provided by user.
   309→
   310→[2] Sapp

steps.content:
Here is the complete audit:

---

## RESEARCH AUDIT: Briefs 05 & 06 vs. Core Documents

---

### GAPS

**GAP-1: Competing agent payment protocols not acknowledged**

Brief 05, Finding 7 lists multiple competing agent payment protocols: OpenAI+Stripe's ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol), Google's AP2, and AWS/Coinbase's x402. The core docs treat MPP as essentially the only protocol. The market thesis (`market_thesis.md`, line 24) says "MPP launched March 2026, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs" and the appendix (`appendix.md`, lines 5-6) describes only MPP. No core document mentions ACP, AP2, or that Stripe is simultaneously involved in both MPP *and* a separate Layer 1 blockchain ($500M raise at $5B valuation per Brief 05, Finding 7). This is a material risk: if Stripe's primary bet is ACP rather than MPP, the "first-mover on mpp.dev" thesis weakens.

*Affected docs:* `market_thesis.md` "Why Now" section, "Risks" section; `appendix.md` Section A.

*Suggestion:* Add a competing protocols subsection to the risks, explicitly naming ACP, AP2, and x402. Acknowledge that Stripe's dual involvement in MPP and its own blockchain creates uncertainty about which protocol wins.

---

**GAP-2: Gartner's 40% agentic AI cancellation prediction is unaddressed**

Brief 05 cites Gartner predicting 40% of agentic AI deployments will be canceled by 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, or poor risk controls. The `market_thesis.md` "Key Assumptions" (line 89) assumes "Agent data consumption will grow significantly in 2026-2027" but does not stress-test against this specific, credible counterpoint.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, Key Assumption #1 and Risks section.

*Suggestion:* Add a risk entry: "Agent adoption may plateau. Gartner predicts 40% of agentic AI deployments canceled by 2027. Mitigation: DataFetch data serves both agent and human consumers via REST (Tier 1)."

---

**GAP-3: The enrichment MCP server ecosystem is completely unmapped**

Brief 06 catalogs 90+ enrichment services already available as MCP servers, including major players like Apollo.io (8+ implementations), ZoomInfo (official hosted MCP), Hunter.io, Lusha, and LeadMagic. None of this landscape appears in any core document. The `market_thesis.md` competitive landscape table (lines 67-74) only lists UK-specific data providers (Endole, Creditsafe, etc.) and misses that agents already have rich enrichment infrastructure via MCP. This matters because DataFetch's "agent discoverability" story (`product_design.md`, lines 325-351) via llms.txt and mpp.dev competes with an already-populated MCP registry ecosystem.

*Affected docs:* `market_thesis.md` Competitive Landscape; `product_design.md` Agent Discoverability.

*Suggestion:* Add a "MCP Ecosystem" row to the competitive landscape. Acknowledge that agents already discover and use enrichment services via MCP registries (mcp.so, Glama.ai, Smithery, Pipedream, Composio). Differentiate DataFetch: UK-specific domain depth, intent-shaped interfaces, and environment model vs. flat tool calls.

---

**GAP-4: Waterfall enrichment pattern not considered**

Brief 06 identifies "Unified enrichment waterfall (try Provider A, fallback to B, then C)" as the #3 biggest opportunity for new MCP servers. The `product_design.md` `Enrichable<T>` abstraction (lines 105-133) resolves dimensions one at a time. There is no discussion of waterfall resolution (e.g., try Companies House first, fall back to FCA Register, then Gazette). This is relevant for data quality and completeness.

*Affected doc:* `spec.md` Enrichment Pipeline; `product_design.md` Enrichable<T> section.

*Suggestion:* Document a waterfall resolution strategy for `Enrichable<T>` dimensions, specifying source priority order and fallback behavior.

---

**GAP-5: "Agent schema" concept maps directly to DataFetch but is not cited**

Brief 05 identifies a novel "Agent Schema Business" concept (lines 213-214): "the company that defines and maintains the canonical data structures an AI agent needs to operate in a specific industry... owns the interoperability layer, similar to how HL7/FHIR became the backbone of health data exchange." DataFetch's intent-shaped interfaces *are* exactly this for UK business data. The core docs never frame it this way. This framing would strengthen the narrative in `market_thesis.md` and `product_design.md`.

*Affected docs:* `market_thesis.md` Core Hypothesis; `product_design.md` Vision.

*Suggestion:* Frame DataFetch's typed interfaces as "the canonical agent schema for UK business intelligence," analogous to HL7/FHIR for health data. This strengthens the moat narrative.

---

**GAP-6: Data moat erosion counterevidence not stress-tested**

Brief 05 explicitly registers counterevidence that "increasingly powerful foundation models reduce the need for proprietary data, as models can 'learn' domain specifics from smaller fine-tuning sets or even zero-shot." The `market_thesis.md` trajectory library moat (lines 57-63) assumes compounding value from accumulated patterns. The counterevidence that better models might reduce the value of accumulated patterns is not addressed.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, Key Assumption #12, Risks section.

---

**GAP-7: LinkedIn enrichment legal risk (Proxycurl shutdown)**

Brief 06 notes Proxycurl shut down in January 2026 after LinkedIn sued (line 241). The `spec.md` and `product_design.md` do not mention director/officer enrichment from LinkedIn or social sources, but the `spec.md` entity resolution section (line 149-153) does director matching across companies. If future enrichment dimensions include LinkedIn-sourced data, this legal precedent matters.

*Affected doc:* `spec.md` Enrichment Pipeline (future consideration).

---

**GAP-8: Construction/property data market size from Brief 05 not reflected**

Brief 05 Finding 6 reports PropTech received $16.7B in VC investment in 2025 (67.9% YoY increase), AI-centered proptech growing at 42% annually. The `market_thesis.md` (lines 41-43) gives much vaguer sizing: "UK proptech market: GBP 6+ billion" and "multi-hundred-million-pound market." The research provides harder numbers that would strengthen the property data market case.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, UK Property Data Market section.

---

### CONTRADICTIONS

**CONTRADICTION-1: MPP creator attribution**

The `appendix.md` (line 6) and `market_thesis.md` (line 24) state MPP was "co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs." Brief 05, Finding 7 (line 128) describes a separate dynamic: "OpenAI and Stripe launched ACP," "Google introduced AP2," and "AWS/Coinbase launched x402" as the payment landscape, while also noting "Stripe and Paradigm are building a Layer 1 blockchain." The core docs present MPP as Stripe's primary agent payment bet, but Brief 05 suggests Stripe is hedging across multiple protocols (ACP and its own blockchain). These are not strictly contradictory but create a misleading impression of Stripe's commitment to MPP specifically.

*Affected docs:* `market_thesis.md` "Why Now" (line 24); `appendix.md` Section A (line 6).

*Suggestion:* Qualify Stripe's involvement: note that Stripe is simultaneously backing ACP with OpenAI and building its own blockchain with Paradigm, making its long-term commitment to MPP uncertain.

---

**CONTRADICTION-2: Clearbit pricing discrepancy**

The `appendix.md` (line 83) lists Clearbit at "$0.05-0.25" per query. Brief 06 lists Clearbit as only available through Pipedream/Composio integrations with no standalone MCP server, and no per-query pricing is confirmed (it is described as API-key-based). While not a direct numerical contradiction, the appendix presents Clearbit pricing with false precision when the actual access model is more complex.

*Affected doc:* `appendix.md`, Section C, International Data Products table.

---

### STALE INFO

**STALE-1: DueDil listed as separate entity**

The `appendix.md` (line 71) lists "DueDil (now Creditsafe)" acknowledging the acquisition, but the `market_thesis.md` competitive landscape table (lines 67-74) does not mention DueDil at all. This is not stale per se, but the appendix and thesis are inconsistent in their competitor coverage.

---

**STALE-2: "mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty" may need verification**

The `market_thesis.md` (line 28) claims "mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed." This was presumably true at time of writing. Given Brief 05's description of rapid protocol proliferation (ACP, AP2, x402 all launching in similar timeframes), the MPP directory's emptiness may change quickly, or alternatively the market may consolidate around a different protocol entirely. This claim has a short shelf life and should be marked as time-sensitive.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, "Why Now" section.

---

### MISSED OPPORTUNITIES

**MISSED-1: The "compliance as moat" framing is underused**

Brief 05, Pattern 2 (line 205-206) articulates: "Rather than viewing compliance as a cost, the most defensible data businesses treat it as the barrier that prevents commodity competitors from entering." The `market_thesis.md` treats GDPR as a risk (line 107) rather than a moat. DataFetch's GDPR compliance work (DPIA, LIA, suppression mechanism in `appendix.md` Section F) should be reframed as competitive advantage, not burden.

*Affected docs:* `market_thesis.md` Risks section; `appendix.md` Section F.

*Suggestion:* In the competitive landscape, add: "GDPR/data governance compliance creates a barrier that discourages casual entrants. Our documented DPIA, LIA, and suppression mechanisms are competitive assets, not just legal requirements."

---

**MISSED-2: Flywheel framing from Brief 05 strengthens the trajectory library narrative**

Brief 05, Pattern 3 (line 208-209) describes the data flywheel: "product usage generates more data, which improves the product, which attracts more users." The `market_thesis.md` trajectory library section (lines 57-63) describes the same dynamic but in more abstract terms. Adopting the explicit "flywheel" language and connecting it to validated examples (Abridge, Scale AI from Brief 05) would make the moat argument more concrete and credible.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, The Trajectory Library section.

*Suggestion:* Add: "This flywheel pattern, where product usage generates data that improves the product, is validated by companies like Scale AI ($2B revenue, $29B valuation) and Abridge in healthcare."

---

**MISSED-3: Capital efficiency argument for data businesses**

Brief 05, Insight 2 (line 216-217) argues data businesses have "higher capital efficiency than agent businesses" and can launch for "$0-$50K" vs. "$500K-$5M for an agent company." DataFetch is a data business. The core docs never make this argument to investors/stakeholders. For a YC-context pitch, this framing is powerful.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, could be added to "The Opportunity" or a new "Why a Data Business" section.

---

**MISSED-4: The enrichment waterfall as a product feature**

Brief 06's identification of "Unified enrichment waterfall" as the #3 opportunity (line 37) suggests DataFetch could differentiate by offering multi-source enrichment resolution transparently. The provenance receipt already tracks sources used (`spec.md` lines 400-426), so extending this to show "tried source A (miss), tried source B (hit)" would add transparency and trust.

*Affected doc:* `spec.md`, Provenance Receipts; `product_design.md`, Provenance section.

---

**MISSED-5: MCP as a distribution channel, not just a competitor**

Brief 06 shows that MCP registries (mcp.so, Glama.ai, Smithery, Composio, Pipedream) are where agents discover enrichment services today. The `product_design.md` Agent Discoverability section (lines 325-351) only mentions llms.txt and mpp.dev directory. Publishing DataFetch as an MCP server on these registries would be an immediate, zero-cost distribution channel that the core docs entirely overlook.

*Affected doc:* `product_design.md`, Agent Discoverability section.

*Suggestion:* Add MCP registry listing as a discoverability channel alongside llms.txt and mpp.dev. Consider offering a DataFetch MCP server that wraps the Tier 1 REST API, making DataFetch discoverable in the same ecosystem where 90+ enrichment providers already live.

---

**MISSED-6: Intent data is the biggest gap in enrichment, and DataFetch could fill it for UK**

Brief 06 identifies intent data as "the biggest gap" in the enrichment ecosystem, with Bombora, 6sense, and Demandbase having zero MCP presence. DataFetch's environment model could incorporate hiring signals, filing behavior changes, and company activity patterns as a form of UK business intent data. This is a positioning angle the core docs do not explore.

*Affected doc:* `product_design.md`, Tier 3 Intent Interfaces; `market_thesis.md`, competitive positioning.

---

**MISSED-7: The "data economy beneath the agent economy" framing**

Brief 05's broader implication (line 224-225): "The agent economy will create a parallel 'data economy' worth tens of billions within 5 years. The companies that build the data substrate for agents will be as foundational as AWS was for cloud computing." This is a stronger, more investor-legible version of DataFetch's thesis than what currently appears in `market_thesis.md`. The AWS analogy is especially powerful.

*Affected doc:* `market_thesis.md`, Core Hypothesis.

*Suggestion:* Consider adding: "DataFetch aims to be part of the data substrate for the agent economy, a layer as foundational as AWS was for cloud computing."

---

### Summary of Findings

| Category | Count | Severity |
|----------|-------|----------|
| GAPS | 8 | 3 high (GAP-1, GAP-3, GAP-5), 3 medium, 2 low |
| CONTRADICTIONS | 2 | 1 medium (CONTRADICTION-1), 1 low |
| STALE INFO | 2 | Both low, but GAP-1 subsumes the staleness risk |
| MISSED OPPORTUNITIES | 7 | 3 high (MISSED-1, MISSED-5, MISSED-7), 4 medium |

**Highest-priority actions:**
1. Address competing payment protocols (GAP-1/CONTRADICTION-1), this is a foundational assumption risk
2. Add MCP registry distribution to the discoverability strategy (MISSED-5), this is a free, immediate win
3. Map the enrichment MCP ecosystem as competitive context (GAP-3)
4. Reframe compliance as moat, not risk (MISSED-1)
5. Adopt the "agent schema" and "data economy substrate" framing (GAP-5, MISSED-7)

1→# Intent-Centric Data Environments: A Novel Architecture for Agent Data Markets
     2→
     3→> Research date: 2026-03-23
     4→> Sources: Paradigm (intents), Anoma (intent machines), envrunai (environments), DataFetch (product context)
     5→> Category: architectural synthesis / R&D exploration
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Executive Summary
    10→
    11→This document synthesizes three paradigms into a novel architecture for how AI agents should consume data services:
    12→
    13→1. **Intent-based architecture** (from crypto/Paradigm/Anoma): Users declare *what* they want, solvers figure out *how*
    14→2. **Governed execution environments** (from envrunai/env.run): Software as typed, branchable, governable codebases that agents navigate by writing code
    15→3. **Agent-native data APIs** (from DataFetch): Per-query paid data enrichment for autonomous agents
    16→
    17→The synthesis: **A data API that presents itself as a typed TypeScript environment where the agent's "query" is executable code composed against intent-shaped interfaces, with branching for cheap exploration against mock data before committing to paid execution against real data.**
    18→
    19→This is not a query language. It is not an API. It is a *data environment* that agents inhabit, explore, and execute within.
    20→
    21→---
    22→
    23→## Part 1: What We Learn From Each Paradigm
    24→
    25→### 1.1 Intent Architecture (Paradigm / Anoma)
    26→
    27→**Core paper**: [Intent-Based Architectures and Their Risks](https://www.paradigm.xyz/2023/06/intents) (Paradigm, June 2023)
    28→
    29→**Key insight**: A transaction is imperative ("do A then B, pay C, get X"). An intent is declarative ("I want X, I'll pay up to C"). The system finds the path.
    30→
    31→**Formal definition**: "A signed set of declarative constraints which allow a user to outsource transaction creation to a third party without relinquishing full control."
    32→
    33→**Architecture layers**:
    34→- **User layer**: Express desired outcome + constraints
    35→- **Propagation layer**: Intents are broadcast to a network of potential executors
    36→- **Solver layer**: Third parties find satisfying computational paths, potentially netting multiple intents together
    37→- **Settlement layer**: Verified execution, final state change
    38→
    39→**What transfers to data**:
    40→
    41→| Crypto Intent Concept | Data Environment Analog |
    42→|----------------------|------------------------|
    43→| Intent (declarative constraint) | Agent's TypeScript program describing desired data derivative |
    44→| Solver (finds execution path) | DataFetch's server-side query planner + enrichment engine |
    45→| Settlement (verified execution) | Provenance receipt proving computation over identified datasets |
    46→| Counterparty discovery | Agent discovering data sources via llms.txt / environment manifest |
    47→| Batch execution (multiple intents → one tx) | Multiple data requirements resolved in a single computation pass |
    48→| Order netting (overlapping intents matched) | Shared intermediate computations cached across agent requests |
    49→
    50→**Critical Paradigm warning that applies here**: "The worst-case outcome is a world in which using an intent-based application entails signing an intent that disappears and then somehow materialises as a transaction with no clarity on how or by whom it was created." The provenance receipt is the answer to this in the data context. The agent must be able to verify *what data was used*, *what computation was performed*, and *what the freshness guarantees are*.
    51→
    52→### 1.2 Anoma's Intent Machine
    53→
    54→**Key technical elements**:
    55→
    56→- **Intent Machine** replaces the Virtual Machine. Instead of executing instructions, it matches and satisfies declarative constraints.
    57→- **Typhon** (consensus/network): Gossips intents, orders transactions, handles settlement
    58→- **Taiga** (privacy/execution): Executes state transitions with zero-knowledge proofs, handles information flow control
    59→- **Solvers**: Specialized nodes that match compatible intents. Can net overlapping requirements. Charge fees for resolution.
    60→- **Information flow control**: Three intent types, transparent (everyone sees everything), shielded (who is hidden, what is visible), private (both hidden). Users choose per-intent.
    61→- **Heterogeneous trust**: Different parties can have different security preferences and still achieve atomic settlement.
    62→
    63→**What transfers to data**:
    64→
    65→The information flow control model maps directly to data access tiers:
    66→- **Transparent**: Public data queries (Companies House, Land Registry), the agent sees the data and the computation
    67→- **Shielded**: The agent gets results but the underlying data source is abstracted (third-party proprietary data contributed to the enrichment, agent doesn't see which provider)
    68→- **Private**: Both the query and the result are private (enterprise use case, compliance-sensitive queries)
    69→
    70→The solver model maps to DataFetch's enrichment engine: the agent doesn't specify *which* data sources to query or *how* to join them. It describes the desired output shape. DataFetch's solver determines the optimal data path.
    71→
    72→### 1.3 Governed Execution Environments (envrunai)
    73→
    74→**Core thesis**: Code agents are better at navigating filesystems and writing code than at calling structured APIs. The right interface for an agent to consume a service is something that looks and feels like a codebase.
    75→
    76→**Key mechanisms**:
    77→
    78→- **Typed TypeScript interfaces**: Not the execution language, but the *interface description language*. Agents read `.ts` module files to understand what the service can do, then write code against those types.
    79→- **Mock data / service emulation**: Agents prototype against synthetic data with identical schemas but randomized values. Cheap exploration before committing to real execution.
    80→- **Branching**: Git-like branching of state. Agent creates exploration branches, tests approaches in parallel, commits the winning trajectory. Branches are cheap (copy-on-write).
    81→- **Governance / invariants**: Hard constraints (deterministic, fail-closed), soft verifiers (advisory signals), relative ranking (multi-candidate comparison). The environment tells the agent what it *can't* do, not what it *should* do.
    82→- **Convergence thesis**: LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time. The LLM is the expensive bootstrap; the code it produces is the durable output.
    83→- **Code mode advantages**: 99%+ context pruning vs tool-call-per-step. The agent chains calls together, surfaces only high-signal decision points for model judgment.
    84→
    85→**What transfers to data**:
    86→
    87→This is the execution model. The agent doesn't call endpoints. It writes TypeScript against typed data interfaces, branches to explore query strategies cheaply, and commits to the approach that produces the desired derivative.
    88→
    89→---
    90→
    91→## Part 2: The Synthesis, Intent-Centric Data Environments
    92→
    93→### 2.1 The Core Idea
    94→
    95→DataFetch's data is not exposed as REST endpoints, SQL schemas, or GraphQL types. It is exposed as **a typed TypeScript environment** that agents clone, explore, and execute within.
    96→
    97→The interfaces are not one-to-one mirrors of the underlying data. They are **intent-shaped**: they represent the *kinds of questions agents want to answer*, not the *tables that store the data*.
    98→
    99→```
   100→Traditional API:         GET /companies?sic_code=6201&incorporated_after=2023-01-01
   101→SQL:                     SELECT * FROM companies WHERE sic_code = '6201' AND ...
   102→Intent-centric env:      const targets = await market.findCompetitors({ sector: "data-enrichment", backed_by: "Y Combinator", vintage: { from: 2023 } });
   103→```
   104→
   105→The difference is not syntactic. The agent doesn't need to know that "data enrichment" maps to SIC codes 6201, 6202, 6311, or that "backed by Y Combinator" requires joining a Crunchbase-derived investor table. The intent interface absorbs that complexity. The DataFetch solver resolves it.
   106→
   107→### 2.2 How It Works End-to-End
   108→
   109→```
   110→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   111→│                        AGENT CONTEXT                             │
   112→│                                                                  │
   113→│  1. Agent clones DataFetch environment (typed .ts modules)       │
   114→│  2. Reads interfaces: market.ts, company.ts, property.ts, ...   │
   115→│  3. Branches to explore query strategies against MOCK DATA       │
   116→│  4. Writes TypeScript composing interfaces toward desired output │
   117→│  5. Tests against mock data (free/cheap, fast)                   │
   118→│  6. Commits winning approach                                     │
   119→│  7. Submits for REAL EXECUTION (paid via MPP)                    │
   120→│                                                                  │
   121→└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
   122→                               │
   123→                               │  Intent (TypeScript program + MPP payment)
   124→                               ▼
   125→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   126→│                    DATAFETCH SOLVER                               │
   127→│                                                                  │
   128→│  1. Receives TypeScript intent                                   │
   129→│  2. Validates against governance (invariants, rate limits)       │
   130→│  3. Plans execution: which data sources, join strategy, cachi

1→# Market Thesis: DataFetch (datafetch.ai)
     2→
     3→## Core Hypothesis
     4→
     5→AI agents are becoming the primary consumers of structured data APIs. The Machine Payments Protocol (mpp.dev) enables frictionless per-query purchasing without signup, API keys, or billing accounts. The first data providers to offer enriched public data via MPP will capture the emerging agent economy's data spend.
     6→
     7→The deeper thesis: REST endpoints are a transitional interface. The endgame is **intent-centric data environments**, where agents don't call APIs but write TypeScript programs against typed, intent-shaped interfaces, explore strategies for free against mock data, and commit to paid execution. This creates a fundamentally different relationship (the agent *works within* DataFetch, not *calls* DataFetch) and a compounding moat via the trajectory library.
     8→
     9→## The Opportunity
    10→
    11→### Supply Side: Free Public Data, Expensive to Use
    12→- UK government publishes vast datasets under OGL v3 (Open Government Licence), freely commercially redistributable
    13→- Raw data is free but fragmented across dozens of sources, inconsistent formats, no cross-referencing
    14→- Existing providers (Endole, Creditsafe, Beauhurst) package this data behind enterprise subscriptions ($5K-$100K/yr)
    15→- No existing provider offers per-query, agent-payable access
    16→
    17→### Demand Side: Agents Need Data Mid-Workflow
    18→- AI agents performing due diligence, lead qualification, property research, compliance checks need data on-the-fly
    19→- Current model: human signs up for subscription, configures API key, agent uses it. Friction-heavy, limits agent autonomy
    20→- MPP model: agent discovers endpoint via llms.txt, pays per-query via HTTP 402, gets data. Zero onboarding
    21→- The agent economy is growing rapidly, every major AI lab is shipping agent frameworks (Claude Computer Use, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK)
    22→
    23→### Why Now
    24→- MPP launched March 2026, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs
    25→- Submitted to IETF as formal internet standard (paymentauth.org)
    26→- Stripe integration means card payments work alongside crypto, same dashboard/settlement
    27→- Sub-cent transactions viable on Tempo chain ($0.001 tx fees, 0.5s finality)
    28→- First-mover window: mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed
    29→- UK OGL data is uniquely well-suited: permissive licensing, rich datasets, global demand for UK company/property data
    30→
    31→## Market Sizing
    32→
    33→### UK Business Data Market
    34→- Creditsafe (essentially a Companies House reseller at core): hundreds of millions GBP revenue
    35→- Dun & Bradstreet UK operations: substantial
    36→- Total UK business data market: estimated GBP 1-2 billion annually
    37→- Even niche vertical products (e.g., construction sector financial health): GBP 1-10M ARR
    38→
    39→### UK Property Data Market
    40→- UK proptech market: GBP 6+ billion
    41→- Property data specifically: multi-hundred-million-pound market
    42→- Landmark Information Group, LonRes, Dataloft, Hometrack all operate here
    43→
    44→### Adjacent Markets
    45→- Global weather data market: USD 3-4 billion
    46→- Sales intelligence (ZoomInfo, Apollo): USD 3+ billion
    47→- Location intelligence: USD 15+ billion globally
    48→
    49→### Our Addressable Slice
    50→- We're not replacing Creditsafe or ZoomInfo. We're serving the agent economy's per-query needs
    51→- Target: the long tail of queries that don't justify a subscription
    52→- If 1M agent queries/month at average $0.25/query = $250K MRR = $3M ARR
    53→- If 10M queries/month = $30M ARR
    54→- These are aspirational but directionally plausible given agent growth trajectory
    55→- Environment tier unlocks higher ARPU: complex analytical intents at $2-5 each, vs $0.05-1.00 for REST. An agent doing competitive analysis might spend $5 per intent but get $500 worth of analytical work done in one shot
    56→
    57→### The Trajectory Library (Compounding Moat)
    58→- Every agent that uses the environment tier contributes (anonymized) query patterns
    59→- Common patterns crystallize into optimized curated interfaces (cheaper, faster)
    60→- Over time, the most common analytical intents become deterministic workflows, near-zero marginal token spend
    61→- DataFetch evolves from "data API" to "library of proven analytical intelligence"
    62→- This is a data network effect: more agent usage -> better interfaces -> more agent usage
    63→- The trajectory library is time-based defensibility, a new entrant with the same idea starts with zero accumulated patterns
    64→
    65→## Competitive Landscape
    66→
    67→| Player | Model | Weakness for Agent Economy |
    68→|--------|-------|---------------------------|
    69→| Endole | Credit-based, GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Requires signup, API key, manual billing |
    70→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | $10K+ minimum, human sales process |
    71→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription $5K+ | Targets VCs/government, not agents |
    72→| OpenCorporates | API from $500/mo | Subscription-only, no per-query |
    73→| Companies House API | Free, rate-limited | Raw data only, no enrichment, 600 req/5 min |
    74→
    75→**Gap**: No one offers enriched UK public data with MPP-native per-query payment. The protocol is weeks old.
    76→
    77→**Deeper gap**: No data provider offers an intent-centric environment where agents can explore query strategies for free before paying. Every existing service charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. The mock-then-commit model (validated by PySyft in production at UN/national stats agencies) aligns cost with value in a way no competitor currently does.
    78→
    79→| Player | Could copy REST + MPP? | Could copy intent environment? |
    80→|--------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
    81→| Endole | Yes, if MPP grows | No, requires new interface paradigm + mock data infrastructure |
    82→| Creditsafe | Yes, but cultural mismatch | No, enterprise DNA incompatible with agent-native exploration |
    83→| OpenCorporates | Possible | Unlikely, data-only, no enrichment layer to power intent resolution |
    84→| LLM providers | Could build generic data agents | Lack domain-specific enrichment + trajectory library |
    85→| Snowflake/Databricks | Could build intent layers over warehouses | Sell infrastructure, not data products |
    86→
    87→## Key Assumptions (to be stress-tested)
    88→
    89→1. Agent data consumption will grow significantly in 2026-2027
    90→2. Per-query pricing is viable at $0.05-$2.00 for enriched public data
    91→3. Enrichment (scoring, cross-referencing, entity resolution) creates enough value to justify markup over free raw data
    92→4. MPP adoption will grow beyond early adopters
    93→5. First-mover advantage in the mpp.dev directory matters
    94→6. UK OGL data licensing permits our commercial model without legal risk
    95→7. A small team can build and maintain the data pipeline at acceptable cost
    96→8. The data refresh cadence we can achieve (daily/weekly) is sufficient for buyers
    97→9. Code-writing agents (Claude, Codex) will become the dominant agent archetype, making the TypeScript environment tier the primary interface within 12-18 months
    98→10. The mock-then-commit exploration model is sufficiently compelling to change agent data consumption patterns (validated by PySyft in adjacent domain, but untested for commercial data APIs)
    99→11. Intent-shaped interfaces (encoding domain knowledge) create meaningful value over schema-mirror typed APIs
   100→12. The trajectory library will compound fast enough to create defensibility before competitors can replicate the architecture
   101→
   102→## Risks
   103→
   104→- **MPP adoption risk**: Protocol is brand new, may not gain traction. Mitigation: also offer traditional API key access
   105→- **Data quality risk**: Enrichment algorithms may produce unreliable scores. Mitigation: start with simple, verifiable enrichments
   106→- **Competition risk**: Established players could add MPP support quickly. Mitigation: move fast, build data quality moat
   107→- **Regulatory risk**: GDPR for director personal data, database rights. Mitigation: legitimate interest basis, DPIA, suppression mechanism
   108→- **Unit economics risk**: Per-query revenue may not cover infrastructure costs at low volume. Mitigation: lean architecture (Cloudflare Workers, serverless)
   109→- **Environment adoption risk**: Code-writing agents may not adopt the TypeScript environment tier if REST is "good enough." Mitigation: REST remains Tier 1, environment is additive. The token economics argument (orders of magnitude cheaper for complex queries) creates strong pull for sophisticated agents
   110→- **Interface authoring risk**: Intent-shaped interfaces require deep domain knowledge to author well. Bad interfaces produce bad agent experiences. Mitigation: start with DataFetch-authored interfaces (Phase 1), evolve to community-proposed + AI-generated as usage patterns emerge
   111→- **Mock data fidelity risk**: If mock data distributions don't match real data well enough, agents' exploration results won't predict real execution outcomes. Mitigation: generate mocks from actual data distributions (not random), validate mock-to-real fidelity systematically
   112→

    61→- DataFetch evolves from "data API" to "library of proven analytical intelligence"
    62→- This is a data network effect: more agent usage -> better interfaces -> more agent usage

     4→Generated by /office-hours + /autoplan on 2026-03-23
     5→
     6→## Vision
     7→
     8→DataFetch is the first proof-of-concept environment for envrun.ai. It demonstrates that agents performing complex data tasks inside a **repo-shaped environment** (typed folder of interfaces, tests, governance, mock data) outperform the same agents using CLIs or REST APIs.
     9→
    10→The innovation is not the data. It is the interaction model: agents work *within* DataFetch rather than *calling* it. Instead of teaching an agent a new CLI with unique verbs and flags, you mount a virtual folder of typed TypeScript interfaces. The agent navigates it like a local codebase, which is what it already knows how to do.
    11→
    12→DataFetch uses UK business and property intelligence as its domain, chosen for permissive licensing (OGL v3), rich cross-referenceable datasets, and complexity that rewards the environment model over flat REST calls.
    13→
    14→### Core Thesis
    15→
    16→Code agents navigating typed folder interfaces outperform the same agents using CLIs/APIs for complex data acquisition tasks. **This must be proven by benchmark before committing to build.**
    17→
    18→### Relationship to envrun.ai
    19→
    20→DataFetch is not a standalone product. It is the first environment built with envkit (envrun.ai's SDK), demonstrating the platform's value proposition with a real domain. The second PoC (an execution-based environment with workflow invariants) validates that the SDK generalizes beyond data.
    21→
    22→| DataFetch Concept | envrun.ai Equivalent |
    23→|---|---|
    24→| TypeScript intent-shaped interfaces | Module interfaces (outer rim) |
    25→| Mock-then-commit exploration | Branching + simulation |
    26→| Real execution (paid via MPP) | Merge to production with governance |
    27→| Governance (cost caps, rate limits) | Invariants + soft verifiers |
    28→| Trajectory convergence | Committed extensions/workflows |
    29→| Enrichable\<T\> (resolve on demand) | Inner rim opt-in access |
    30→| Provenance receipts | Traces |
    31→
    32→## Problem Statement
    33→
    34→Code agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) are excellent at navigating codebases: reading files, writing code, branching, testing. But when they need external services, they fall back to CLIs and APIs, each a unique DSL. `stripe customers list --limit 10` is different from `gh pr list --state open` is different from `kubectl get pods`. The agent has to learn each one. Error handling, output parsing, and state management differ for every tool.
    35→
    36→The workaround costs:
    37→- Agents spend tokens learning each CLI's syntax
    38→- Multi-step workflows require extensive glue code between tools
    39→- No free exploration of paywalled data (every API call costs money)
    40→- No branching (can't try 3 approaches in parallel)
    41→- No trajectory reuse (same glue code gets rewritten every session)
    42→
    43→### Demand Evidence
    44→
    45→First-principles thesis. No direct demand from external users.
    46→
    47→Founder observation from using OpenClaw: "Whenever agents have access to folder interfaces and can treat the project as local, even if they're not touching the core logic but they just understand the interfaces, they just seem to perform better than just giving them CLIs and MCPs or APIs."
    48→
    49→Supporting structural evidence:
    50→- Cloudflare demonstrated 99.9% token reduction with code-mode (Mar 2026)
    51→- Anthropic demonstrated 98.7% token reduction independently (Mar 2026)
    52→- Both converged on the same pattern: agents writing code against typed interfaces instead of calling tools one-at-a-time
    53→
    54→## The Interaction Model
    55→
    56→### Three Access Tiers (Long-Term Vision)
    57→
    58→Every data domain on DataFetch is accessible through three tiers. The PoC focuses on Tier 3 (environment-first), with Tier 1 endpoints as a secondary access path. Tier 2 is deferred.
    59→
    60→| Tier | Interface | Agent Requirement | Price Model |
    61→|------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
    62→| Tier 1: REST API | Standard endpoints (`GET /entity/:id/enriched`) | Any HTTP-capable agent | Per-endpoint MPP |
    63→| Tier 2: Natural Language Intent | Agent describes query in English, DataFetch translates | Any agent | Per-intent MPP (deferred) |
    64→| Tier 3: Code Environment | Agent navigates folder of typed interfaces, explores mock data, commits to paid execution | Code-writing agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) | Compute-based MPP (explore free, execute paid) |
    65→
    66→**PoC priority:** Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary (compatibility). Tier 2 deferred.
    67→
    68→### Intent-Shaped Interfaces
    69→
    70→Interfaces encode **domain intelligence**, not data schemas. The agent describes *what* it wants to know. The environment resolves *how*.
    71→
    72→**Bad (schema-mirror):**
    73→```typescript
    74→interface CompaniesTable {
    75→  getById(number: string): Company;
    76→  search(query: { name?: string; sic?: string[] }): Company[];
    77→}
    78→```
    79→
    80→**Good (intent-shaped):**
    81→```typescript
    82→interface MarketIntelligence {
    83→  findCompetitors(criteria: {
    84→    sector: string | string[];
    85→    backed_by?: string;
    86→    vintage?: { from?: number; to?: number };
    87→  }): Promise<CompanySet>;
    88→
    89→  enrichWithTeam(
    90→    companies: CompanySet,
    91→    dimensions: ('headcount' | 'leadership' | 'location_breakdown')[]
    92→  ): Promise<EnrichedCompanySet>;
    93→
    94→  rankBy(
    95→    companies: EnrichedCompanySet,
    96→    metric: 'growth_rate' | 'financial_health' | 'hiring_velocity'
    97→  ): Promise<RankedCompanySet>;
    98→}
    99→```
   100→
   101→The agent doesn't need to know that "data enrichment" maps to SIC codes 6201, 6202, 6311, or that "backed by Y Combinator" requires joining an investor table. The intent interface absorbs domain complexity.
   102→
   103→Over time, the agents' glue code (novel compositions of explore/purchase calls) gets mined to produce simpler, more intent-centric curated interfaces. The interface layer evolves from agent usage, not just author design.
   104→
   105→### The `Enrichable<T>` Abstraction
   106→
   107→Not all data dimensions are materialized upfront. Some are expensive to compute, some require cross-referencing, some are proprietary. The agent sees the full type surface and cost of each dimension, composes its intent without triggering resolution, and resolution happens only at purchase time.
   108→
   109→```typescript
   110→// Enrichable<T>: a dimension that exists but is not materialized.
   111→// The agent sees the type surface and cost, but resolution requires purchase().
   112→type Enrichable<T> = {
   113→  available: true;
   114→  cost: { usd: number; description: string };
   115→  resolve: () => Promise<T>;  // Only callable inside purchase() context
   116→};
   117→
   118→type Company = {
   119→  number: string;
   120→  name: string;
   121→  status: 'active' | 'dissolved' | 'liquidation';
   122→  sic_codes: string[];
   123→  incorporated: Date;
   124→  // Always available (free via explore):
   125→  officers_count: number;
   126→  // Enrichable (costs money, resolved via purchase):
   127→  financials?: Enrichable<FinancialProfile>;
   128→  risk_score?: Enrichable<number>;
   129→  director_network?: Enrichable<DirectorGraph>;
   130→};
   131→```
   132→
   133→In envrun.ai terms, always-available fields are the **outer rim** (public interface). Enrichable dimensions are the **inner rim** (opt-in, paid access). Governance controls which enrichments an agent can request and at what cost.
   134→
   135→### Mock-Then-Commit: Explore Before You Pay
   136→
   137→Every other data API charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. DataFetch inverts this:
   138→
   139→1. Agent enters the environment folder, reads TypeScript interfaces and AGENTS.md
   140→2. Mock data has identical schemas, realistic distributions, but synthetic values
   141→3. Agent branches (`git branch`) to try different query compositions in parallel (free, instant)
   142→4. Agent compares result shape and cardinality across branches
   143→5. Agent commits the winning approach via `purchase()` for real execution (paid via MPP)
   144→6. Real data returned + provenance receipt
   145→
   146→This pattern maps directly to envrun.ai's branching + simulation model: branch = isolated copy of state, merge = governance-checked commit to production.
   147→
   148→### Provenance: The Trust Layer
   149→
   150→Every real execution (purchase) returns a provenance receipt:
   151→- What data sources were used (named, versioned)
   152→- What filters and joins were applied
   153→- Row counts before and after filtering
   154→- Whether the result is reproducible (and until when)
   155→- Drill-down availability and cost for underlying data
   156→- Itemized pricing breakdown
   157→
   158→The agent (or its human principal) can verify the result came from real, identified data and that the computation is auditable. In envrun.ai terms, this is the **trace** for the committed trajectory.
   159→
   160→### The Convergence Play (Future Vision)
   161→
   162→LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time:
   163→
   164→1. First time an agent needs a particular analytical pattern, it writes the intent from scratch
   165→2. That trajectory gets saved as a reusable function (envrun.ai: committed extension)
   166→3. Next time any agent needs similar intelligence, the trajectory runs deterministically
   167→4. Over time, common intents become optimized curated interfaces, near-zero marginal token s
