1→# Economics of Data Goods and the Copy Problem
     2→
     3→Research brief on the fundamental economic properties of data that prevent liquid data markets, and the academic/industry work addressing them.
     4→
     5→---
     6→
     7→## 1. The Non-Rivalrous, Non-Excludable Nature of Data
     8→
     9→### Core Problem
    10→
    11→Data is fundamentally different from physical goods: it is **non-rivalrous** (one person's use does not diminish another's) and difficult to make **excludable** (once shared, the sender loses control). This creates market failures that prevent liquid trading.
    12→
    13→### Key Papers
    14→
    15→**Jones, Charles I. and Christopher Tonetti. "Nonrivalry and the Economics of Data." American Economic Review, 110(9): 2819-2858, 2020.**
    16→- The seminal paper on data nonrivalry. Data (location history, medical records, driving data) can be used by many firms simultaneously. Nonrivalry leads to increasing returns and implies an important role for market structure and property rights.
    17→- Firms fearing creative destruction may choose to **hoard data**, leading to inefficient use of nonrival data. Giving data property rights to consumers can generate near-optimal allocations, as consumers balance privacy concerns against economic gains from selling data broadly.
    18→- Social gains exist from data being used broadly across firms, even with privacy considerations.
    19→- URL: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20191330
    20→- Full PDF: https://christophertonetti.com/files/papers/JonesTonetti_DataNonrivalry.pdf
    21→
    22→**Goldfarb, Avi and Catherine Tucker. "Digital Economics." Journal of Economic Literature, 57(1): 3-43, 2019.**
    23→- Examines how digital technology has reduced five distinct economic costs: **search costs, replication costs, transportation costs, tracking costs, and verification costs**. The near-zero replication cost is the root of the copy problem.
    24→- URL: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jel.20171452
    25→
    26→**UN DESA Working Paper 164. "Economic Properties of Data and the Monopolistic Tendencies of Data Platforms." 2020.**
    27→- The economic characteristics of data (non-rivalry, economies of scale and scope) favour data aggregation in big datasets. Non-rivalry implies the need for exclusive rights to incentivise data production when it is costly. The balance between access and exclusion is at the centre of the data regime debate.
    28→- Making data excludable by one firm does not stop others from understanding preferences if other data pieces are accessible.
    29→- URL: https://www.un.org/esa/desa/papers/2020/wp164_2020.pdf
    30→
    31→### Arrow's Information Paradox
    32→
    33→Kenneth Arrow (1962) observed that the value of information is inherently difficult to trade: its utility is unknown to the buyer until revealed, but once revealed, the buyer possesses it without having paid. This "buyers' inspection paradox" creates information asymmetry between sellers (who know data quality) and buyers (who do not), producing adverse selection.
    34→
    35→**Leppala, Samuli. "Arrow's Paradox and Markets for Nonproprietary Information." Cardiff Economics Working Paper E2013/2.**
    36→- Formalizes Arrow's paradox and explores conditions under which markets for information can function despite it.
    37→- URL: http://patrickminford.net/wp/E2013_2.pdf
    38→
    39→**Rahaman, Nasim et al. "Language Models Can Reduce Asymmetry in Information Markets." arXiv:2403.14443, 2024.**
    40→- Proposes a simulated digital marketplace where LLM-powered agents buy and sell information on behalf of participants. Agents can assess the quality of privileged information while having the ability to "forget," allowing vendors to grant temporary access and reducing risk of unauthorized retention.
    41→- A novel technical approach to Arrow's paradox using AI agents as trusted intermediaries.
    42→- URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.14443
    43→
    44→**"Sell Data to AI Algorithms Without Revealing It" (Trustworthy Influence Protocol / TIP). arXiv:2512.06033, 2024.**
    45→- A privacy-preserving framework enabling buyers to quantify the utility of external data without decrypting raw assets. Integrates Homomorphic Encryption with gradient-based influence functions for precise, blinded scoring of data points against a buyer's specific AI model.
    46→- Directly addresses Arrow's paradox: lets buyers evaluate data value without seeing it.
    47→- URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.06033
    48→
    49→### Data as an Experience Good
    50→
    51→Data exhibits properties of an **experience good** (Nelson, 1970) or **credence good** (Darby & Karni, 1973), where quality cannot be verified before purchase.
    52→
    53→**Stahl, Florian et al. "Selecting Data Assets in Data Marketplaces." Business & Information Systems Engineering, Springer, 2025.**
    54→- Data assets are intangible and their value is highly context-dependent. Data consumers struggle to evaluate quality and relevance without first accessing them. Data providers are hesitant to reveal detailed information due to sovereignty and IP concerns. This reflects Arrow's Information Paradox directly.
    55→- Proposes DQSM (Data Quality and Selection Mechanism) using ML and Explainable AI to assess data asset value.
    56→- URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12599-025-00940-8
    57→
    58→**Stucke, M.E. and Grunes, A.P. "Data as the New Oil: Parallels, Challenges, and Regulatory Implications." NBER Chapter, 2024-2025.**
    59→- Data differs from oil by the fundamental difficulty of pricing information (Arrow's paradox). Ex ante, it is very hard to know whether an AI model would provide information that is actually valuable.
    60→- URL: https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15121/revisions/c15121.rev0.pdf
    61→
    62→**Stahl, Florian et al. "Markets for Data." Industrial and Corporate Change, 29(3): 645-660, Oxford Academic, 2020.**
    63→- Applies Roth's market design theory to data markets. A central concern is safety and quality verification: if a buyer cannot assess data origins (and thus quality and legality), information asymmetries are aggravated and the market becomes inefficient.
    64→- Addresses "thickness" (liquidity): an efficient market needs sufficient pool of participants willing to transact. In markets for unique, context-specific data, lack of thickness is a major factor leading to inefficiency.
    65→- URL: https://academic.oup.com/icc/article/29/3/645/5804957
    66→
    67→---
    68→
    69→## 2. Compute-Without-Copy Paradigms
    70→
    71→### Core Problem
    72→
    73→The traditional data transaction model requires data to move from seller to buyer, at which point the seller loses control. "Compute-without-copy" (or "compute-to-data") inverts this: computation moves to the data, and only results are returned.
    74→
    75→### Key Papers and Platforms
    76→
    77→**McConaghy, Trent et al. "Ocean Protocol: Tools for the Web3 Data Economy." Springer, 2022.**
    78→- Ocean Protocol's Compute-to-Data feature allows compute access on privately held data that never leaves the data owner's premises. Algorithms travel to the data rather than data traveling to the algorithm.
    79→- Implemented using Data NFTs (ERC721) and Datatokens (ERC20) for granular permissioning, pricing, whitelisting, and expiration controls.
    80→- URL: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-07535-3_16
    81→- Whitepaper: https://oceanprotocol.com/tech-whitepaper.pdf
    82→
    83→**Privacy-Preserving Blockchain Platform for a Data Marketplace. ACM Distributed Ledger Technologies, 2023.**
    84→- Proposes a blockchain framework embodying compute-without-copy: users that generate data store it in external servers, while blockchain records transactions and performs access control. Data generators have complete ownership and control.
    85→- URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3573894
    86→
    87→**Warnat-Herresthal, Stefanie et al. "When Federated Learning Meets Privacy-Preserving Computation." ACM Computing Surveys, 2024.**
    88→- Federated Learning is a direct embodiment of compute-to-data: models are trained on local devices using private data and only local models are aggregated, avoiding central collection of raw data.
    89→- URL: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3679013
    90→
    91→**Driessen, Stefan et al. "Understanding How Privacy-Preserving Technologies Transform Data Marketplace Platforms: The Case of Multi-Party Computation." ResearchGate/Delft University, 2019.**
    92→- MPC increases platform openness and shifts control to data providers, but introduces a "trust paradox" where MPC influences trust both positively and negatively simultaneously.
    93→- MPC enables data marketplaces to employ "privacy-as-a-service" business models beyond simple privacy-preserving data exchange.
    94→- URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341072138
    95→
    96→**UN Handbook on Privacy-Preserving Computation Techniques.**
    97→- Differential privacy provides information-theoretic output privacy: it quantifies and limits information about individual records leaked by releasing aggregate computation results. Highly relevant to compute-without-copy where only computation results, not raw data, are exposed.
    98→- URL: https://unstats.un.org/bigdata/task-teams/privacy/UN%20Handbook%20for%20Privacy-Preserving%20Techniques.pdf
    99→
   100→### Maturity Summary
   101→
   102→| Approach | Maturity | Performance | Agent Applicability |
   103→|----------|----------|-------------|---------------------|
   104→| Federated Learning | Production (Google, Apple) | Moderate overhead | High (model training) |
   105→| Secure MPC | Early production | High overhead | Medium (joint computation) |
   106→| TEEs (SGX, TDX) | Production | Low overhead | High (sandboxed execution) |
   107→| Homo

1→# Market Thesis: DataFetch (datafetch.ai)
     2→
     3→## Core Hypothesis
     4→
     5→AI agents are becoming the primary consumers of structured data APIs. The Machine Payments Protocol (mpp.dev) enables frictionless per-query purchasing without signup, API keys, or billing accounts. The first data providers to offer enriched public data via MPP will capture the emerging agent economy's data spend.
     6→
     7→The deeper thesis: REST endpoints are a transitional interface. The endgame is **intent-centric data environments**, where agents don't call APIs but write TypeScript programs against typed, intent-shaped interfaces, explore strategies for free against mock data, and commit to paid execution. This creates a fundamentally different relationship (the agent *works within* DataFetch, not *calls* DataFetch) and a compounding moat via the trajectory library.
     8→
     9→## The Opportunity
    10→
    11→### Supply Side: Free Public Data, Expensive to Use
    12→- UK government publishes vast datasets under OGL v3 (Open Government Licence), freely commercially redistributable
    13→- Raw data is free but fragmented across dozens of sources, inconsistent formats, no cross-referencing
    14→- Existing providers (Endole, Creditsafe, Beauhurst) package this data behind enterprise subscriptions ($5K-$100K/yr)
    15→- No existing provider offers per-query, agent-payable access
    16→
    17→### Demand Side: Agents Need Data Mid-Workflow
    18→- AI agents performing due diligence, lead qualification, property research, compliance checks need data on-the-fly
    19→- Current model: human signs up for subscription, configures API key, agent uses it. Friction-heavy, limits agent autonomy
    20→- MPP model: agent discovers endpoint via llms.txt, pays per-query via HTTP 402, gets data. Zero onboarding
    21→- The agent economy is growing rapidly, every major AI lab is shipping agent frameworks (Claude Computer Use, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK)
    22→
    23→### Why Now
    24→- MPP launched March 2026, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs
    25→- Submitted to IETF as formal internet standard (paymentauth.org)
    26→- Stripe integration means card payments work alongside crypto, same dashboard/settlement
    27→- Sub-cent transactions viable on Tempo chain ($0.001 tx fees, 0.5s finality)
    28→- First-mover window: mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed
    29→- UK OGL data is uniquely well-suited: permissive licensing, rich datasets, global demand for UK company/property data
    30→
    31→## Market Sizing
    32→
    33→### UK Business Data Market
    34→- Creditsafe (essentially a Companies House reseller at core): hundreds of millions GBP revenue
    35→- Dun & Bradstreet UK operations: substantial
    36→- Total UK business data market: estimated GBP 1-2 billion annually
    37→- Even niche vertical products (e.g., construction sector financial health): GBP 1-10M ARR
    38→
    39→### UK Property Data Market
    40→- UK proptech market: GBP 6+ billion
    41→- Property data specifically: multi-hundred-million-pound market
    42→- Landmark Information Group, LonRes, Dataloft, Hometrack all operate here
    43→
    44→### Adjacent Markets
    45→- Global weather data market: USD 3-4 billion
    46→- Sales intelligence (ZoomInfo, Apollo): USD 3+ billion
    47→- Location intelligence: USD 15+ billion globally
    48→
    49→### Our Addressable Slice
    50→- We're not replacing Creditsafe or ZoomInfo. We're serving the agent economy's per-query needs
    51→- Target: the long tail of queries that don't justify a subscription
    52→- If 1M agent queries/month at average $0.25/query = $250K MRR = $3M ARR
    53→- If 10M queries/month = $30M ARR
    54→- These are aspirational but directionally plausible given agent growth trajectory
    55→- Environment tier unlocks higher ARPU: complex analytical intents at $2-5 each, vs $0.05-1.00 for REST. An agent doing competitive analysis might spend $5 per intent but get $500 worth of analytical work done in one shot
    56→
    57→### The Trajectory Library (Compounding Moat)
    58→- Every agent that uses the environment tier contributes (anonymized) query patterns
    59→- Common patterns crystallize into optimized curated interfaces (cheaper, faster)
    60→- Over time, the most common analytical intents become deterministic workflows, near-zero marginal token spend
    61→- DataFetch evolves from "data API" to "library of proven analytical intelligence"
    62→- This is a data network effect: more agent usage -> better interfaces -> more agent usage
    63→- The trajectory library is time-based defensibility, a new entrant with the same idea starts with zero accumulated patterns
    64→
    65→## Competitive Landscape
    66→
    67→| Player | Model | Weakness for Agent Economy |
    68→|--------|-------|---------------------------|
    69→| Endole | Credit-based, GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Requires signup, API key, manual billing |
    70→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | $10K+ minimum, human sales process |
    71→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription $5K+ | Targets VCs/government, not agents |
    72→| OpenCorporates | API from $500/mo | Subscription-only, no per-query |
    73→| Companies House API | Free, rate-limited | Raw data only, no enrichment, 600 req/5 min |
    74→
    75→**Gap**: No one offers enriched UK public data with MPP-native per-query payment. The protocol is weeks old.
    76→
    77→**Deeper gap**: No data provider offers an intent-centric environment where agents can explore query strategies for free before paying. Every existing service charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. The mock-then-commit model (validated by PySyft in production at UN/national stats agencies) aligns cost with value in a way no competitor currently does.
    78→
    79→| Player | Could copy REST + MPP? | Could copy intent environment? |
    80→|--------|----------------------|-------------------------------|
    81→| Endole | Yes, if MPP grows | No, requires new interface paradigm + mock data infrastructure |
    82→| Creditsafe | Yes, but cultural mismatch | No, enterprise DNA incompatible with agent-native exploration |
    83→| OpenCorporates | Possible | Unlikely, data-only, no enrichment layer to power intent resolution |
    84→| LLM providers | Could build generic data agents | Lack domain-specific enrichment + trajectory library |
    85→| Snowflake/Databricks | Could build intent layers over warehouses | Sell infrastructure, not data products |
    86→
    87→## Key Assumptions (to be stress-tested)
    88→
    89→1. Agent data consumption will grow significantly in 2026-2027
    90→2. Per-query pricing is viable at $0.05-$2.00 for enriched public data
    91→3. Enrichment (scoring, cross-referencing, entity resolution) creates enough value to justify markup over free raw data
    92→4. MPP adoption will grow beyond early adopters
    93→5. First-mover advantage in the mpp.dev directory matters
    94→6. UK OGL data licensing permits our commercial model without legal risk
    95→7. A small team can build and maintain the data pipeline at acceptable cost
    96→8. The data refresh cadence we can achieve (daily/weekly) is sufficient for buyers
    97→9. Code-writing agents (Claude, Codex) will become the dominant agent archetype, making the TypeScript environment tier the primary interface within 12-18 months
    98→10. The mock-then-commit exploration model is sufficiently compelling to change agent data consumption patterns (validated by PySyft in adjacent domain, but untested for commercial data APIs)
    99→11. Intent-shaped interfaces (encoding domain knowledge) create meaningful value over schema-mirror typed APIs
   100→12. The trajectory library will compound fast enough to create defensibility before competitors can replicate the architecture
   101→
   102→## Risks
   103→
   104→- **MPP adoption risk**: Protocol is brand new, may not gain traction. Mitigation: also offer traditional API key access
   105→- **Data quality risk**: Enrichment algorithms may produce unreliable scores. Mitigation: start with simple, verifiable enrichments
   106→- **Competition risk**: Established players could add MPP support quickly. Mitigation: move fast, build data quality moat
   107→- **Regulatory risk**: GDPR for director personal data, database rights. Mitigation: legitimate interest basis, DPIA, suppression mechanism
   108→- **Unit economics risk**: Per-query revenue may not cover infrastructure costs at low volume. Mitigation: lean architecture (Cloudflare Workers, serverless)
   109→- **Environment adoption risk**: Code-writing agents may not adopt the TypeScript environment tier if REST is "good enough." Mitigation: REST remains Tier 1, environment is additive. The token economics argument (orders of magnitude cheaper for complex queries) creates strong pull for sophisticated agents
   110→- **Interface authoring risk**: Intent-shaped interfaces require deep domain knowledge to author well. Bad interfaces produce bad agent experiences. Mitigation: start with DataFetch-authored interfaces (Phase 1), evolve to community-proposed + AI-generated as usage patterns emerge
   111→- **Mock data fidelity risk**: If mock data distributions don't match real data well enough, agents' exploration results won't predict real execution outcomes. Mitigation: generate mocks from actual data distributions (not random), validate mock-to-real fidelity systematically

1→# Market Thesis: DataFetch (datafetch.ai)
     2→
     3→## Core Hypothesis
     4→
     5→AI agents are becoming the primary consumers of structured data APIs. The Machine Payments Protocol (mpp.dev) enables frictionless per-query purchasing without signup, API keys, or billing accounts. The first data providers to offer enriched public data via MPP will capture the emerging agent economy's data spend.
     6→
     7→The deeper thesis: REST endpoints are a transitional interface. The endgame is **intent-centric data environments**, where agents don't call APIs but write TypeScript programs against typed, intent-shaped interfaces, explore strategies for free against mock data, and commit to paid execution. This creates a fundamentally different relationship (the agent *works within* DataFetch, not *calls* DataFetch) and a compounding moat via the trajectory library.
     8→
     9→## The Opportunity
    10→
    11→### Supply Side: Free Public Data, Expensive to Use
    12→- UK government publishes vast datasets under OGL v3 (Open Government Licence), freely commercially redistributable
    13→- Raw data is free but fragmented across dozens of sources, inconsistent formats, no cross-referencing
    14→- Existing providers (Endole, Creditsafe, Beauhurst) package this data behind enterprise subscriptions ($5K-$100K/yr)
    15→- No existing provider offers per-query, agent-payable access
    16→
    17→### Demand Side: Agents Need Data Mid-Workflow
    18→- AI agents performing due diligence, lead qualification, property research, compliance checks need data on-the-fly
    19→- Current model: human signs up for subscription, configures API key, agent uses it. Friction-heavy, limits agent autonomy
    20→- MPP model: agent discovers endpoint via llms.txt, pays per-query via HTTP 402, gets data. Zero onboarding
    21→- The agent economy is growing rapidly, every major AI lab is shipping agent frameworks (Claude Computer Use, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK)
    22→
    23→### Why Now
    24→- MPP launched March 2026, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs
    25→- Submitted to IETF as formal internet standard (paymentauth.org)
    26→- Stripe integration means card payments work alongside crypto, same dashboard/settlement
    27→- Sub-cent transactions viable on Tempo chain ($0.001 tx fees, 0.5s finality)
    28→- First-mover window: mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty, a handful of services listed
    29→- UK OGL data is uniquely well-suited: permissive licensing, rich datasets, global demand for UK company/property data
    30→
    31→## Market Sizing
    32→
    33→### UK Business Data Market
    34→- Creditsafe (essentially a Companies House reseller at core): hundreds of millions GBP revenue
    35→- Dun & Bradstreet UK operations: substantial
    36→- Total UK business data market: estimated GBP 1-2 billion annually
    37→- Even niche vertical products (e.g., construction sector financial health): GBP 1-10M ARR
    38→
    39→### UK Property Data Market
    40→- UK proptech market: GBP 6+ billion
    41→- Property data specifically: multi-hundred-million-pound market
    42→- Landmark Information Group, LonRes, Dataloft, Hometrack all operate here
    43→
    44→### Adjacent Markets
    45→- Global weather data market: USD 3-4 billion
    46→- Sales intelligence (ZoomInfo, Apollo): USD 3+ billion
    47→- Location intelligence: USD 15+ billion globally
    48→
    49→### Our Addressable Slice
    50→- We're not replacing Creditsafe or ZoomInfo. We're serving the agent economy's per-query needs
    51→- Target: the long tail of queries that don't justify a subscription
    52→- If 1M agent queries/month at average $0.25/query = $250K MRR = $3M ARR
    53→- If 10M queries/month = $30M ARR
    54→- These are aspirational but directionally plausible given agent growth trajectory
    55→- Environment tier unlocks higher ARPU: complex analytical intents at $2-5 each, vs $0.05-1.00 for REST. An agent doing competitive analysis might spend $5 per intent but get $500 worth of analytical work done in one shot
    56→
    57→### The Trajectory Library (Compounding Moat)
    58→- Every agent that uses the environment tier contributes (anonymized) query patterns
    59→- Common patterns crystallize into optimized curated interfaces (cheaper, faster)
    60→- Over time, the most common analytical intents become deterministic workflows, near-zero marginal token spend
    61→- DataFetch evolves from "data API" to "library of proven analytical intelligence"
    62→- This is a data network effect: more agent usage -> better interfaces -> more agent usage
    63→- The trajectory library is time-based defensibility, a new entrant with the same idea starts with zero accumulated patterns

1→# Product Design: DataFetch, envrun.ai's First Proof-of-Concept Environment
     2→
     3→Status: APPROVED
     4→Generated by /office-hours + /autoplan on 2026-03-23
     5→
     6→## Vision
     7→
     8→DataFetch is the first proof-of-concept environment for envrun.ai. It demonstrates that agents performing complex data tasks inside a **repo-shaped environment** (typed folder of interfaces, tests, governance, mock data) outperform the same agents using CLIs or REST APIs.
     9→
    10→The innovation is not the data. It is the interaction model: agents work *within* DataFetch rather than *calling* it. Instead of teaching an agent a new CLI with unique verbs and flags, you mount a virtual folder of typed TypeScript interfaces. The agent navigates it like a local codebase, which is what it already knows how to do.
    11→
    12→DataFetch uses UK business and property intelligence as its domain, chosen for permissive licensing (OGL v3), rich cross-referenceable datasets, and complexity that rewards the environment model over flat REST calls.
    13→
    14→### Core Thesis
    15→
    16→Code agents navigating typed folder interfaces outperform the same agents using CLIs/APIs for complex data acquisition tasks. **This must be proven by benchmark before committing to build.**
    17→
    18→### Relationship to envrun.ai
    19→
    20→DataFetch is not a standalone product. It is the first environment built with envkit (envrun.ai's SDK), demonstrating the platform's value proposition with a real domain. The second PoC (an execution-based environment with workflow invariants) validates that the SDK generalizes beyond data.
    21→
    22→| DataFetch Concept | envrun.ai Equivalent |
    23→|---|---|
    24→| TypeScript intent-shaped interfaces | Module interfaces (outer rim) |
    25→| Mock-then-commit exploration | Branching + simulation |
    26→| Real execution (paid via MPP) | Merge to production with governance |
    27→| Governance (cost caps, rate limits) | Invariants + soft verifiers |
    28→| Trajectory convergence | Committed extensions/workflows |
    29→| Enrichable\<T\> (resolve on demand) | Inner rim opt-in access |
    30→| Provenance receipts | Traces |
    31→
    32→## Problem Statement
    33→
    34→Code agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) are excellent at navigating codebases: reading files, writing code, branching, testing. But when they need external services, they fall back to CLIs and APIs, each a unique DSL. `stripe customers list --limit 10` is different from `gh pr list --state open` is different from `kubectl get pods`. The agent has to learn each one. Error handling, output parsing, and state management differ for every tool.
    35→
    36→The workaround costs:
    37→- Agents spend tokens learning each CLI's syntax
    38→- Multi-step workflows require extensive glue code between tools
    39→- No free exploration of paywalled data (every API call costs money)
    40→- No branching (can't try 3 approaches in parallel)
    41→- No trajectory reuse (same glue code gets rewritten every session)
    42→
    43→### Demand Evidence
    44→
    45→First-principles thesis. No direct demand from external users.
    46→
    47→Founder observation from using OpenClaw: "Whenever agents have access to folder interfaces and can treat the project as local, even if they're not touching the core logic but they just understand the interfaces, they just seem to perform better than just giving them CLIs and MCPs or APIs."
    48→
    49→Supporting structural evidence:
    50→- Cloudflare demonstrated 99.9% token reduction with code-mode (Mar 2026)
    51→- Anthropic demonstrated 98.7% token reduction independently (Mar 2026)
    52→- Both converged on the same pattern: agents writing code against typed interfaces instead of calling tools one-at-a-time
    53→
    54→## The Interaction Model
    55→
    56→### Three Access Tiers (Long-Term Vision)
    57→
    58→Every data domain on DataFetch is accessible through three tiers. The PoC focuses on Tier 3 (environment-first), with Tier 1 endpoints as a secondary access path. Tier 2 is deferred.
    59→
    60→| Tier | Interface | Agent Requirement | Price Model |
    61→|------|-----------|-------------------|-------------|
    62→| Tier 1: REST API | Standard endpoints (`GET /entity/:id/enriched`) | Any HTTP-capable agent | Per-endpoint MPP |
    63→| Tier 2: Natural Language Intent | Agent describes query in English, DataFetch translates | Any agent | Per-intent MPP (deferred) |
    64→| Tier 3: Code Environment | Agent navigates folder of typed interfaces, explores mock data, commits to paid execution | Code-writing agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) | Compute-based MPP (explore free, execute paid) |
    65→
    66→**PoC priority:** Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary (compatibility). Tier 2 deferred.
    67→
    68→### Intent-Shaped Interfaces
    69→
    70→Interfaces encode **domain intelligence**, not data schemas. The agent describes *what* it wants to know. The environment resolves *how*.
    71→
    72→**Bad (schema-mirror):**
    73→```typescript
    74→interface CompaniesTable {
    75→  getById(number: string): Company;
    76→  search(query: { name?: string; sic?: string[] }): Company[];
    77→}
    78→```
    79→
    80→**Good (intent-shaped):**
    81→```typescript
    82→interface MarketIntelligence {
    83→  findCompetitors(criteria: {
    84→    sector: string | string[];
    85→    backed_by?: string;
    86→    vintage?: { from?: number; to?: number };
    87→  }): Promise<CompanySet>;
    88→
    89→  enrichWithTeam(
    90→    companies: CompanySet,
    91→    dimensions: ('headcount' | 'leadership' | 'location_breakdown')[]
    92→  ): Promise<EnrichedCompanySet>;
    93→
    94→  rankBy(
    95→    companies: EnrichedCompanySet,
    96→    metric: 'growth_rate' | 'financial_health' | 'hiring_velocity'
    97→  ): Promise<RankedCompanySet>;
    98→}
    99→```
   100→
   101→The agent doesn't need to know that "data enrichment" maps to SIC codes 6201, 6202, 6311, or that "backed by Y Combinator" requires joining an investor table. The intent interface absorbs domain complexity.
   102→
   103→Over time, the agents' glue code (novel compositions of explore/purchase calls) gets mined to produce simpler, more intent-centric curated interfaces. The interface layer evolves from agent usage, not just author design.
   104→
   105→### The `Enrichable<T>` Abstraction
   106→
   107→Not all data dimensions are materialized upfront. Some are expensive to compute, some require cross-referencing, some are proprietary. The agent sees the full type surface and cost of each dimension, composes its intent without triggering resolution, and resolution happens only at purchase time.
   108→
   109→```typescript
   110→// Enrichable<T>: a dimension that exists but is not materialized.
   111→// The agent sees the type surface and cost, but resolution requires purchase().
   112→type Enrichable<T> = {
   113→  available: true;
   114→  cost: { usd: number; description: string };
   115→  resolve: () => Promise<T>;  // Only callable inside purchase() context
   116→};
   117→
   118→type Company = {
   119→  number: string;
   120→  name: string;
   121→  status: 'active' | 'dissolved' | 'liquidation';
   122→  sic_codes: string[];
   123→  incorporated: Date;
   124→  // Always available (free via explore):
   125→  officers_count: number;
   126→  // Enrichable (costs money, resolved via purchase):
   127→  financials?: Enrichable<FinancialProfile>;
   128→  risk_score?: Enrichable<number>;
   129→  director_network?: Enrichable<DirectorGraph>;
   130→};
   131→```
   132→
   133→In envrun.ai terms, always-available fields are the **outer rim** (public interface). Enrichable dimensions are the **inner rim** (opt-in, paid access). Governance controls which enrichments an agent can request and at what cost.
   134→
   135→### Mock-Then-Commit: Explore Before You Pay
   136→
   137→Every other data API charges the moment you call it, even if the result isn't what you wanted. DataFetch inverts this:
   138→
   139→1. Agent enters the environment folder, reads TypeScript interfaces and AGENTS.md
   140→2. Mock data has identical schemas, realistic distributions, but synthetic values
   141→3. Agent branches (`git branch`) to try different query compositions in parallel (free, instant)
   142→4. Agent compares result shape and cardinality across branches
   143→5. Agent commits the winning approach via `purchase()` for real execution (paid via MPP)
   144→6. Real data returned + provenance receipt
   145→
   146→This pattern maps directly to envrun.ai's branching + simulation model: branch = isolated copy of state, merge = governance-checked commit to production.
   147→
   148→### Provenance: The Trust Layer
   149→
   150→Every real execution (purchase) returns a provenance receipt:
   151→- What data sources were used (named, versioned)
   152→- What filters and joins were applied
   153→- Row counts before and after filtering
   154→- Whether the result is reproducible (and until when)
   155→- Drill-down availability and cost for underlying data
   156→- Itemized pricing breakdown
   157→
   158→The agent (or its human principal) can verify the result came from real, identified data and that the computation is auditable. In envrun.ai terms, this is the **trace** for the committed trajectory.
   159→
   160→### The Convergence Play (Future Vision)
   161→
   162→LLM execution converges toward deterministic software over time:
   163→
   164→1. First time an agent needs a particular analytical pattern, it writes the intent from scratch
   165→2. That trajectory gets saved as a reusable function (envrun.ai: committed extension)
   166→3. Next time any agent needs similar intelligence, the trajectory runs deterministically
   167→4. Over time, common intents become optimized curated interfaces, near-zero marginal token s

1→# Technical Specification: DataFetch (datafetch.ai)
     2→
     3→## Architecture Overview
     4→
     5→### Phase 1: REST API Layer
     6→
     7→```
     8→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
     9→│                   DATA INGESTION                 │
    10→│  Bulk downloads (CH, LR, EPC) -> daily refresh   │
    11→│  APIs (CH streaming, CQC, FHRS) -> near-realtime│
    12→│  Scrapers (planning portals) -> scheduled crawls │
    13→└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
    14→                       v
    15→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    16→│               ENRICHMENT PIPELINE                │
    17→│  Normalization -> Entity Resolution -> Scoring   │
    18→│  Cross-referencing -> Geocoding -> Classification│
    19→│  (Dagster orchestration)                         │
    20→└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
    21→                       v
    22→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    23→│                PRODUCTION STORE                   │
    24→│  PostgreSQL (structured) + search index          │
    25→│  Redis (cache) + S3 (raw archive)                │
    26→└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
    27→                       v
    28→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    29→│                  API LAYER (MPP)                  │
    30→│  Hono on Cloudflare Workers                      │
    31→│  mppx middleware for per-endpoint pricing        │
    32→│  llms.txt for agent discoverability              │
    33→└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    34→```
    35→
    36→### Phase 4: Intent-Centric Environment Layer
    37→
    38→Adds a second access path on top of the same data infrastructure:
    39→
    40→```
    41→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    42→│                        AGENT CONTEXT                             │
    43→│                                                                  │
    44→│  1. Agent clones DataFetch environment (typed .ts modules)       │
    45→│  2. Reads intent-shaped interfaces: market.ts, property.ts, ... │
    46→│  3. Branches to explore query strategies against MOCK DATA       │
    47→│  4. Writes TypeScript composing interfaces toward desired output │
    48→│  5. Tests against mock data (free, fast)                         │
    49→│  6. Commits winning approach                                     │
    50→│  7. Submits for REAL EXECUTION (paid via MPP)                    │
    51→│                                                                  │
    52→└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
    53→                               │
    54→                               │  Intent (TypeScript program + MPP payment)
    55→                               v
    56→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    57→│                    DATAFETCH SOLVER                               │
    58→│                                                                  │
    59→│  1. Receives TypeScript intent                                   │
    60→│  2. Validates against governance (invariants, rate limits, caps) │
    61→│  3. Plans execution: which data sources, join strategy, caching  │
    62→│  4. Executes computation server-side against production store    │
    63→│  5. Generates provenance receipt                                 │
    64→│  6. Returns derivative data + receipt                            │
    65→│                                                                  │
    66→└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
    67→                               │
    68→                               │  Derivative data + provenance receipt
    69→                               v
    70→┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    71→│                        AGENT CONTEXT                             │
    72→│                                                                  │
    73→│  Receives compact result:                                        │
    74→│  - N entities matching intent (not raw records)                  │
    75→│  - Enrichment dimensions resolved as requested                   │
    76→│  - Provenance: sources, versions, filters, query hash            │
    77→│  - Drill-down endpoints for any row (paid, on-demand)            │
    78→│                                                                  │
    79→└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    80→```
    81→
    82→Both layers share the same data ingestion, enrichment pipeline, and production store. The environment layer adds: TypeScript interface modules, mock data generation, intent solver, and provenance receipt generation.
    83→
    84→## Data Ingestion
    85→
    86→### Companies House
    87→
    88→**Bulk Data (daily):**
    89→- Source: Companies House bulk data product (CSV/JSON)
    90→- Contains: ~5M active companies, officers, PSCs, charges, filing history
    91→- Refresh: Daily snapshot download via Companies House data products page
    92→- Storage: Raw files to S3, parsed records to PostgreSQL
    93→
    94→**Streaming API (near-realtime):**
    95→- Source: Companies House streaming API
    96→- Events: New filings, company updates, officer appointments/resignations
    97→- Consumer: Long-running process that applies deltas to production DB
    98→- Latency: Minutes from filing to availability
    99→
   100→**Accounts Data (iXBRL):**
   101→- Source: Companies House document API
   102→- Format: iXBRL (inline XBRL tagged HTML)
   103→- Extraction: Parse XBRL tags to extract: revenue, profit/loss, total assets, total liabilities, net assets, employee count
   104→- Challenge: Not all companies file digitally. Micro-entities file minimal data. Only ~40% of companies file accounts with useful financial detail
   105→- Storage: Extracted financial metrics in dedicated table, linked to company record
   106→
   107→### Land Registry
   108→
   109→**Price Paid Data (monthly):**
   110→- Source: gov.uk bulk download (CSV)
   111→- Contains: Every residential transaction in England & Wales since 1995 (~28M records)
   112→- Fields: Price, date, postcode, property type, tenure, new/old, address
   113→- Refresh: Monthly update file (incremental)
   114→
   115→**CCOD/OCOD (quarterly):**
   116→- Source: gov.uk bulk download
   117→- CCOD: ~3.5M titles owned by UK companies (title number, tenure, address, company, CH number, price paid)
   118→- OCOD: ~100K titles owned by overseas entities
   119→- Cross-reference: CCOD company numbers link directly to Companies House
   120→
   121→**EPC Register (monthly):**
   122→- Source: Open Data Communities bulk download
   123→- Contains: Energy Performance Certificates for ~20M properties
   124→- Fields: Address, EPC rating (A-G), floor area, wall type, heating type, estimated energy cost
   125→- Cross-reference: Address matching to Land Registry records
   126→
   127→### Additional Sources
   128→

1→# Appendix: Reference Data & Market Context
     2→
     3→## A. MPP Protocol Reference
     4→
     5→### What is MPP?
     6→Machine Payments Protocol, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs (March 2026). An HTTP authentication scheme that standardizes the 402 Payment Required status code.
     7→
     8→### Core Flow
     9→1. Client requests resource -> `GET /endpoint`
    10→2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)
    11→3. Client pays (signs blockchain tx, provides card token, etc.)
    12→4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
    13→5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header
    14→
    15→### Transaction Modes
    16→- **Charge (one-time):** Immediate settlement per request. Good for discrete API calls
    17→- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency
    18→
    19→### SDKs
    20→| Language | Package | Install |
    21→|----------|---------|---------|
    22→| TypeScript | mppx | npm install mppx |
    23→| Python | pympp | pip install pympp |
    24→| Rust | mpp-rs | cargo add mpp |
    25→
    26→### Key Resources
    27→- Protocol overview: mpp.dev/overview
    28→- Server quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/server
    29→- Agent quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/agent
    30→- IETF spec: paymentauth.org
    31→- Stripe blog: stripe.com/blog/machine-payments-protocol
    32→
    33→## B. UK Open Government Licence (OGL v3) Summary
    34→
    35→**Permits:** Copy, publish, distribute, transmit, adapt, exploit commercially and non-commercially
    36→**Requires:** Acknowledge the source, provide link to licence
    37→**Does NOT require:** Payment, registration, or permission
    38→
    39→### OGL-Covered Datasets Used
    40→- Companies House basic company data
    41→- Land Registry Price Paid Data
    42→- Land Registry CCOD/OCOD
    43→- EPC Register
    44→- Charity Commission register
    45→- CQC provider data
    46→- FHRS food hygiene ratings
    47→- Ofsted inspection data
    48→- Census / ONS statistical data
    49→- The Gazette (insolvency notices)
    50→- Met Office DataPoint
    51→- police.uk crime data
    52→- HMRC trade statistics
    53→
    54→### NOT OGL (require separate licensing)
    55→- Ordnance Survey premium products (AddressBase, MasterMap)
    56→- Royal Mail PAF (postcode/address data)
    57→- Land Registry National Polygon Dataset (GBP 4,500+/yr)
    58→- Individual Land Registry title registers (GBP 3/title, no bulk redistribution)
    59→
    60→## C. Competitor Pricing Reference
    61→
    62→### UK Company Data
    63→
    64→| Provider | Model | Price Point | Enrichment Level |
    65→|----------|-------|-------------|------------------|
    66→| Companies House API | Free | 0 (rate-limited) | Raw data only |
    67→| Endole | Pay-as-you-go | GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Scored, basic network |
    68→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | GBP 10K+/yr minimum | Full credit scoring |
    69→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription | GBP 5K-30K/yr | Growth/innovation signals |
    70→| OpenCorporates | API subscription | $500+/mo | Cross-jurisdiction, no scoring |

    75→- Comparable to Endole on enriched (GBP 0.25)
    76→- Below DueDil on compliance checks (GBP 1.00 vs 1.50+)
    77→- Zero friction: no signup, no subscription, no API key
    78→
    79→### International Data Products (for comparison)

    81→| Provider | Data Type | Per-Query Price |
    82→|----------|-----------|-----------------|

    89→## D. Companies House Data Schema (Key Fields)
    90→
    91→### Company Profile
    92→- company_number (PK)
    93→- company_name

    95→- company_type (ltd, plc, llp, etc.)

    99→- sic_codes (array of 5-digit codes)

   118→- psc_id
   119→- company_number (FK)
   120→- name or corporate_name
   121→- natures_of_control (array: ownership-of-shares-25-to-50-percent, voting-rights-75-to-100-percent, etc.)
   122→- nationality, country_of_residence
   123→- date_of_birth (month, year)
   124→- address
   125→- ceased_on (if no longer a PSC)
   126→- For corporate PSCs: identification.legal_authority, identification.place_registered, identification.registration_number
   127→
   128→### Charges
   129→- charge_id
   130→- company_number (FK)
   131→- status (outstanding, fully-satisfied, part-satisfied)
   132→- created_on, delivered_on, satisfied_on
   133→- persons_entitled (lender names)
   134→- particulars (description of charged property)
   135→- classification (nature-of-charge, etc.)
   136→
   137→## E. Financial Health Score Methodology (Draft)
   138→
   139→### Input Variables
   140→
   141→**From Accounts (40% weight):**
   142→- Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (target: > 1.5)
   143→- Debt to equity = total liabilities / net assets (target: < 2.0)
   144→- Net assets trend (increasing = positive signal)
   145→- Revenue growth YoY (where available)
   146→- Profit margin (where available)
   147→
   148→**From Filing Behaviour (25% weight):**
   149→- Average days late (0 = perfect, >30 = concerning)
   150→- Percentage of filings late
   151→- Currently overdue filings count
   152→- Trend: improving or worsening
   153→
   154→**From Charges (15% weight):**
   155→- Active charges count
   156→- Recent charge activity (new charges in last 12 months)
   157→- Charge satisfaction rate
   158→
   159→**From Gazette/Insolvency (15% weight):**
   160→- Winding-up petitions (severe negative signal)
   161→- Strike-off action (moderate negative)
   162→- Administrative receiver appointed (severe)
   163→
   164→**From Company Age/Status (5% weight):**
   165→- Companies < 2 years old get a slight penalty (less track record)
   166→- Dormant companies scored separately
   167→
   168→### Score Bands
   169→- 80-100: Strong financial position
   170→- 60-79: Adequate, no immediate concerns
   171→- 40-59: Caution, some risk indicators
   172→- 20-39: Significant risk, multiple negative signals
   173→- 0-19: Severe risk, active insolvency indicators
   174→
   175→### Known Limitations
   176→- ~60% of UK companies file micro-entity or abbreviated accounts with minimal financial detail
   177→- Score for these companies relies heavily on filing behaviour and charges (lower confidence)
   178→- Financial data can be up to 21 months old at time of filing (9 month filing deadline + 12 month accounting period)
   179→- Score should always be accompanied by confidence indicator and data freshness
   180→
   181→## F. GDPR Compliance Plan
   182→
   183→### Personal Data Processed
   184→- Director/secretary names
   185→- Director date of birth (month/year only)
   186→- Director correspondence addresses (not residential)
   187→- PSC names, nationality, country of residence
   188→
   189→### Lawful Basis
   190→- Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f))
   191→- Data is published by Companies House under statutory authority
   192→- Processing serves legitimate business interests (credit checking, due diligence, compliance)
   193→- Balanced against individual rights: data is already public, we add enrichment not new personal data
   194→
   195→### Required Actions
   196→1. Privacy policy explaining processing activities
   197→2. Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) documented
   198→3. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for systematic profiling
   199→4. Right to object mechanism (suppression list)
   200→5. Data subject access request (DSAR) process
   201→6. Respect Companies House residential address suppression
   202→7. Do not attempt to derive full dates of birth
   203→8. Consider ICO registration if not already registered
   204→
   205→## G. Potential Product Expansion Path
   206→
   207→```
   208→Phase 1 (Months 1-2): Company Intelligence API
   209→  |
   210→  v
   211→Phase 2 (Months 2-4): + Property Intelligence
   212→  |
   213→  v
   214→Phase 3 (Months 4-6): + Planning Pipeline + Trade Intelligence
   215→  |
   216→  v
   217→Phase 4 (Months 6-12): + Climate Risk + Tech/Hiring Signals
   218→  |
   219→  v
   220→Phase 5 (Year 2): + Niche products (Care, Charity, Food, Hyperlocal)
   221→  |
   222→  v
   223→Phase 6 (Year 2+): International expansion (US SEC, EU company registries)
   224→```

1→# Privacy-Preserving Computation for Data Marketplaces
     2→
     3→> Research date: 2026-03-24
     4→> Category: technical landscape / privacy engineering
     5→> Scope: Technologies organized by what they protect, assessed for agent-native marketplace applicability
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Executive Summary
    10→
    11→Privacy-preserving computation (PPC) is a $4-5B market in 2025, growing at ~28% CAGR. The landscape divides cleanly into five protection categories: input privacy, input verification, governance, output privacy, and output verification. Each is at a different maturity level, and each has different implications for agent-native data marketplaces where the "user" is autonomous code rather than a human analyst.
    12→
    13→The key finding: **no single technology solves the full stack**. Production systems combine 2-3 techniques (e.g., federated learning + differential privacy + policy engines). For an agent-native marketplace like DataFetch, the most practical near-term stack is: governance via policy engines (mature, low overhead), output privacy via differential privacy (proven at scale), input verification via digital signatures + provenance (production-ready), and compute-to-data sandboxes (PySyft model) as the primary input privacy mechanism, deferring heavier cryptographic approaches (FHE, SMPC) to specific high-value use cases.
    14→
    15→---
    16→
    17→## 1. INPUT PRIVACY (Data Hidden from Processor)
    18→
    19→### 1.1 Homomorphic Encryption (HE)
    20→
    21→**What it does:** Allows computation on encrypted data without decryption. The processor never sees plaintext.
    22→
    23→**Current practical maturity: Late research / early production**
    24→
    25→- The global HE market was valued at ~$195M in 2024, projected to reach $725M by 2032 (21% CAGR).
    26→- 92% of market share is Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), not partial schemes.
    27→- NYU's Orion framework (2025) demonstrated FHE on a 139M-parameter object detection model, ~500x larger than prior FHE demonstrations.
    28→
    29→**Performance overhead: 100-10,000x slower than plaintext operations**
    30→
    31→- CKKS scheme outperforms TFHE for most arithmetic operations on datasets of 65,536 32-bit integers.
    32→- Bootstrapping (noise refresh) requires seconds per operation on current hardware.
    33→- Simple operations (addition of two 32-bit numbers) take milliseconds; multiplication chains degrade rapidly.
    34→- Leveled FHE (no bootstrapping) is practical for shallow circuits but limits computation depth.
    35→
    36→**Key libraries and vendors:**
    37→
    38→| Library/Vendor | Type | Notes |
    39→|---|---|---|
    40→| OpenFHE | OSS library | Most feature-complete, combines PALISADE + HElib + HEAAN + FHEW |
    41→| Microsoft SEAL | OSS library | Enterprise-friendly, easier to use, less customizable |
    42→| Apple Swift HE | OSS library | Released July 2024, Swift-native |
    43→| Zama | Vendor + OSS | Concrete framework, TFHE-focused, Rust/Python bindings |
    44→| Duality Technologies | Vendor | FHE + TEE + FL hybrid, Oracle/Microsoft/Google Cloud partnerships |
    45→| Enveil | Vendor | Encrypted search/analytics, CIA-backed (In-Q-Tel), custom FHE primitives |

    58→### 1.2 Federated Machine Learning
    59→
    60→**What it does:** Trains models across decentralized data sources without centralizing data. Each participant trains locally and shares only model updates (gradients/weights).
    61→
    62→**Current practical maturity: Production for specific use cases**
    63→
    64→- Google Gboard is the canonical deployment (millions of Android devices, next-word prediction).
    65→- Only 5.2% of federated learning research has reached real-world clinical deployment.
    66→- EU Data Protection Supervisor (2025) highlighted FL as a key GDPR compliance technology.

    72→|---|---|---|

    75→| PySyft (OpenMined) | Remote data science, Datasites | Production-ready for approved-code workflows |
    76→| Google TFF | TensorFlow Federated | Production (Gboard, Chrome) |
    77→| Meta (internal) | Cross-device FL | Internal production |
    78→
    79→**Performance overhead: 2-10x training time, communication is the bottleneck**
    80→
    81→- In a 15-hospital deployment, naive implementations spent more time communicating than training.
    82→- Communication overhead far exceeds computational overhead when many clients participate.
    83→- Non-IID data across participants causes model drift, requiring 1.5-3x more rounds to converge.

    90→5. Privacy not fully guaranteed: gradient inversion attacks can reconstruct training data
    91→

    93→
    94→FL is well-suited when the agent needs to train or fine-tune models across multiple data providers. Less relevant for the common case of an agent querying structured data.    104→### 1.3 Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC)
   105→
   106→**What it does:** Multiple parties jointly compute a function over their private inputs without revealing those inputs to each other. No trusted third party required.
   107→
   108→**Current practical maturity: Early production for specific verticals**
   109→
   110→- Global MPC market: ~$888M in 2024, projected $2.72B by 2034 (~11-12% CAGR).
   111→- Finance sector leads adoption (digital asset custody, key management).

   116→
   117→- Sub-second to sub-minute latency achievable on intranet (low-latency links, up to ~10 parties).

   119→- Reinforcement learning-based protocol tuning (Sayyadi et al., 2025) achieved 25-31% reduction in execution time and communication cost.
   120→- Multiplication-heavy workloads and high-cardinality operations are the worst case.

   143→## 2. INPUT VERIFICATION (Authenticity of Data)
   144→
   145→### 2.1 Digital Signatures for Data Provenance
   146→
   147→**What it does:** Cryptographically binds data to its origin, ensuring integrity (not tampered) and authenticity (came from claimed source).
   148→
   149→**Current practical maturity: PRODUCTION (widely deployed)**
   150→
   151→- Sigstore (OpenSSF graduated project, Linux Foundation): keyless signing with short-lived certificates and transparency logs. Used across software supply chains.
   152→- SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts): provenance framework using in-toto attestations. Verifies artifact origin, creator identity, and CI/CD pipeline.
   153→- C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity): developed by Adobe, Microsoft, Intel. Cryptographic content credentials for media provenance. Production-deployed in Adobe products, Microsoft Bing.
   154→- Sigstore model-transparency project: extends signing to ML models, ensuring model integrity post-training.
   155→- Verifiable Credentials (VCs) + Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs): W3C standards for tamper-evident, portable attestations. Production use in supply chain tracking, academic credentials.
   156→
   157→**Performance overhead: NEGLIGIBLE**
   158→
   159→- Signing: milliseconds (ECDSA, Ed25519).
   160→- Verification: milliseconds.
   161→- Storage overhead: small metadata payload per artifact.
   162→
   163→**Agent-native applicability: HIGH**
   164→
   165→Digital signatures are the natural foundation for DataFetch's provenance receipts. Every data response can carry a signature from the provider, verifiable by the agent without human intervention. The C2PA model (cryptographic content credentials) maps directly to data marketplace provenance. Sigstore's transparency log model provides auditability. This is the most mature and lowest-overhead technology in the entire landscape.
   166→
   167→**Key citations:**
   168→- SLSA Provenance and Software Attestation: [Legit Security](https://www.legitsecurity.com/blog/slsa-provenance-blog-series-part-2-deeper-dive-into-slsa-provenance)
   169→- Sigstore Model Transparency: [GitHub](https://github.com/sigstore/model-transparency)
   170→- Verifiable Credentials and DIDs Technical Landscape (2025): [GS1](https://ref.gs1.org/docs/2025/VCs-and-DIDs-tech-landscape)
   171→- Digital Authenticity and Provenance Act 2025
   172→
   173→---
   174→
   175→### 2.2 Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Selective Disclosure
   176→
   177→**What it does:** Allows a prover to demonstrate a statement is true without revealing the underlying data. In data marketplaces: prove data properties (freshness, completeness, coverage) without exposing the data itself.
   178→
   179→**Current practical maturity: Production for specific applications, research for general-purpose**
   180→
   181→- ZKP market valued at $1.28B in 2024, projected $7.59B by 2033.
   182→- ZK-KYC market: $83.6M in 2025, growing at 40.5% CAGR.
   183→- Production deployments: Google Wallet + Sparkasse banks (ZK-based age verification), OKX Proof of Reserves (monthly attestations).
   184→- zkVMs (RISC Zero, SP1 by Succinct): compile arbitrary Rust programs into ZK proofs of correct execution. This is a game-changer for verifiable data processing.
   185→- ZKML (Kudelski Security): ZK proofs that ML inference was computed correctly without revealing model weights.
   186→
   187→**Performance overhead: HIGH but rapidly improving**
   188→
   189→- ZK proof generation: seconds to minutes for complex circuits.
   190→- Verification: milliseconds (succinct proofs).
   191→- The asymmetry (expensive to prove, cheap to verify) is favorable for marketplaces where the provider proves once and many agents verify.
   192→
   193→**Agent-native applicability: HIGH (for verification), MEDIUM (for privacy)**
   194→
   195→ZKPs enable a provider to prove "this dataset contains >10,000 UK companies updated within the last 7 days" without revealing the dataset. This maps directly to DataFetch's `explore()` pattern where agents need to verify data quality before purchasing. The zkVM model (prove arbitrary computation) is particularly relevant: a provider could prove their enrichment pipeline ran correctly.
   196→
   197→**Key citations:**
   198→- ZK proofs in blockchain finance, opportunity vs reality (2025): [Nethermind](https://www.nethermind.io/blog/zero-knowledge-proofs-in-blockchain-finance-opportunity-vs-reality)
   199→- ZKML: Verifiable ML using ZKPs: [Kudelski Security](https://kudelskisecurity.com/modern-ciso-blog/zkml-verifiable-machine-learning-using-zero-knowledge-proof)
   200→- ZK proof AI in 2026: [Calibraint](https://www.calibraint.com/blog/zero-knowledge-proof-ai-2026)
   201→- Blockchain + ZKP data security transaction method (2024): [MDPI Electronics](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/13/21/4260)
   202→
   203→---
   204→
   205→### 2.3 Blockchain-Based Verification
   206→
   207→**What it does:** Provides immutable, append-only ledgers for recording data transactions, provenance, and access events. Smart contracts automate verification logic.
   208→
   209→**Current practical maturity: PRODUCTION (but with caveats)**
   210→
   211→- Ethereum + Solidity remain dominant for smart contract-based verification.
   212→- Hyperledger Fabric for permissioned enterprise use cases.
   213→- EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 address blockchain + GDPR compliance, noting tension between immutability and right to erasure.
   214→- Production: OKX Proof of Reserves, supply chain tracking (VeChain, IBM Food Trust).
   215→
   216→**Performance overhead: MODERATE**
   217→
   218→- On-chain transactions: seconds to minutes (block time dependent), $0.01-$10+ per transaction (chain dependent).
   219→- Off-chain computation + on-chain verification (ZK-Rollups): higher throughput, lower per-transaction cost.
   220→- Storage: expensive on-chain, so most systems store hashes on-chain and data off-chain.
   221→
   222→**Agent-native applicability: MEDIUM**
   223→
   224→Blockchain adds verifiable audit trails for data purchases, but the latency and cost make it unsuitable as a primary data transport. Better suited as a settlement/audit layer. For DataFetch, blockchain could record purchase receipts and provenance hashes, while actual data delivery happens off-chain. The MPP protocol (Stripe + Tempo Labs) already handles payment settlement, potentially reducing the need for blockchain as a payment rail.
   225→
   226→**Key citations:**
   227→- EDPB Guidelines on Blockchain and Data Protection (2025): [EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-04/edpb_guidelines_202502_blockchain_en.pdf)
   228→- Blockchain-driven smart contracts for authorization (2025): [MDPI Electronics](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/15/3104)
   229→- Blockchain-enabled policy-based access control for health records (2025): [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11784709/)
   230→
   231→---
   232→
   233→## 3. GOVERNANCE (Access Control Orchestration)
   234→
   235→### 3.1 RBAC/ABAC for Data
   236→
   237→**What it does:** Role-Based (RBAC) and Attribute-Based (ABAC) Access Control determine who can access what data under what conditions.
   238→
   239→**Current practical maturity: PRODUCTION (industry standard)**
   240→
   241→- RBAC is the default in virtually every enterprise system. Well-understood, easy to audit.
   242→- ABAC extends RBAC with contextual attributes (time, location, device, data sensitivity, security clearance).
   243→- Most organizations use RBAC + ABAC hierarchically: broad access via RBAC, fine-grained via ABAC.
   244→
   245→**Performance overhead: NEGLIGIBLE**
   246→
   247→- Policy evaluation: sub-millisecond for simple rules, low-millisecond for complex ABAC.
   248→- The overhead is in policy management, not computation.
   249→
   250→**Limitation for data marketplaces:** RBAC/ABAC are designed for known users within an organization. For a marketplace with dynamic, anonymous agents, you need capability-based or token-based access control. The traditional "assign a role to a user" model doesn't map cleanly to "an agent presents a payment token and gets scoped access."
   251→
   252→**Agent-native applicability: MEDIUM (needs adaptation)**
   253→
   254→RBAC/ABAC are the right primitives but need to be extended for agent contexts. Key adaptations:
   255→- Capabi
