1→# Appendix: Reference Data & Market Context
     2→
     3→## A. MPP Protocol Reference
     4→
     5→### What is MPP?
     6→Machine Payments Protocol, co-created by Stripe and Tempo Labs (March 2026). An HTTP authentication scheme that standardizes the 402 Payment Required status code.
     7→
     8→### Core Flow
     9→1. Client requests resource -> `GET /endpoint`
    10→2. Server returns 402 with `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` header (challenge: amount, currency, accepted methods)
    11→3. Client pays (signs blockchain tx, provides card token, etc.)
    12→4. Client retries with `Authorization: Payment` header (payment credential)
    13→5. Server verifies payment, returns resource + `Payment-Receipt` header
    14→
    15→### Transaction Modes
    16→- **Charge (one-time):** Immediate settlement per request. Good for discrete API calls
    17→- **Session (streaming):** Payment channel for streaming data. Sub-cent costs, sub-millisecond latency
    18→
    19→### SDKs
    20→| Language | Package | Install |
    21→|----------|---------|---------|
    22→| TypeScript | mppx | npm install mppx |
    23→| Python | pympp | pip install pympp |
    24→| Rust | mpp-rs | cargo add mpp |
    25→
    26→### Key Resources
    27→- Protocol overview: mpp.dev/overview
    28→- Server quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/server
    29→- Agent quickstart: mpp.dev/quickstart/agent
    30→- IETF spec: paymentauth.org
    31→- Stripe blog: stripe.com/blog/machine-payments-protocol
    32→
    33→## B. UK Open Government Licence (OGL v3) Summary
    34→
    35→**Permits:** Copy, publish, distribute, transmit, adapt, exploit commercially and non-commercially
    36→**Requires:** Acknowledge the source, provide link to licence
    37→**Does NOT require:** Payment, registration, or permission
    38→
    39→### OGL-Covered Datasets Used
    40→- Companies House basic company data
    41→- Land Registry Price Paid Data
    42→- Land Registry CCOD/OCOD
    43→- EPC Register
    44→- Charity Commission register
    45→- CQC provider data
    46→- FHRS food hygiene ratings
    47→- Ofsted inspection data
    48→- Census / ONS statistical data
    49→- The Gazette (insolvency notices)
    50→- Met Office DataPoint
    51→- police.uk crime data
    52→- HMRC trade statistics
    53→
    54→### NOT OGL (require separate licensing)
    55→- Ordnance Survey premium products (AddressBase, MasterMap)
    56→- Royal Mail PAF (postcode/address data)
    57→- Land Registry National Polygon Dataset (GBP 4,500+/yr)
    58→- Individual Land Registry title registers (GBP 3/title, no bulk redistribution)
    59→
    60→## C. Competitor Pricing Reference
    61→
    62→### UK Company Data
    63→
    64→| Provider | Model | Price Point | Enrichment Level |
    65→|----------|-------|-------------|------------------|
    66→| Companies House API | Free | 0 (rate-limited) | Raw data only |
    67→| Endole | Pay-as-you-go | GBP 0.25-0.80/report | Scored, basic network |
    68→| Creditsafe | Enterprise subscription | GBP 10K+/yr minimum | Full credit scoring |
    69→| Beauhurst | Annual subscription | GBP 5K-30K/yr | Growth/innovation signals |
    70→| OpenCorporates | API subscription | $500+/mo | Cross-jurisdiction, no scoring |
    71→| DueDil (now Creditsafe) | API credits | GBP 0.50-2.00/check | Compliance/KYB focused |
    72→
    73→### Our Proposed Positioning
    74→- Below Endole on basic lookups (GBP 0.05 vs 0.25)
    75→- Comparable to Endole on enriched (GBP 0.25)
    76→- Below DueDil on compliance checks (GBP 1.00 vs 1.50+)
    77→- Zero friction: no signup, no subscription, no API key
    78→
    79→### International Data Products (for comparison)
    80→
    81→| Provider | Data Type | Per-Query Price |
    82→|----------|-----------|-----------------|
    83→| Clearbit | Company enrichment | $0.05-0.25 |
    84→| Apollo.io | Contact + company | $0.01-0.05 |
    85→| BuiltWith | Technology profiles | $0.10-0.50 |
    86→| SimilarWeb | Traffic data | $0.01-0.10 |
    87→| Crunchbase | Startup/funding | $0.05-0.20 |
    88→
    89→## D. Companies House Data Schema (Key Fields)
    90→
    91→### Company Profile
    92→- company_number (PK)
    93→- company_name
    94→- company_status (active, dissolved, liquidation, etc.)
    95→- company_type (ltd, plc, llp, etc.)
    96→- date_of_creation
    97→- date_of_cessation
    98→- registered_office_address (premises, address_line_1, address_line_2, locality, region, postal_code, country)
    99→- sic_codes (array of 5-digit codes)
   100→- accounts.next_due, accounts.last_made_up_to
   101→- confirmation_statement.next_due, confirmation_statement.last_made_up_to
   102→- has_charges, has_insolvency_history
   103→- jurisdiction
   104→
   105→### Officer (Director/Secretary)
   106→- officer_id
   107→- company_number (FK)
   108→- name (surname, forename)
   109→- officer_role (director, secretary, llp-member, etc.)
   110→- appointed_on, resigned_on
   111→- date_of_birth (month, year only)
   112→- nationality
   113→- country_of_residence
   114→- occupation
   115→- address (correspondence address, not residential)
   116→
   117→### PSC (Person of Significant Control)
   118→- psc_id
   119→- company_number (FK)
   120→- name or corporate_name
   121→- natures_of_control (array: ownership-of-shares-25-to-50-percent, voting-rights-75-to-100-percent, etc.)
   122→- nationality, country_of_residence
   123→- date_of_birth (month, year)
   124→- address
   125→- ceased_on (if no longer a PSC)
   126→- For corporate PSCs: identification.legal_authority, identification.place_registered, identification.registration_number
   127→
   128→### Charges
   129→- charge_id
   130→- company_number (FK)
   131→- status (outstanding, fully-satisfied, part-satisfied)
   132→- created_on, delivered_on, satisfied_on
   133→- persons_entitled (lender names)
   134→- particulars (description of charged property)
   135→- classification (nature-of-charge, etc.)
   136→
   137→## E. Financial Health Score Methodology (Draft)
   138→
   139→### Input Variables
   140→
   141→**From Accounts (40% weight):**
   142→- Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities (target: > 1.5)
   143→- Debt to equity = total liabilities / net assets (target: < 2.0)
   144→- Net assets trend (increasing = positive signal)
   145→- Revenue growth YoY (where available)
   146→- Profit margin (where available)
   147→
   148→**From Filing Behaviour (25% weight):**
   149→- Average days late (0 = perfect, >30 = concerning)
   150→- Percentage of filings late
   151→- Currently overdue filings count
   152→- Trend: improving or worsening
   153→
   154→**From Charges (15% weight):**
   155→- Active charges count
   156→- Recent charge activity (new charges in last 12 months)
   157→- Charge satisfaction rate
   158→
   159→**From Gazette/Insolvency (15% weight):**
   160→- Winding-up petitions (severe negative signal)
   161→- Strike-off action (moderate negative)
   162→- Administrative receiver appointed (severe)
   163→
   164→**From Company Age/Status (5% weight):**
   165→- Companies < 2 years old get a slight penalty (less track record)
   166→- Dormant companies scored separately
   167→
   168→### Score Bands
   169→- 80-100: Strong financial position
   170→- 60-79: Adequate, no immediate concerns
   171→- 40-59: Caution, some risk indicators
   172→- 20-39: Significant risk, multiple negative signals
   173→- 0-19: Severe risk, active insolvency indicators
   174→
   175→### Known Limitations
   176→- ~60% of UK companies file micro-entity or abbreviated accounts with minimal financial detail
   177→- Score for these companies relies heavily on filing behaviour and charges (lower confidence)
   178→- Financial data can be up to 21 months old at time of filing (9 month filing deadline + 12 month accounting period)
   179→- Score should always be accompanied by confidence indicator and data freshness
   180→
   181→## F. GDPR Compliance Plan
   182→
   183→### Personal Data Processed
   184→- Director/secretary names
   185→- Director date of birth (month/year only)
   186→- Director correspondence addresses (not residential)
   187→- PSC names, nationality, country of residence
   188→
   189→### Lawful Basis
   190→- Legitimate interest (Article 6(1)(f))
   191→- Data is published by Companies House under statutory authority
   192→- Processing serves legitimate business interests (credit checking, due diligence, compliance)
   193→- Balanced against individual rights: data is already public, we add enrichment not new personal data
   194→
   195→### Required Actions
   196→1. Privacy policy explaining processing activities
   197→2. Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) documented
   198→3. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for systematic profiling
   199→4. Right to object mechanism (suppression list)
   200→5. Data subject access request (DSAR) process
   201→6. Respect Companies House residential address suppression
   202→7. Do not attempt to derive full dates of birth
   203→8. Consider ICO registration if not already registered
   204→
   205→## G. Potential Product Expansion Path
   206→
   207→```
   208→Phase 1 (Months 1-2): Company Intelligence API
   209→  |
   210→  v
   211→Phase 2 (Months 2-4): + Property Intelligence
   212→  |
   213→  v
   214→Phase 3 (Months 4-6): + Planning Pipeline + Trade Intelligence
   215→  |
   216→  v
   217→Phase 4 (Months 6-12): + Climate Risk + Tech/Hiring Signals
   218→  |
   219→  v
   220→Phase 5 (Year 2): + Niche products (Care, Charity, Food, Hyperlocal)
   221→  |
   222→  v
   223→Phase 6 (Year 2+): International expansion (US SEC, EU company registries)
   224→```

1→# Clean Rooms, Compute-to-Data, and Sandbox Environments
     2→
     3→**Research Brief for DataFetch / envrun.ai**
     4→**Mode:** Deep Landscape Scan | **Date:** 2026-03-24 | **Sources:** 50+
     5→
     6→---
     7→
     8→## 1. Executive Summary
     9→
    10→This brief maps the full landscape of platforms where data stays in place and computation comes to it, organized into four tiers: enterprise clean rooms (Snowflake, Databricks, AWS, Google ADH, Habu/LiveRamp), privacy-preserving compute platforms (OpenMined/PySyft, Ocean Protocol, Oasis Network, Duality Technologies, Cape Privacy), sandboxed environment models (TEEs, confidential computing, container isolation), and "mock-then-commit" design patterns (synthetic preview, schema-only access, try-before-buy).
    11→
    12→**Key findings for DataFetch positioning:**
    13→
    14→1. Enterprise clean rooms are locked inside cloud vendor ecosystems and designed for SQL-literate humans, not agents. Cross-cloud interop remains painful.
    15→2. PySyft's Datasite model is the closest existing precedent to DataFetch's explore/purchase pattern: mock data for free development, code submission for real execution, data owner approval. But PySyft targets researchers, not agents, and has no payment layer.
    16→3. Ocean Protocol proved compute-to-data at scale (1.7M nodes) but remains crypto-native with blockchain settlement, creating friction for enterprise adoption.
    17→4. The "mock-then-commit" pattern (explore synthetic data free, pay for real execution) has strong precedents in API sandboxes (Plaid, Stripe test mode), Snowflake Marketplace trials, and PySyft's dual-data model, but nobody has built it as an agent-native experience with micropayment settlement.
    18→5. Confidential computing hardware (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA) is production-ready for VM-level isolation at ~10% overhead, making TEE-based sandboxes viable for DataFetch's execution layer.

    21→
    22→## 2. CLEAN ROOM PLATFORMS
    23→
    24→### 2.1 Snowflake Data Clean Rooms
    25→
    26→**Architecture:** Provider-consumer model built on Snowflake's Secure Data Sharing. Data never leaves each party's Snowflake account (zero data movement). Two variants exist:
    27→
    28→- **Framework-Based DCR (Legacy):** Combines Snowflake features (tables, views, shares, streams, tasks, row access policies, Python UDFs) as building blocks. Complex to implement.
    29→- **Native DCR (Current):** Fully native feature, simplified after Snowflake's acquisition of **Samooha** (December 2023). Samooha's UI was named one of Fast Company's most innovative data science products of 2024. Now integrated as a Snowflake Native App on Snowflake Marketplace.
    30→
    31→**How queries work:** Providers create aggregation query templates using **Jinja** (Python templating). Consumers cannot reference data directly; they request dimensions according to a prior agreement, and the provider generates a query returning only aggregated results. Sensitive fields are hashed before sharing for join operations without exposing raw values.
    32→
    33→**Privacy features:** Data anonymization/masking, differential privacy (some use cases), fine-grained access controls, audit trails, data lineage tracking. GDPR and CCPA compliance support built in.
    34→
    35→**Pricing:** No additional access fees from Snowflake. Cost is based on **compute and storage credits** (standard Snowflake billing). As of September 2024, collaborators can set monthly credit consumption limits. Costs can be unpredictable for complex queries on large datasets.
    36→
    37→**Limitations:**
    38→- **Ecosystem lock-in:** All parties typically need Snowflake accounts. Cross-cloud collaboration requires same cloud/region deployment with data replication.
    39→- **SQL-first interface:** Powerful for SQL users but inaccessible without custom UIs for non-technical stakeholders.
    40→- **Template rigidity:** Query templates must be pre-agreed; ad-hoc exploration is constrained.
    41→- Named a Leader in the **2025 IDC MarketScape for Data Clean Rooms**.
    42→
    43→**Availability:** AWS, Azure, GCP (select regions).
    44→
    45→**Sources:**
    46→- [NTT DATA Deep Dive](https://us.nttdata.com/en/blog/2024/january/a-deep-dive-into-snowflakes-data-clean-rooms)
    47→- [Snowflake Documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cleanrooms/introduction)
    48→- [Snowflake Clean Rooms Cost](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cleanrooms/cleanroom-cost)
    49→- [Flexera Guide 2026](https://www.flexera.com/blog/finops/snowflake-data-clean-rooms/)
    50→
    51→---
    52→
    53→### 2.2 Databricks Clean Rooms
    54→
    55→**Architecture:** Built on the **Lakehouse** (Delta Lake + Apache Spark), using **Delta Sharing** for multicloud data exchange and **Unity Catalog** for cross-workload governance.
    56→
    57→**Key differentiator from Snowflake:** Notebook-based workflow. Users add SQL or Python notebooks with analysis code, partners review/approve, then it runs. This is closer to a compute-to-data model than Snowflake's template-based approach.
    58→
    59→**Cross-platform capability:** **Lakehouse Federation** exposes external systems (Snowflake, BigQuery, traditional warehouses) as foreign catalogs in Unity Catalog. External tables can be shared in clean rooms without copying data into Databricks.
    60→
    61→**Data type support:** Handles both **structured and unstructured data**, making it suitable for AI/ML collaboration (unlike Snowflake's primarily structured focus).
    62→
    63→**Query interface:** Python, SQL, notebooks (vs. Snowflake's SQL/Jinja templates).
    64→
    65→**Generally available** on AWS and Azure.
    66→
    67→**Limitations:**
    68→- **Engineering-heavy:** No dedicated UI for marketers or business teams. Notebook workflows require engineering support.
    69→- **Accessibility gap:** Slows time-to-value for non-technical collaborators.
    70→
    71→**Comparison matrix:**
    72→
    73→| Dimension | Databricks | Snowflake |
    74→|-----------|-----------|-----------|
    75→| Architecture | Lakehouse (Delta Lake + Spark) | Data Cloud (columnar warehouse) |
    76→| Data types | Structured + unstructured | Primarily structured |
    77→| Query interface | Python, SQL, notebooks | SQL / Jinja templates |
    78→| Cross-platform | Yes (Lakehouse Federation + Delta Sharing) | Requires same cloud/region |
    79→| AI/ML | Strong (native Spark, MLflow) | Moderate (Snowpark, Cortex) |
    80→| Governance | Unity Catalog | Horizon Catalog |
    81→| Best for | AI-driven, cross-platform, regulated | SQL-first analytics |
    82→
    83→**Sources:**
    84→- [Databricks Clean Rooms GA Blog](https://www.databricks.com/blog/databricks-clean-rooms-now-generally-available-aws-and-azure)
    85→- [Databricks Clean Rooms FAQ](https://www.databricks.com/blog/top-10-questions-you-asked-about-databricks-clean-rooms-answered)
    86→- [Perficient Comparison](https://blogs.perficient.com/2025/06/27/databricks-vs-snowflake-clean-rooms-financial-research-collaboration/)
    87→
    88→---
    89→
    90→### 2.3 AWS Clean Rooms
    91→
    92→**Service model:** Fully managed AWS service where multiple parties join data in a secure collaboration workspace. Data stays in **Amazon S3** with processing via AWS Clean Rooms' own compute layer.
    93→
    94→**Integration with AWS ecosystem:**
    95→- **AWS Glue** for ETL and table configuration
    96→- **Amazon S3** for data storage
    97→- **AWS Entity Resolution** for record matching
    98→- **CloudWatch** for monitoring
    99→- **Analysis Rules** with configurable aggregate functions, join controls, query results controls
   100→
   101→**Three privacy layers:**
   102→1. **Analysis Rules:** Fine-grained SQL/Spark query constraints (what columns, what aggregations, what joins are allowed).
   103→2. **Differential Privacy (GA April 2024):** Fully managed, injects calibrated noise, enforces privacy budgets, blocks unsafe joins. Supports CTEs and aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM). No expertise required from partners.
   104→3. **Cryptographic Computing for Clean Rooms (C3R):** Open-source Java SDK (free). Enables private set intersection (PSI) where data remains encrypted at rest, in transit, and in use. Available for both Spark SQL and SQL engines.
   105→
   106→**ML capabilities (Clean Rooms ML):** Lookalike modeling, custom ML model deployment (bring your own model), PySpark support.
   107→
   108→**Pricing:** Pay per **Clean Rooms Processing Unit (CRPU)-hour** for SQL/PySpark queries. ML custom modeling priced per million records. Lookalike modeling priced per training/segment generation.
   109→
   110→**Limitations:**
   111→- AWS ecosystem-centric (though S3 is broadly used).
   112→- Less mature marketplace/listing ecosystem compared to Snowflake.
   113→- CJEU September 2025 ruling implies parties using Clean Rooms in EU likely remain joint controllers under GDPR.
   114→
   115→**Sources:**
   116→- [AWS Clean Rooms Features](https://aws.amazon.com/clean-rooms/features/)

   118→- [AWS Clean Rooms Differential Privacy](https://aws.amazon.com/clean-rooms/differential-privacy/)
   119→- [AWS Clean Rooms Documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/clean-rooms/latest/userguide/what-is.html)

   122→
   123→### 2.4 Google Ads Data Hub (ADH)
   124→
   125→**What it is:** Google's clean room solution (launched 2017, first major clean room product). Lets advertisers upload first-party data to BigQuery and join it with Google's event-level ad campaign data.
   126→
   127→**Restricted to advertising?** Effectively yes. ADH provides measurement, campaign insights, and audience activation specifically for **Google advertising** (Search, Display, YouTube, Shopping). It offers little value outside Google's ad ecosystem.
   128→
   129→**Key limitations:**
   130→1. **Walled garden:** Analysis only within Google's platform. No cross-platform neutrality, no insight into Meta, Amazon, etc.
   131→2. **Aggregated output only:** Results aggregated over user groups. Raw/user-level data cannot be inspected (prevents re-identification).
   132→3. **Requires substantial first-party data:** Most effective when running multiple Google platforms with a large CRM dataset.
   133→4. **Steep learning curve:** Functionality differs significantly from standard data warehousing, even for clean room experts.
   134→5. **EU consent enforcement (March 2024):** All customers must attest appropriate consent under EU user consent policy for any first-party data used.
   135→6. **Not a general-purpose clean room:** Designed specifically for ad measurement and attribution.
   136→
   137→**Relevance to DataFetch:** Limited. ADH demonstrates the walled-garden clean room model but is not a precedent for general-purpose data collaboration or agent-native workflows.
   138→
   139→**Sources:**
   140→- [Google ADH Developer Docs](https://developers.google.com/ads-data-hub)
   141→- [Improvado ADH Guide 2026](https://improvado.io/blog/google-ads-data-hub)
   142→- [InfoTrust ADH Introduction](https://infotrust.com/articles/introduction-to-ads-data-hub/)
   143→
   144→---
   145→
   146→### 2.5 Habu (Acquired by LiveRamp)
   147→
   148→**The deal:** LiveRamp acquired Habu in January 2024 for approximately **$200 million** ($170M cash + stock + $16M retention).
   149→
   150→**What Habu was:** A cross-cloud clean room specialist founded in 2018 (by Krux/Salesforce DMP alumni). Native applications for walled garden platforms including Google ADH, Amazon Marketing Cloud, and multiple cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, Databricks, Snowflake).
   151→
   152→**Why it matters:** Habu solved the fundamental limitation of vendor-specific clean rooms. A large enterprise (e.g., Pepsi) must work with ADH for YouTube, Amazon Marketing Cloud for Amazon analytics, Azure for Microsoft/LinkedIn, Walmart's clean room, and Disney's clean room. No single cloud vendor's clean room covers all of these. Habu provided an **interoperable layer across all of them**.
   153→
   154→**Combined offering:** Through LiveRamp + Habu, companies get one platform to:
   155→- Measure campaigns across all walled gardens, programmatic, and media channels
   156→- Connect data seamlessly across any cloud, warehouse, or clean room
   157→- Expand beyond marketing into supply chain optimization, inventory management
   158→
   159→**Market context:**
   160→- One-third of companies extensively using data clean rooms (Deloitte Digital study).
   161→- ~90% expect increased usage over next 12 months.
   162→- The clean room vendor landscape has consolidated: Epsilon (Publicis), Acxiom (IPG), Samooha (Snowflake), Habu (LiveRamp).
   163→
   164→**Financial impact:** Expected $18M revenue contribution in FY25; 200+ markets globally via Habu's walled garden/publisher network.
   165→
   166→**Sources:**
   167→- [LiveRamp Acquisition Blog](https://liveramp.com/blog/liveramp-habu-accelerate-data-collaboration)
   168→- [AdExchanger Analysis](https://www.adexchanger.com/platforms/liveramp-acquires-habu-as-walled-gardens-put-the-squeeze-on-indie-data-collaboration-tech/)
   169→- [Marketing Dive](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/liveramp-habu-data-clean-room-death-cookie-deprecation/705189/)
   170→
   171→---
   172→
   173→### 2.6 Clean Room Summary for DataFetch
   174→
   175→| Platform | Cross-Cloud | Agent-Ready | Payment Layer | Mock Data | Open/Closed |
   176→|----------|-------------|-------------|---------------|-----------|-------------|
   177→| Snowflake DCR | No (same account) | No (SQL templates) | Snowflake credits | No (trial listings only) | Closed |
   178→| Databricks CR | Partial (Federation) | No (notebooks) | Databricks billing | No | Closed |
   179→| AWS Clean Rooms | No (AWS-centric) | No (managed service) | CRPU-hours | No | Closed |
   180→| Google ADH | No (Google only) | No | Google billing | No | Closed (walled garden) |
   181→| Habu/LiveRamp | **Yes** | No | Enterprise contracts | No | Closed |
   182→| Decentriq | Yes (TEE-based) | No | Enterprise contracts | No | Partially open |
   183→
   184→**Gap for DataFetch:** None of these platforms are designed for autonomous agents. They all assume human operators (SQL analysts, data scientists, marketers). None offer mock-data exploration as a first-class pattern. None integrate micropayment settlement. This is the whitespace.
   185→
   186→---
   187→
   188→## 3. PRIVACY-PRESERVING COMPUTE PLATFORMS
   189→
   190→### 3.1 OpenMined / PySyft Datasites
   191→
   192→**Current state (2025-2026):** PySyft is the most mature open-source implementation of the compute-to-data paradigm. Maintained by the OpenMined Foundation with a community of 17,000+ technologists.
   193→
   194→**Core concept: Datasites.** "Like websites, but for data." While web servers let you download files, Datasites let you send code to data and receive only results.
   195→
   196→**How agents/users submit code:**
   197→
   198→1. **Connect** to a Datasite (client-server architecture).
   199→2. **Browse mock datasets:** Every Asset has a dual behavior, a pointer to private data + an accessible mock counterpart. Data scientists/guests can only access mock data. Admins see real data.
   200→3. **Develop locally against mock data.** Write analysis code using standard Python. Test it locally. Results from mock data are explicitly "completely meaningless for actual research."
   201→4. **Submit code request:** Wrap function with `syft.syft_function_single_use` decorator, specifying which assets to use. This creates a `UserCode` object within a Project.
   202→5. **Data owner reviews and approves.** The owner inspects the code, understands its purpose via the Project context, and grants/denies execution.
   203→6. **Remote execution on real data.** A Job is created for asynchronous, non-blocking execution. Users can run parallel requests and monitor progress.
   204→7. **Download approved results.**
   205→
   206→**Advanced features:**
   207→- **Projects API:** Multi-Datasite collaboration. A Project spans multiple Datasites, establishing research purpose upfront.
   208→- **MapReduce / nested jobs:** Cluster deployment enables distributed computation across nodes.
   209→- **Airgapped deployment:** High-side servers can be physically isolated from the internet for maximum security.
   210→- **Differential privacy:** Privacy budgets set by data owners, automatically enforced.
   211→- **Third-party library support:** Arbitrary Python libraries allowed in submitted functions.
   212→
   213→**What PySyft gets right for DataFetch's model:**
   214→- The mock/real dual-data model is exactly the "explore for free, pay for real" pattern.
   215→- Code-to-data (not data-to-code) is the right architecture for sensitive data.
   216→- Approval workflow provides governance without data exposure.
   217→
   218→**What PySyft lacks (DataFetch opportunity):**
   219→- No payment layer. No monetization infrastructure.
   220→- No agent-native interface. Assumes human Jupyter notebook users.
   221→- No schema-level browsing optimized for machine consumption.
   222→- No typed folder interfaces or code-mode patterns.
   223→- Approval is manual (human data owner must review). No automated policy engine for programmatic approval.
   224→
   225→**Sources:**
   226→- [PySyft GitHub](https://github.com/OpenMined/PySyft)
   227→- [PySyft Documentation](https://docs.openmined.org/)
   228→- [Datasite Server Docs](https://docs.openmined.org/en/latest/components/datasite-server.html)
   229→- [Code API Docs](https://docs.openmined.org/en/latest/components/code-api.html)
   230→- [UK GOV AI Assurance: PySyft](https://www.gov.uk/ai-assurance-techniques/openmined-privacy-preserving-third-party-audits-on-unreleased-digital-assets-with-pysyft)
   231→
   232→---
   233→
   234→### 3.2 Ocean Protocol Compute-to-Data
   235→
   236→**Maturity:** Significantly more mature than commonly assumed. Since **Ocean Nodes** launch (August 15, 2024), **1.7 million+ nodes** deployed across **70+ countries**.
   237→
   238→**How it works:** Instead of selling raw data, owners offer **compute access** to private data, controlling which algorithms can run. Example: sensitive health records can permit an algorithm to calculate average patient age without revealing individual records.

360→
   361→**Core approach:** All processing happens under **encryption-in-use** inside Trusted Execution Environments. Neither Decentriq (platform operator), the cloud provider, nor other participants can access raw data.
   362→
   363→**Decentriq v3 (key milestone):** World's first analytics platform deployed in production using **AMD SEV-SNP**. Enables data scientists to use existing ML workloads and frameworks on production-size datasets with confidential computing guarantees.
   364→
   365→**Privacy model:**
   366→- Each participant encrypts data so only the TEE can decrypt it.
   367→- Data segregation keeps each contributor's data isolated.
   368→- Only aggregated data or approved audience insights leave the clean room.
   369→- Raw/user-level data never transfers between parties.
   370→
   371→**GDPR precedent:** CJEU ruling in *EDPS v. SRB* confirmed confidential computing as the **gold standard for GDPR-compliant data collaboration**.
   372→
   373→**Industry deployments:**
   374→- **Swiss Re:** Sensitive analytics workflows, proprietary ML models in TEEs.
   375→- **Healthcare:** Patient data lifecycle protection from ingestion to analysis.
   376→- **Advertising/Media:** Brand/publisher data collaboration without exposure.
   377→
   378→**Tools:** Python, R, ML frameworks supported within the clean room.
   379→
   380→**Relevance to DataFetch:** Decentriq validates that TEE-based clean rooms work in production and satisfy GDPR requirements. Their AMD SEV-SNP deployment is relevant technical precedent for DataFetch's execution environment. Decentriq is enterprise/B2B focused, not agent-native, leaving the agent interface gap open.
   381→
   382→**Sources:**
   383→- [Decentriq Platform](https://www.decentriq.com)
   384→- [Decentriq v3 Announcement](https://www.decentriq.com/article/decentriq-v3-confidential-data-clean-rooms-for-scale)
   385→- [Decentriq vs Snowflake Comparison](https://www.decentriq.com/article/decentriq-vs-snowflake-data-clean-rooms-compared)
   386→
   387→---
   388→
   389→## 4. SANDBOX / ENVIRONMENT MODELS
   390→
   391→### 4.1 How Exfiltration Boundaries Are Enforced
   392→
   393→Modern data sandboxes use layered enforcement:
   394→
   395→**Layer 1: Process Isolation**
   396→- Application runs in separate address space with no access to system memory or privileged operations.
   397→- Container-based sandboxes (Docker) are the most common approach for LLM/AI sandboxing.
   398→- Each sandbox gets a temporary, virtualized file system.
   399→
   400→**Layer 2: Network Restrictions**
   401→- Restricted network stacks limit outbound connections.
   402→- DNS tunneling, side-channel, and covert channel prevention.
   403→- Syscall whitelisting blocks unauthorized I/O operations.
   404→
   405→**Layer 3: Output Controls**
   406→- Data Loss Prevention (DLP) rules block unauthorized data movement.
   407→- Role-based access control (RBAC) and attribute-based access control (ABAC).
   408→- Differential privacy on query results (noise injection, privacy budgets).
   409→- Aggregation minimums (e.g., results must cover N+ records).
   410→
   411→**Layer 4: Behavioral Monitoring**
   412→- Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) detects risky patterns in near-real time.
   413→- ML-based anomaly detection on data access patterns.
   414→- Audit trails for all operations.
   415→
   416→**Key academic reference:** "Data Sandboxing" (IEEE, 2006) established system call interposition as the foundational mechanism for confidentiality policy enforcement. Still the theoretical basis for modern implementations.
   417→
   418→**Sources:**
   419→- [IEEE: Data Sandboxing Technique](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel5/4041138/4041139/04041169.pdf)
   420→- [SandGarden: LLM Sandbox Environments](https://www.sandgarden.com/learn/llm-sandbox)
   421→
   422→---
   423→
   424→### 4.2 Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for Data Processing
   425→
   426→**Production-ready hardware options (2025):**
   427→
   428→| Technology | Vendor | Isolation Level | Overhead | Best For |
   429→|------------|--------|----------------|----------|----------|
   430→| **SGX** | Intel | Process/Enclave | Low-medium | Small enclave workloads, ML model protection |
   431→| **TDX** | Intel | VM (Trust Domain) | ~10% | Confidential VMs in cloud |
   432→| **SEV-SNP** | AMD | VM | ~10% | Cloud VMs (Azure, GCP use this) |
   433→| **CCA (Realms)** | ARM | VM/Realm | Variable | Mobile, IoT, embedded |
   434→| **GPU-CC** | NVIDIA | GPU Domain | Emerging | AI/ML secure inference |
   435→
   436→**Key architectural differences:**
   437→
   438→- **Intel SGX (process-level):** Smallest trusted computing base (TCB), but requires application modification and has larger side-channel attack surface. Memory encrypted, unreadable even by OS/hypervisor.
   439→- **Intel TDX / AMD SEV-SNP / ARM CCA (VM-level):** Larger TCB but enhanced compatibility and scalability. Full VM isolation including memory/state encryption. Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP provide remote attestation.
   440→- **ARM CCA:** Uses "Realms" architecture. Monitor acts as gatekeeper between Normal, Secure, and Realm worlds. Resources can be dynamically added/retrieved.
   441→
   442→**Remote attestation:** All major TEE platforms provide tamper-proof attestation, allowing remote clients to verify both hardware specs and exact software running inside the enclave. This is critical for DataFetch, as data owners need to verify what code will execute on their data.
   443→
   444→**Known vulnerabilities:**
   445→- **Side-channel attacks:** Cache access patterns, branch prediction, speculative execution can leak data. Primarily affects Intel SGX.
   446→- **Rollback/replay attacks:** Reverting enclave to previous state or reusing stale data.
   447→- **~10% performance overhead** for typical workloads; more severe for I/O-heavy operations due to encrypt/decrypt on data movement.
   448→
   449→**NVIDIA GPU Confidential Computing (emerging, 2025):**
   450→- Extends trust boundary from CPUs to GPUs.
   451→- Encapsulates AI computation pipeline within unified protected domain.
   452→- Clear separation of roles: model owners, data owners, compute providers.
   453→- Critical for DataFetch's future AI/ML workloads on sensitive data.
   454→
   455→**Sources:**
   456→- [Cisco Confidential Computing White Paper](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/servers-unified-computing/computing-overview-wp.html)
   457→- [Medium: SGX, SEV-SNP, ARM CCA Comparison](https://medium.com/@zlhk100/confidential-computing-solution-case-studies-intel-sgx-amd-sev-snp-and-arm-cca-comparison-b29d53401f77)
   458→- [Confidential Computing in 2025](https://medium.com/@aaron.mathis/confidential-computing-what-it-is-and-why-it-matters-in-2025-0a0567e2bcea)
   459→- [NVIDIA GPU CC Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.02770v1)
   460→- [Survey of Confidential Computing (IET 2024)](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1049/cmu2.12759)
   461→
   462→---
   463→
   464→### 4.3 Confidential Computing Consortium & Standardization
   465→
   466→The **Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC)** is driving cross-platform standardization. Members include Microsoft, Google, Intel, AMD, ARM, Facebook/Meta, and Decentriq.
   467→
   468→Goals:
   469→- Synchronization across Intel SGX, AMD SEV, and ARM CCA.
   470→- Enable secure multi-cloud deployment.
   471→- Post-quantum security research.
   472→- AI-assisted security operations.
   473→
   474→**Cloud provider support (2025):**
   475→- **Azure:** AMD SEV-SNP confidential VMs (production), Intel TDX (preview).
   476→- **GCP:** AMD SEV-SNP + NVIDIA GPU confidential VMs (production).
   477→- **AWS:** Nitro Enclaves (proprietary approach, not CCC-standard TEE).
   478→
   479→---

   481→## 5. MOCK-THEN-COMMIT PATTERNS
   482→
   483→### 5.1 PySyft: The Purest Precedent
   484→
   485→PySyft's dual-data model is the closest existing implementation of "explore synthetic data for free, pay for real execution":
   486→
   487→**How it works:**
   488→1. Every dataset has two versions: **private (real) data** and **mock (fake) data**.

# Research Audit: Briefs 13-14 vs. Core Documents

## GAPS

### GAP-1: Clean Room Market Size Not Reflected in Market Thesis
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 1 ("$2 billion market in 2025, projected to reach $10 billion by 2033") and Brief 13, Section 6.3 (same figures plus synthetic data market $0.51B->$2.67B, data marketplace $1.49B->$5.73B, privacy-preserving computation $4-5B at 28% CAGR).
**Missing from:** `market_thesis.md`, Market Sizing section.
The market thesis sizes the UK business data market, property data market, and adjacent markets, but never mentions the clean room / data collaboration market or the privacy-preserving computation market. These are adjacent TAM segments that contextualize where DataFetch sits and could strengthen the "Our Addressable Slice" argument by showing the white space between enterprise clean rooms ($376K/year) and DataFetch's per-query model.
**Suggestion:** Add a subsection under Market Sizing titled "Adjacent Infrastructure Markets" citing the $2B->$10B clean room market and the fact that no player in that market serves agents with micropayment.

### GAP-2: Databricks MCP Server Marketplace Not in Competitive Landscape
**Source:** Brief 14, Sections 3.2 and 7 (Databricks hosts MCP servers with LSEG, S&P Global, Moody's, ATTOM as launch partners, creating a direct bridge between clean room data and AI agents).
**Missing from:** `market_thesis.md`, Competitive Landscape table. The table lists Endole, Creditsafe, Beauhurst, OpenCorporates, and Companies House API. The "Could copy?" table mentions "Snowflake/Databricks" in one row but only says "Could build intent layers over warehouses / Sell infrastructure, not data products." It does not mention that Databricks is already shipping MCP servers for data providers on its marketplace, which is the closest existing thing to DataFetch's vision.
**Suggestion:** Add Databricks MCP Marketplace as a row in the Competitive Landscape table with weakness: "Enterprise pricing ($50/collaborator/day min), no mock data, no micropayment, platform lock-in." Also update the "Could copy?" table to note Databricks is already moving in this direction.

### GAP-3: Delta Sharing as an Open Protocol Not Mentioned Anywhere
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 5.3 and Brief 13, Section 2.2 (Delta Sharing is "the only open cross-platform data sharing protocol, published as a VLDB paper with 15+ client implementations").
**Missing from:** All core docs. Delta Sharing is relevant to DataFetch's architecture as a potential upstream data consumption protocol. ATTOM launched property data via both MCP server and Delta Sharing. DataFetch could consume data via Delta Sharing for cross-cloud interoperability.
**Suggestion:** Add Delta Sharing to `spec.md` as a potential future data ingestion protocol, or to `product_design.md` under Proprietary Data Sources as an alternative/complement to PySyft for accessing external datasets.

### GAP-4: "End of Clean Room Era" Thesis Not Captured
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 1 and 5.2 Path 3 (AdExchanger 2025 argues clean room technology is dissolving into background infrastructure rather than remaining standalone).
**Missing from:** All core docs. This thesis directly supports DataFetch's positioning: if clean rooms become background plumbing, the agent-facing interface layer (which DataFetch provides) becomes the primary value capture point.
**Suggestion:** Add to `market_thesis.md` Risks or Key Assumptions section: "If the 'end of clean room era' thesis plays out (AdExchanger 2025), DataFetch's agent-native layer becomes the primary interface through which agents access all data, regardless of underlying privacy infrastructure."

### GAP-5: Clean Room Adoption Friction Statistics Not Used
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 4.2 (41% integration friction, 38% scaling challenges, 34% expertise gap, 33% difficulty driving action from insights, from Skai 2025 report).
**Missing from:** `market_thesis.md` and `product_design.md`. These statistics powerfully quantify why the enterprise clean room model cannot serve the developer/agent segment DataFetch targets. They would strengthen the "Gap" argument in the competitive landscape.
**Suggestion:** Add to `market_thesis.md` competitive section: "Enterprise clean rooms face severe adoption friction: 41% cite integration challenges, 34% lack expertise, and average deployment costs $376K/year with 6+ dedicated staff (IAB/Skai 2025). This structural barrier creates the gap DataFetch exploits."

### GAP-6: Confidential Computing Hardware Maturity Not in Spec
**Source:** Brief 13, Section 4.2 (Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, ARM CCA all production-ready at ~10% overhead; NVIDIA GPU confidential computing emerging).
**Missing from:** `spec.md`. The spec mentions TEEs only in the PySyft section with the phrase "shielded source" and says TEEs are future scope. Brief 13 establishes that TEE hardware is production-ready NOW at acceptable overhead, which is relevant to DataFetch's execution environment security model.
**Suggestion:** Add a brief subsection to `spec.md` under a "Security Architecture" or "Future: Execution Environment" heading noting that AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX provide VM-level isolation at ~10% overhead and are supported by Azure and GCP in production, making TEE-based execution viable when DataFetch needs it.

### GAP-7: Synthetic Data Market Growth Not Referenced
**Source:** Brief 13, Section 5.5 (Synthetic data market $0.51B in 2025 to $2.67B by 2030 at 39.4% CAGR; ~60% of data for AI/analytics is synthetically generated per Gartner; EU AI Act requires testing synthetic alternatives before processing personal data).
**Missing from:** All core docs. DataFetch's mock data layer is essentially a synthetic data product. The EU AI Act requirement and market growth validate the mock-then-commit pattern as not just a nice feature but a regulatory and market trend.
**Suggestion:** Add to `market_thesis.md` under "Why Now" or to `product_design.md` under "Mock-Then-Commit": "The synthetic data market is projected to reach $2.67B by 2030 (39.4% CAGR), and the EU AI Act requires testing synthetic alternatives before processing personal data, validating mock-first exploration as a regulatory and market trend, not just a UX choice."

### GAP-8: Ocean Protocol Scale Not Referenced
**Source:** Brief 13, Section 3.2 (1.7M+ nodes across 70+ countries, proving compute-to-data at scale).
**Missing from:** All core docs. Ocean Protocol validates that the compute-to-data model works at massive scale, even if its crypto-native settlement creates friction. This is useful supporting evidence for the core thesis.
**Suggestion:** Brief mention in `market_thesis.md` competitive landscape or assumptions: "Ocean Protocol has proven compute-to-data at scale (1.7M nodes, 70+ countries) but remains crypto-native. DataFetch applies the same principle with fiat-native micropayment settlement."

### GAP-9: Cape Privacy's Failure as a Cautionary Tale
**Source:** Brief 13, Section 3.4 (Cape Privacy raised $25M, went dormant as a compute platform, pivoted entirely to an MVNO. Lesson: "combine privacy tech with a compelling product surface, not the other way around").
**Missing from:** All core docs. This is a directly relevant cautionary tale about building privacy-preserving computation platforms without a compelling product surface. It validates DataFetch's approach of leading with the agent experience rather than the privacy tech.
**Suggestion:** Add to `market_thesis.md` Risks section or product design Premises: "Cape Privacy ($25M raised) failed as a standalone encrypted computation platform, validating our approach of leading with agent-native product surface rather than privacy technology."

### GAP-10: Automated Policy Engine vs. Manual Approval
**Source:** Brief 13, Section 6.1 recommendation 5 ("Approval model: Policy engine (not human review). Data owners define rules, agent code validated against policy before execution") and Section 3.1 on PySyft's manual approval bottleneck.
**Missing from:** `spec.md` governance section. The spec describes vitest invariants for cost caps and rate limits, but does not explicitly describe an automated policy engine for data access approval. The spec's governance model is agent-side (vitest invariants the agent runs), not provider-side (data owner defining what operations are allowed). Brief 13 recommends a policy engine approach that maps well to the `Enrichable<T>` access control mentioned in the spec but is not articulated as a distinct architectural component.
**Suggestion:** Add to `spec.md` governance section: "Provider-side policy engine: data owners define allowed operations, aggregation minimums, and privacy budgets. Agent code is validated against provider policy before execution, enabling automated approval without human-in-the-loop bottlenecks."

### CONTRADICTION-1: Phase Numbering Inconsistency
**Source:** `product_design.md` describes Phases 1, 2, 3.
**Conflict:** `spec.md` labels the intent-centric environment layer as "Phase 4" (line 305: "Intent-Centric Environment Layer (Phase 4)") and the REST API as "Phase 1" (line 5: "Phase 1: REST API Layer").
In `product_design.md`, Phase 1 is the thesis validation (hardcoded folder + benchmark), Phase 2 is DataFetch PoC + envkit extraction, Phase 3 is the second PoC. The spec's "Phase 1: REST API Layer" and "Phase 4: Intent-Centric Environment Layer" follow a completely different numbering scheme. The product design says the environment (Tier 3) is the **primary** PoC focus built first, while the spec frames REST as Phase 1 and the environment as Phase 4 (built later).
**Impact:** This creates confusion about build order. The product design explicitly says "PoC priority: Tier 3 first (proves the thesis), Tier 1 as secondary." The spec's phase numbering implies REST first, environment later.
**Suggestion:** Align the spec's phase numbering with the product design, or add a note in the spec clarifying that "Phase 1/4" refer to architectural layers not build order, and that the product design governs build sequence.

### CONTRADICTION-2: Snowflake/Databricks Competitive Assessment
**Source:** `market_thesis.md` competitive table says Snowflake/Databricks "Sell infrastructure, not data products" and "Could build intent layers over warehouses" (framed as hypothetical/unlikely).
**Conflict:** Brief 14, Section 3.2 documents that Databricks **already** hosts MCP servers from LSEG, S&P Global, Moody's, and ATTOM on its marketplace, with a Supervisor Agent for multi-agent orchestration. This is not hypothetical. Databricks is actively shipping agent-accessible data products. Snowflake has Cortex Agents operating within clean room boundaries (Brief 14, Section 3.1).
**Impact:** The market thesis understates the competitive threat from Databricks specifically.
**Suggestion:** Update the Snowflake/Databricks row to: "Already shipping MCP-served data products (Databricks) and Cortex Agents (Snowflake), but without mock data, micropayment, or code-mode interfaces. Enterprise pricing ($50/collaborator/day) and platform lock-in remain barriers to agent adoption."

## STALE INFO

### STALE-1: Clean Room Market Not Addressed Despite Being Directly Relevant
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 2.1 documents rapid consolidation (Samooha->Snowflake Dec 2023, Habu->LiveRamp Jan 2024, InfoSum->WPP 2024). Brief 13, Section 2.5 gives Habu acquisition details ($200M).
**In core docs:** `market_thesis.md` and `appendix.md` do not mention clean rooms at all, despite the briefs establishing that clean room evolution toward agent integration is the most significant competitive dynamic. The "Competitive Landscape" section in the market thesis appears to have been written before the clean room research was conducted.
**Suggestion:** Add a "Clean Room Landscape" subsection to the competitive landscape acknowledging the market consolidation and clean rooms' movement toward agent integration, while differentiating DataFetch's approach.

### STALE-2: Appendix Expansion Path Does Not Reflect Environment-First Strategy
**Source:** `appendix.md` Section G shows a product expansion path: "Phase 1 (Months 1-2): Company Intelligence API" -> "Phase 2 (Months 2-4): + Property Intelligence" etc.
**Conflict with:** `product_design.md` which establishes the environment (Tier 3) as the primary access path built first, with REST as secondary. The appendix expansion path describes a REST-API-first rollout with no mention of the environment layer, envkit, or the benchmark-first approach.
**Suggestion:** Update appendix expansion path to reflect the product design: Phase 1 = Thesis Validation (benchmark), Phase 2 = DataFetch PoC on envkit, Phase 3 = Second PoC, with REST endpoints as a secondary access path within Phase 2.

### OPPORTUNITY-1: "Plaid for Agent Data" Positioning
**Source:** Brief 14, Section 9.3 ("Plaid provides a unified API for accessing bank data across thousands of financial institutions. DataFetch could become the unified environment for accessing enriched data across multiple providers. Plaid's sandbox established the mock-then-commit pattern in fintech"). **Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (lines 34-38) describes credit-based systems as "most common for data products," noting psychological benefits ("spending 5 credits vs $0.50"), pre-purchase driving upfront revenue, and expiry driving recurring purchases.

**Impact:** The research identifies credit-based systems as the industry standard for data products. The core docs should at minimum acknowledge this model and explain *why* it was rejected in favor of pure MPP per-query pricing. This is a deliberate design choice that should be documented as a tradeoff, not simply omitted.
**Suggested addition to `product_design.md`, Pricing Philosophy section:**
> "Credit-based pricing (common in data products for psychological framing and upfront revenue) was evaluated and rejected. MPP per-query pricing better serves agent autonomy (no pre-purchase needed) and aligns with the zero-onboarding thesis, though it sacrifices upfront cash collection and recurring purchase mechanics."

### GAP 2: Entity Resolution as Highest-Value Enrichment
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (line 46) explicitly states entity resolution (linking "J Smith" across companies) is "hardest and most valuable enrichment."
**Core docs:** `spec.md` (lines 145-158) covers entity resolution technically but treats it as just another pipeline step. No core document identifies it as the *primary value driver* or the *hardest technical challenge*. The competitive moat discussion in `market_thesis.md` (lines 57-63) mentions cross-referencing but doesn't elevate entity resolution specifically.
**Impact:** The research positions entity resolution as the key defensible capability. The core docs should reflect this strategic importance.
**Suggested addition to `market_thesis.md`, Competitive Landscape section:**
> "Entity resolution (linking individuals across companies, addresses, and filings) is the hardest and most valuable enrichment in business data. It is the primary technical moat: easy to start, extremely hard to do well at scale."

### GAP 3: Geocoding/Spatial Enrichment Missing
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (line 50) lists "Geocoding/spatial: Address normalization, proximity analysis, area profiling" as a high-value enrichment pattern.
**Core docs:** `spec.md` mentions address normalization (line 158) but only as an entity resolution challenge. No geocoding pipeline is described. `product_design.md` lists `area/:postcode/profile` as an endpoint (line 282) but the spec has no geocoding infrastructure to support it. The enrichment pipeline in `spec.md` (lines 143-186) lists entity resolution, scoring, and filing behavior, but not geocoding.
**Suggested addition to `spec.md`, Enrichment Pipeline section:** Add a "Geocoding & Spatial" subsection describing how addresses are normalized and geolocated to support the area profile endpoint.

### GAP 4: NLP Extraction from Unstructured Filings
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (line 49) identifies "NLP extraction: Structured data from unstructured filings (PDFs, iXBRL). Transforms free PDFs into valuable structured data."
**Core docs:** `spec.md` (lines 100-105) mentions iXBRL parsing but frames it narrowly as tag extraction, not as a broader NLP capability. No mention of extracting structured data from PDF filings (annual reports, charge documents, prospectuses). The research identifies this as a distinct high-value enrichment pattern.
**Impact:** This is a missed enrichment category. Many Companies House filings are PDF-only. NLP extraction could expand the coverage beyond the ~40% that file digitally (spec.md line 104).

### GAP 5: MCP Registry Ecosystem Entirely Absent from Core Docs
**Research brief:** `04-data-peers.md` documents an explosive MCP ecosystem (~19,000 servers, 7+ registries, official Linux Foundation governance, progressive discovery). This is the infrastructure layer through which AI agents discover and consume tools/data in 2026.
**Core docs:** None of the four core documents mention MCP registries. `product_design.md` discusses discoverability only via `llms.txt` and `mpp.dev` directory (lines 325-347). The spec mentions no MCP server implementation.
**Impact:** This is a significant distribution gap. If ~19,000 MCP servers exist and agents discover tools through MCP registries, DataFetch should be listed as an MCP server, not just via llms.txt. The research explicitly states (line 11): "API data services are rapidly evolving from traditional developer tools into AI-native infrastructure, with MCP servers and structured schemas becoming key differentiators."
**Suggested addition to `product_design.md`, Agent Discoverability section:**
> "### MCP Registry
> DataFetch will be published as an MCP server on the official MCP registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) and listed on community directories (MCP.so, Glama). MCP is the de facto standard for agent-tool discovery in 2026, with ~19,000 servers. An MCP server wrapping Tier 1 endpoints provides protocol-level discoverability alongside llms.txt and mpp.dev."

**Core docs:** `product_design.md` uses `AGENTS.md` (line 349) for agent-readable context, but never references the SKILL.md standard. DataFetch could publish a SKILL.md that teaches agents how to work with the environment.
**Impact:** The target users (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) all support the SKILL.md format. Publishing a DataFetch skill on skills.sh would provide an additional high-visibility distribution channel.
**Suggested addition to `product_design.md`, Agent Discoverability section:**

**Research brief:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 374-376) identifies a critical constraint: "Agents can realistically connect to only 2-3 MCP servers before accuracy drops, pushing the ecosystem toward progressive disclosure patterns." **Core docs:** The environment model in `product_design.md` implicitly addresses this (agents load only the interfaces they need), but the token economics advantage is not explicitly framed as a competitive advantage against MCP-based competitors. The Cloudflare/Anthropic 98-99% token reduction data (product_design.md lines 50-52) is mentioned but not connected to the MCP context window problem.
**Suggested addition to `market_thesis.md`:** Frame the environment model as a direct solution to the MCP context bloat problem identified in the research.

### GAP 8: Network Effects from Monitoring
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (line 55) notes: "Network effects possible via monitoring (more customers = better signal on what data to prioritize refreshing)."
**Core docs:** The trajectory library (market_thesis.md lines 57-63) captures *query pattern* network effects, but not *data freshness prioritization* network effects. These are complementary: more users querying certain companies signals which companies to refresh more frequently.
**Suggested addition:** Add data freshness prioritization as a network effect alongside trajectory convergence.

**Core docs:** No mention of integrating with these platforms.
**Impact:** These are potential distribution channels, especially for Tier 1 REST endpoints. An OpenTools listing would let agents consume DataFetch via a single unified API call.

## CONTRADICTIONS

### CONTRADICTION 1: Pricing Band Misalignment
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (lines 58-63) defines UK company data unit economics:
- Below GBP 0.05: "hard to sustain unless billions of queries"
- GBP 0.10-0.30: "basic enrichment over free Companies House data"

**Core docs:** `product_design.md` (line 278) prices `GET /search/company` at GBP 0.02, and `GET /company/:number` at GBP 0.05 (line 274). `appendix.md` (line 74) explicitly positions basic lookups "below Endole" at GBP 0.05.

**Conflict:** The research says below GBP 0.05 is "hard to sustain unless billions of queries." The core docs price the search endpoint at GBP 0.02 and basic lookups at GBP 0.05 (which is the sustainability floor).

**Resolution needed:** Either justify the below-floor pricing (e.g., search at GBP 0.02 is explicitly a loss leader, which product_design.md line 357 does note), or revise prices upward to match the research's sustainability analysis. At minimum, `market_thesis.md` should acknowledge the unit economics tension.

### CONTRADICTION 2: Endole Pricing Characterization
**Research brief:** `03-business-models.md` (line 12) states Endole pricing is "GBP 0.25-0.80/report, pay-as-you-go."
**Core docs:** `market_thesis.md` (line 69) describes Endole as "Credit-based, GBP 0.25-0.80/report."
**Conflict:** Minor but notable. The research says "pay-as-you-go" while the market thesis says "credit-based." These are different models (pay-as-you-go implies direct per-transaction billing; credit-based implies pre-purchased credits). The research brief on business models (lines 34-38) describes credit-based as a distinct model. Both may be partially correct (Endole uses credits that function as pay-as-you-go), but the characterization should be consistent.

### CONTRADICTION 3: OpenAI Deprecating Assistants API
**Research brief:** `04-data-peers.md` (line 367) states: "OpenAI deprecated Assistants API in favor of MCP (sunset mid-2026)."
**Core docs:** No core document reflects this. `product_design.md` (line 64) lists "Codex" as a target agent but doesn't acknowledge the MCP pivot. If OpenAI is deprecating their proprietary tool-use framework in favor of MCP, this strengthens the case for DataFetch having an MCP server, contradicting the current MCP-absent approach.

### STALE 1: "Protocol is weeks old" Framing
**Core doc:** `market_thesis.md` (line 75): "No one offers enriched UK public data with MPP-native per-query payment. The protocol is weeks old."
**Research context:** The market thesis was written around March 2026. This "weeks old" framing will become stale quickly. More importantly, the research (04-data-peers.md) shows the agent infrastructure ecosystem moves extremely fast (MCP went from ~100 to ~19,000 servers in ~16 months). The first-mover window may be shorter than assumed.
**Suggestion:** Replace temporal language with version-anchored language: "MPP launched March 2026. The mpp.dev/services directory currently lists fewer than a dozen services."

### STALE 2: MCP Server Count / Ecosystem Maturity
**Research brief:** `04-data-peers.md` documents a mature MCP ecosystem as of March 2026 (19,000 servers, Linux Foundation governance, official registry API, progressive discovery).
**Core docs:** None of the core documents reference MCP at all, which makes them read as if the agent-tool ecosystem is nascent. The ecosystem is actually quite mature and DataFetch risks being invisible if it doesn't participate.

---

### OPPORTUNITY 1: DataFetch as an MCP Server + Environment Hybrid
**Research insight:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 355-361) identifies a three-layer architecture: Protocol (MCP), Knowledge (Skills), Data (API services). DataFetch currently only exists at the Data layer (REST + environment). By also existing at the Protocol layer (MCP server) and Knowledge layer (SKILL.md), DataFetch would be present at all three layers, maximizing discoverability.
**Suggestion:** Tier 1 REST endpoints should be exposed as an MCP server (simple wrapper). The environment interaction model should be published as a SKILL.md. This gives DataFetch presence in MCP registries, skills.sh, llms.txt, and mpp.dev simultaneously.

**Research insight:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 275-283) describes Apify as the leading web data extraction platform with 10,000+ Actors, MCP integration, and dynamic tool discovery.
**Core docs:** `spec.md` (line 13) mentions "Scrapers (planning portals) -> scheduled crawls" but doesn't specify tooling.
**Suggestion:** Apify could handle the scraping components of the data pipeline (planning portals, non-API sources), reducing custom scraper maintenance.

### OPPORTUNITY 3: Historical Tracking as Subscription Revenue
**Research insight:** `03-business-models.md` (line 48): "Historical tracking: Change detection, trend analysis. Best as monitoring subscriptions."
**Core docs:** `product_design.md` (line 318) explicitly rejects subscriptions: "Pay-per-query only." But monitoring/alerts (e.g., "notify me when this company files new accounts" or "alert if risk score drops below 40") is the one subscription model that could work alongside MPP. The agent pays per-query for the monitoring setup, then pays per-notification. This creates recurring revenue without traditional subscriptions.
**Suggestion:** Consider a monitoring tier where agents register webhooks (paid via MPP per-registration and per-notification). This captures the recurring revenue opportunity the research identifies without violating the no-subscription principle.

### OPPORTUNITY 4: The "Price on Decision Value" Principle
**Research insight:** `03-business-models.md` (line 41): "Price on decision value, not production cost. A GBP 0.50 risk score preventing a GBP 50K bad debt is trivially justified. Same data sold as 'public records lookup' only commands GBP 0.05."
**Core docs:** `product_design.md` (line 360) states this principle ("Price on the value of the decision the data supports") but doesn't apply it consistently. The agent persona for Compliance (persona 4, line 382) notes "highest per-query spend ($1-2), regulated demand, mandatory use case" but the risk-report endpoint is only GBP 1.00 (product_design.md line 275). For AML/KYB compliance where the decision value is avoiding regulatory fines (tens of thousands of pounds), GBP 1.00 may be significantly underpriced.
**Suggestion:** Consider a compliance-specific pricing tier at GBP 2.00-5.00 for AML/KYB reports, justified by decision value. The research's pricing band (lines 30-31) shows compliance/regulatory use cases commanding $0.50-2.00, and "deep investigative" commands $2.00-10.00.

### OPPORTUNITY 5: Sub-Registry / Downstream Catalog Opportunity
**Research insight:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 40-41) notes the official MCP registry "supports sub-registries, allowing organizations to create opinionated downstream catalogs."
**Core docs:** If envrun.ai is a platform for environments, it could operate a sub-registry of MCP servers specifically for data environments. This would give the platform a discovery/distribution advantage.

**Research insight:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 374-376): "Every MCP server loads tool definitions at session startup... Agents can realistically connect to only 2-3 MCP servers before accuracy drops."
**Core docs:** The environment model inherently solves this (agent loads a local folder, not remote tool definitions), but this advantage is never explicitly marketed.
**Suggestion:** Add to `market_thesis.md`: "The environment model sidesteps the MCP context window tax. While agents connecting to 2-3 MCP servers consume 20,000+ tokens in tool definitions before their first query, the environment folder loads only the interfaces relevant to the agent's task."

### OPPORTUNITY 7: Convergence of Skills and MCP
**Research insight:** `04-data-peers.md` (lines 239-246) describes the "Skills Over MCP Interest Group" exploring skill distribution through MCP primitives. If skills merge into MCP, DataFetch's environment model (which is essentially a rich skill) could be distributed through MCP directly.

# Knowledge Audit: Full Synthesis

## Cross-Agent Analysis

7 agents reviewed 14 research briefs against 4 core documents. Here are the consolidated findings, deduplicated and prioritized.

### Summary Statistics

| Category | Total Findings (raw) | After Dedup |
|----------|---------------------|-------------|
| Gaps | 62 | ~40 unique |
| Contradictions | 15 | ~8 unique |
| Stale Info | 12 | ~5 unique |
| Missed Opportunities | 46 | ~25 unique |

---

## CRITICAL ISSUES (appear across 3+ agent reports)

### 1. Phase Numbering Mismatch (spec.md vs product_design.md)
**Agents: 2, 5, 7** | Affects: `spec.md`, `product_design.md`, `appendix.md`

`spec.md` labels REST as "Phase 1" and environment as "Phase 4". `product_design.md` labels benchmark as Phase 1, PoC as Phase 2, second PoC as Phase 3. `appendix.md` Section G shows yet another REST-first expansion path. These are three conflicting roadmaps. Product design says "Tier 3 first", spec implies REST first.

**Fix:** Align all docs to product_design.md phasing (the APPROVED doc). Relabel spec sections as architectural layers, not build phases.

---

### 2. MCP Registry/Ecosystem Completely Absent
**Agents: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6** | Affects: `product_design.md`, `market_thesis.md`

~19,000 MCP servers exist. 90+ enrichment services already available as MCP servers. Agents discover tools through MCP registries (mcp.so, Glama, Smithery, Composio). DataFetch has zero MCP presence. The only discoverability channels mentioned are llms.txt and mpp.dev. The target agents (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) all use MCP. Perplexity dropped MCP due to 72% context window waste, which actually validates DataFetch's folder-interface approach.

**Fix:** Add MCP registry listing to `product_design.md` Agent Discoverability as a Tier 1 REST distribution channel. Frame the environment model as the MCP-alternative for complex queries.

---

### 3. Competing Payment Protocols Not Acknowledged
**Agents: 2, 3, 6** | Affects: `market_thesis.md`, `appendix.md`

ACP (OpenAI+Stripe), AP2 (Google, with "Mandates"), UCP (Google+Shopify, Walmart, Target), x402 (AWS/Coinbase), L402 (Bitcoin Lightning) all exist. Stripe is simultaneously involved in MPP AND building its own L1 blockchain ($500M raise). Core docs treat MPP as the only protocol.

**Fix:** Add a "Protocol Landscape" subsection to `market_thesis.md` Risks naming all competing protocols. Add "Adjacent Protocols" to `appendix.md` Section A. Acknowledge Stripe's dual-betting.

---

### 4. "Protocol is weeks old" and Time-Sensitive Language
**Agents: 1, 2, 3, 6** | Affects: `market_thesis.md`

"The protocol is weeks old" (line 75) and "mpp.dev/services directory is nearly empty" (line 28) will rot immediately.

**Fix:** Replace with date-anchored language: "MPP launched March 18, 2026. The mpp.dev/services directory has fewer than 10 services listed as of March 2026."

---

### 5. "Pay-per-query ONLY" Contradicts API Key Fallback
**Agents: 1, 6** | Affects: `product_design.md`, `market_thesis.md`

Design Principle 4 says "No subscriptions, no API keys, no accounts. MPP is the only authentication." But `market_thesis.md` line 104 says "Mitigation: also offer traditional API key access." And 90%+ of current agent data consumption uses pre-provisioned API keys.

**Fix:** Reconcile. Change Principle 4 to: "MPP-native payment with traditional API key access as a compatibility layer during adoption ramp."

---

### 6. Code Execution Security Model Absent
**Agents: 5, 6** | Affects: `spec.md`

Agents submit TypeScript that executes server-side via the solver. No security model exists for this. PySyft's `exec()`-based sandbox is known-weak. Prompt injection could cause misleading purchases. No discussion of sandboxing, AST validation, or injection prevention.

**Fix:** Add a "Code Execution Security" section to `spec.md` covering TypeScript AST validation, V8 isolate sandboxing (Cloudflare Workers provides this), and injection attack vectors.

---

### 7. Arrow's Information Paradox Not Named

## Completeness Principle — Boil the Lake

AI-assisted coding makes the marginal cost of completeness near-zero. When you present options:

- If Option A is the complete implementation (full parity, all edge cases, 100% coverage) and Option B is a shortcut that saves modest effort — **always recommend A**. The delta between 80 lines and 150 lines is meaningless with CC+gstack. "Good enough" is the wrong instinct when "complete" costs minutes more.
- **Lake vs. ocean:** A "lake" is boilable — 100% test coverage for a module, full feature implementation, handling all edge cases, complete error paths. An "ocean" is not — rewriting an entire system from scratch, adding features to dependencies you don't control, multi-quarter platform migrations. Recommend boiling lakes. Flag oceans as out of scope.
- **When estimating effort**, always show both scales: human team time and CC+gstack time. The compression ratio varies by task type — use this reference:

| Task type | Human team | CC+gstack | Compression |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Boilerplate / scaffolding | 2 days | 15 min | ~100x |
| Test writing | 1 day | 15 min | ~50x |
| Feature implementation | 1 week | 30 min | ~30x |
| Bug fix + regression test | 4 hours | 15 min | ~20x |
| Architecture / design | 2 days | 4 hours | ~5x |
| Research / exploration | 1 day | 3 hours | ~3x |

- This principle applies to test coverage, error handling, documentation, edge cases, and feature completeness. Don't skip the last 10% to "save time" — with AI, that 10% costs seconds.

**Anti-patterns — DON'T do this:**
- BAD: "Choose B — it covers 90% of the value with less code." (If A is only 70 lines more, choose A.)
- BAD: "We can skip edge case handling to save time." (Edge case handling costs minutes with CC.)
- BAD: "Let's defer test coverage to a follow-up PR." (Tests are the cheapest lake to boil.)
- BAD: Quoting only human-team effort: "This would take 2 weeks." (Say: "2 weeks human / ~1 hour CC.")

## Model & Reasoning

**Model:** No model is hardcoded — codex uses whatever its current default is (the frontier
agentic coding model). This means as OpenAI ships newer models, /codex automatically
uses them. If the user wants a specific model, pass `-m` through to codex.

**Reasoning effort:** All modes use `xhigh` — maximum reasoning power. When reviewing code, breaking code, or consulting on architecture, you want the model thinking as hard as possible.

**Web search:** All codex commands use `--enable web_search_cached` so Codex can look up
docs and APIs during review. This is OpenAI's cached index — fast, no extra cost.

If the user specifies a model (e.g., `/codex review -m gpt-5.1-codex-max`
or `/codex challenge -m gpt-5.2`), pass the `-m` flag through to codex.

- **Binary not found:** Detected in Step 0. Stop with install instructions.
- **Auth error:** Codex prints an auth error to stderr. Surface the error:
  "Codex authentication failed. Run `codex login` in your terminal to authenticate via ChatGPT."
- **Timeout:** If the Bash call times out (5 min), tell the user:
  "Codex timed out after 5 minutes. The diff may be too large or the API may be slow. Try again or use a smaller scope."
- **Empty response:** If `$TMPRESP` is empty or doesn't exist, tell the user:
  "Codex returned no response. Check stderr for errors."
- **Session resume failure:** If resume fails, delete the session file and start fresh.

## Assessment

The audit found some real holes, but it also over-collected research trivia. The core docs have about six credibility problems, a second tier of worthwhile cleanups, and a long tail of noise.

### MUST-FIX

1. **Roadmap incoherence.** The approved design says benchmark first, then PoC, then second PoC, and explicitly says DataFetch is not a standalone product. The spec and appendix read like a REST-first product roadmap using the same phase labels for different things. That is the biggest embarrassment risk.

2. **The benchmark is not credible as written.** The flagship task depends on investor/YC/headcount-style data, but the listed data sources do not include an investor source, and the environment side gets higher-level curated abstractions that the REST side does not. That would prove curation advantage, not repo-shape advantage. **This was the biggest blind spot the agents missed.**

3. **Execution and payment security model is underspecified.** The spec says "receive TypeScript, validate, execute" but gives no real sandbox, no network/file/process isolation story, no prompt-injection/payment-injection model, and only partial handling of payment failure.

4. **Business model coherence.** "MPP only, no API keys" directly conflicts with the market thesis fallback to traditional API keys, and pricing is split across GBP, USD, and USDC with no explicit customer-facing/settlement policy.

5. **Distribution and payment-protocol reality.** Not "become just another MCP server," but the docs need an explicit MCP/skills compatibility stance for target agents, and an explicit "MPP first, x402-compatible, ACP/AP2/UCP watched" stance instead of acting like MPP is the whole board.

6. **Competitive/date language is stale.** "Protocol is weeks old" and "directory nearly empty" will rot immediately, and Snowflake/Databricks treatment understates actual threat.

### NICE-TO-HAVE

- Mention clean rooms and Databricks as adjacent infrastructure/partnership surface
- PySyft: add one sentence that manual approval and latency make it future-only and non-core
- Revisit GBP 0.02 search price and explain as capped loss-leader
- Simple interface versioning policy
- Elevate entity resolution as a core moat (in spec but not prominent in thesis)
- Tighten property endpoint claims so every field maps to a legal source

### REJECTED

- **Arrow's information paradox naming.** Docs already explain the problem. Label is academic perfume.
- **Cryptographic provenance as core requirement.** Over-engineering for this stage.
- **EU Data Governance Act** for current UK public-data PoC.
- **Survey-stat padding** (enterprise adoption %, CH macroeconomic value, Gartner scare quotes, A2A acronym collecting)
- **Most of the slogan hunt.** "Governance-as-code", "Enrichable<T> as intent capture", and "token efficiency vs MCP" are useful. "Data economy substrate", "provenance receipt = invoice", and similar are hype.

### BLIND SPOTS THE AGENTS MISSED

- **The benchmark task is infeasible with currently declared data inventory.** (No investor data source exists to support "backed by Y Combinator" queries)
- **The benchmark is methodologically confounded.** It will not prove the thesis cleanly, as the environment gets curated abstractions the REST baseline doesn't.
- **The docs never choose one identity for DataFetch:** standalone business or envrun.ai proof artifact. That ambiguity causes half the roadmap confusion.

1. Pick a single source of truth for what DataFetch is, rewrite all phase language
2. Fix the benchmark task, data dependencies, and evaluation design
3. Add a real execution/payment security model
4. Resolve auth/pricing/currency contradictions
5. Add MCP/distribution and protocol positioning, refresh competition/date claims

### mpp.dev Directory
Listed on mpp.dev/services for protocol-level discoverability.

### MCP Registry (Tier 1 Distribution)
DataFetch Tier 1 REST endpoints are published as an MCP server on the official MCP registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) and community directories (mcp.so, Glama). With ~19,000 MCP servers in the ecosystem as of early 2026, this is the primary discovery mechanism for agents using tool-calling. The MCP server wraps REST endpoints for compatibility; the environment (Tier 3) is the recommended path for code agents capable of navigating typed folders.

Note: MCP tool-calling carries significant context window overhead (~20,000+ tokens in tool definitions before the first query). The environment model sidesteps this entirely, the agent loads only the interfaces relevant to its task. This is a structural advantage, not just a UX preference.

### Agent Skill (SKILL.md)
DataFetch publishes a SKILL.md following the agentskills.io specification, installable via `npx skills add datafetch/uk-business`. The skill teaches code agents how to navigate the environment folder, compose intents, and use explore/purchase. This targets the 19+ agents that support the standard (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, etc.).

### AGENTS.md (Environment)

### mpp.dev Directory
Listed on mpp.dev/services for protocol-level discoverability.

### MCP Registry (Tier 1 Distribution)
DataFetch Tier 1 REST endpoints are published as an MCP server on the official MCP registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) and community directories (mcp.so, Glama). With ~19,000 MCP servers in the ecosystem as of early 2026, this is the primary discovery mechanism for agents using tool-calling. The MCP server wraps REST endpoints for compatibility; the environment (Tier 3) is the recommended path for code agents capable of navigating typed folders.

Note: MCP tool-calling carries significant context window overhead (~20,000+ tokens in tool definitions before the first query). The environment model sidesteps this entirely, the agent loads only the interfaces relevant to its task. This is a structural advantage, not just a UX preference.

### Agent Skill (SKILL.md)
DataFetch publishes a SKILL.md following the agentskills.io specification, installable via `npx skills add datafetch/uk-business`. The skill teaches code agents how to navigate the environment folder, compose intents, and use explore/purchase. This targets the 19+ agents that support the standard (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, etc.).

Agent-readable context file in the environment root. Describes what the environment is, what interfaces are available, how to explore, how to purchase, and governance rules. AGENTS.md is the canonical agent context file (emerging open standard, supported by Sourcegraph, OpenAI, Google), with CLAUDE.md as a symlink for Claude Code compatibility.
